Also note that the stuff in square brackets is not explicitly stated in Japanese, the meaning in this case however is that of the English sentence. suru: to do Remark: Most resources teach this as "to do", but in fact it is more general. Don't worry about this for now, it's covered in more detail later.

hiragana: やくそく する
meaning: [I] promise. The verb "suru" is slightly special. Together with a noun, you can omit the "wo"-particle, the entire compound then acts as a verb. When you look up such a noun on jisho, you'll notice the word type to be "noun, suru verb". suru: to do Remark: Most resources teach this as "to do", but in fact it is more general. Don't worry about this for now, it's covered in more detail later.

hiragana: でんわ は しない
meaning: As for phoning/calling, [I] don't do [it]. shinai: negative of suru The negative form of suru is one out of few verb conjugation exceptions (Tae Kim p. 46).

hiragana: つよく なった な
meaning: [You] became strong. natta: past of naru

hiragana: いかない
meaning: [I] don't go. ikanai: negative of iku

hiragana: きょう は こない よ
meaning: As for today [the panda] doesn't come. They're talking about the panda who doesn't attend his job at the zoo today. konai: negative of kuru. The negative form of kuru is one out of few verb conjugation exceptions (Tae Kim p. 46).

hiragana: ぼく が かった
meaning: I won. Note that the plain past tense of "katsu - to win" and "kau - to buy" is the same.

hiragana: こなかった
meaning: [Someone] didn't come. konakatta: past negative of kuru

kanji: 私ずっと分からなかった
hiragana: わたし ずっと わからなかった
meaning: I never realized [this]. wakaranakatta: past negative of wakaru

hiragana: いただきます
meaning: "itadakimasu" is actually a phrase Japanese people say before starting a meal. The dictionary form is "itadaku", but I think the teineigo-form is used more often. itadaku: to receive itadakimasu: polite / teineigo conjugation of itadaku A plain verb is made more polite by somehow appending "-masu".

hiragana: はなします
meaning: hanashimasu: polite/teineigo of hanasu (to speak, talk) A plain verb is made more polite by somehow appending "-masu".
source: Mahoutsukai no Yome (The Ancient Magus Bride) ep 1-12

hiragana: わかります
meaning: wakarimasu: polite/teineigo of wakaru (to understand) In this example, the "u" of "masu" is pronounced very clearly. It is usually omitted, see next card. Fast Japanese speakers even tend to skip more vowels.

hiragana: わかります
meaning: wakarimasu: polite/teineigo of wakaru (to understand)

hiragana: さあ いそぎます よ
meaning: isogimasu: polite/teineigo of isogu (to hurry) sa: well now; all right (it's sort of a filler, safe to ignore here I'd say)

hiragana: たのみます よ
meaning: tanomimasu: polite/teineigo of tanomu (to request; to beg; to ask)

hiragana: さけ
meaning: sake: alcoholic beverage Remark: In western languages, "sake" refers to Japanese rice wine. In Japanese, sake is a broader category that refers to any type of alcoholic beverage, no matter where it comes from. The Japanese rice wine is called nihonshu/日本酒 in Japanese.

hiragana: おさけ のみます
meaning: [We] drink sake [there]. nomimasu: polite/teineigo of nomu (to drink) osake: polite/teineigo for sake (alcoholic beverage) Some nouns also have a teineigo form. In this case they start with an additional "o/お" or "go/ご". Note that "o" or "go" can't be added to all nouns, you'll need to learn this from the respective context. I'll add some more examples soon.
source: Terrace House- Boys & Girls in the City

hiragana: よぶ
meaning: yobu: to call out (to); to call; to invoke Obviously, the speaker wants to yobu someone with his phone. Do you remember the Japanese word for phone?
source: The Daily Lives of High School Boys (EP 1-12)

hiragana: わたし も たべます
meaning: I also [will] eat [this]! The speaker says this in anticipation of some super delicious food someone else has already tasted. tabemasu: polite/teineigo of taberu (to eat) Remark: You could also translate this as "I also want to eat this" in English, which was the translation of this card up to deck version 14. Since there's a dedicated form for saying "want to" in Japanese (covered later), I changed the translation.

hiragana: ぺんぎん を みます
meaning: [I] see a penguin. pengin: penguin mimasu: polite/teineigo of miru (to see)

hiragana: ぜったい かちます
meaning: [I will] totally win (the speaker is talking to his teacher and wants to convince him). An interesting point here is that Japanese does not have a future tense. The present tense is used for both present and future, future is either expressed by context as in this example (the date of the contest is known to both). Or if it is unknown, it is stated by using time words as "tomorrow" or "next week". That's actually a lot simpler than in English. For this reason, some people also avoid the term "present tense" and say that there's past and non-past only. kachimasu: polite/teineigo of katsu (to win) zettai: definitely; absolutely; unconditionally

hiragana: はいはい まちます よ
meaning: Ok, ok, [I'll] wait! machimasu: polite/teineigo of matsu (to wait)

hiragana: かいます
meaning: kaimasu: polite/teineigo of kau (to buy)
source: Ouran High School Host Club (jp eng)

hiragana: おれ も たたかいます
meaning: [I will] also fight. tatakaimasu: polite/teineigo of tatakau (to fight, to wage war)

kanji: すみません少し急ぎます
hiragana: すみません すこし いそぎます
meaning: Sorry, [I need to] hurry a bit. sukoshi: small quantity; a little; few

hiragana: けいさつ よびます よ
meaning: [Hey, don't do that! I'll] call the police! yobimasu: polite/teineigo of yobu (to call out (to); to call; to invoke) keisatsu: police

hiragana: さいご まで たたかいます
meaning: [I] fight till the end. saigo: end; conclusion

hiragana: やくそく します
meaning: [I] promise [this to you]. shimasu: polite/teineigo of suru (to do) "suru" is one out of two conjugation exceptions for teneigo / -masu.

hiragana: また きます
meaning: [I] come again. mata: again; once more kimasu: polite/teineigo of kuru (to come) "kuru" is the other one out of two conjugation exceptions for teneigo / -masu.

hiragana: ぼく も いきます
meaning: ikimasu: polite/teineigo of iku (to go)

hiragana: おります
meaning: orimasu: polite/teineigo of oriru (to descend (e.g. a mountain); to go down; to get off (bus / train)
source: JoJos Bizarre Adventure 黄金の風 (26-39)

hiragana: だいじ な はなし が あります
meaning: Important conversation is there -> [I] need to talk about [something] important. arimasu: polite/teineigo of aru (to be there, to exist for inanimate things)
source: Terrace House-Boys x Girls Next Door

hiragana: しあわせ に なります
meaning: [Something] will become happiness / good fortune. Probably something these people are about to do makes them happy. narimasu: polite/teineigo of naru (to become, to get)

hiragana: ねむく なります
meaning: nemui: sleepy Refresher: Replacing "i" by "ku" in an i-adjective makes it an adverb (i.e. it can be used to describe a verb, just as in this example).
source: さよなら絶望先生 (Sayonara, Zetsubou-Sensei)

kanji: 好きな人がいますよね
hiragana: すき な ひと が います よ ね
romaji: suki na hito ga imasu yo ne
meaning: There's a person you like, right? imasu: polite/teineigo of iru (to be there, to exist for animate things)
source: Boku no Hero Academia S3 (ep 1-25 jp_en)

hiragana: ええ あそびます わ よ
meaning: asobimasu: polite/teineigo of asobu (to play) wa yo: female emphatic sentence-ending particle​

kanji: 僕は書きますよ内申書に
hiragana: ぼく は かきます よ ないしんしょ に
romaji: boku ha kakimasu yo naishinsho ni
meaning: kakimasu: polite/teineigo of kaku (to write) naishinsho means "school record (on a student); transcript (of grades)". It's not a frequent word, so just ignore it - I couldn't find a better example for "kakimasu".

kanji: おもしろいことになるよたぶんね
hiragana: おもしろい こと に なる よ たぶん ね
romaji: omoshiroi koto ni naru yo tabun ne
meaning: [Something] becomes an interesthing thing / matter. perhaps... tabun: perhaps; probably
source: Ouran High School Host Club (jp eng)

kanji: すみませんすぐ行きます
hiragana: すみません すぐ いきます
meaning: Sorry, [I] go immediately! sugu: immediately; at once; right away sugu can also mean soon, which is a little less urgent.

kanji: 多分すぐ死にますよ俺は
hiragana: たぶん すぐ しにます よ おれ は
romaji: tabun sugu shinimasu yo ore ha
meaning: Maybe I soon die. This sentence is just for the sake of completeness to conclude the teineigo-conjugation of verbs. It contains "shinu", which ends on the rare "nu". shinimasu: polite/teineigo of shinu (to die)

hiragana: のみもの を のみます か
meaning: nomimono: beverage (notice the similarity to nomu - to drink) ka (always written in Hiragana as か): Question marker particle "ka" explicitly marks a sentence as question. I'm sure you remember all those questions without "ka": In casual speech it is often omitted, the question is formed by intonation.

hiragana: いきます か
meaning: [Do you] go [there]? ka (always written in Hiragana as か): Question marker particle "ka" explicitly marks a sentence as question. I'm sure you remember all those questions without "ka": In casual speech it is often omitted, the question is formed by intonation.

hiragana: しらない の か
meaning: [You] don't know [this]?

hiragana: わたし は いきません
meaning: As for me, [I] don't go. ikimasen: negative polite/teineigo of iku (to go) The negative polite teineigo form is simply built by using "-masen" instead of "-masu".

hiragana: わかりません
meaning: wakarimasen: negative polite/teineigo of wakaru (to understand)

hiragana: おもいません
meaning: omoimasen: negative polite/teineigo of omou (to think, to believe)

hiragana: ありません
meaning: arimasen: negative polite/teineigo of aru (to be, to exist)

hiragana: いみ が わかりません
meaning: As for the meaning [of something that just happened], [I] don't understand.

hiragana: やくそく は できません
meaning: As for promise, [I] can't do. yakusoku: promise dekimasen: negative polite/teineigo of dekiru (to be able to)

hiragana: せんせい いません か
meaning: Teacher, aren't [you] there? imasen: negative polite/teineigo of iru (to be there, to exist for animate things)

hiragana: はい しません
meaning: This sentence could be the answer to the order "Don't do this" - yes, [I] don't do [it]. Or the question "So he doesn't do his homework?" - yes, [he] doesn't do [it]. shimasen: negative polite/teineigo of suru (to do)
source: Honzuki - Ascendance of a Bookworm S1 (JP Only)

hiragana: ありません でした
meaning: [Something inanimate] wasn't there. In order to get the negative past teineigo, simply add "deshita" to the negative form.

hiragana: しりません でした
meaning: [I] didn't know [this] / [I] wasn't aware [of this]. In order to get the negative past teineigo, simply add "deshita" to the negative form.

kanji: 喧嘩にもなりませんでしたよ
hiragana: けんか に も なりません でした よ
romaji: kenka ni mo narimasen deshita yo
meaning: [Something, maybe a conversation] didn't become a fight (the speaker was asked: "Did you fight"? before). Ignore the "mo" in this sentence for now: We learned it meant "also", but in negative sentences it's used a bit different. I'll explain this in more detail later. kenka: quarrel; brawl; fight Remark: The "ni" particle is often used together with "naru" in practice, see ref.
source: Sakurasou no Pet na Kanojo (jp eng)

kanji: 全然分かりませんでした
hiragana: ぜんぜん わかりません でした
meaning: [I] completely didn't understand -> in the sense: I understood nothing. zenzen: wholly; entirely; completely

hiragana: わかりました
meaning: "got it." wakarimashita: past polite/teineigo of wakaru (to unterstand) The past polite/teineigo form is simply built by using "-mashita" instead of "-masu".

hiragana: わすれました
meaning: [I] forgot [it]. wasuremashita: past polite/teineigo of wasureru (to forget) The past polite/teineigo form is simply built by using "-mashita" instead of "-masu".

hiragana: できました か
meaning: Could [you] do/finish [it]? Meaning: Are you done? is it done? dekimashita: past polite/teineigo of dekiru (to be able to, to finish) The past polite/teineigo form is simply built by using "-mashita" instead of "-masu".

kanji: はいありがとうございました
hiragana: はい ありがとう ございました
meaning: Remember "arigatou gozaimasu" as polite way to thank someone? If the thing you're thanking for happened a while a go in the past, you use "gozaimashita". "gozaimasu" is used to thank fo something that happened just now.

hiragana: おそく なりました
meaning: Literally, the sentence reads [something] became late. It means that either the speaker or someone else was late.

hiragana: たべました ね
meaning: [We] ate [everything on the table, didn't we].

hiragana: つよく なりました
meaning: [You / it / someone] became strong.

hiragana: かいました
meaning: [I] bought [it].
source: Ouran High School Host Club (jp eng)

hiragana: やくそく しました よ
meaning: [Someone / I] made a promise.

hiragana: おいしい です
meaning: [It's] tasty. desu: politeness marker According to Tae Kim, Everything that does not end on a verb will become polite by adding "desu" (p. 79). That may be a bit vague, but you'll face "desu" so often that it will become easily clear from context. Technically, it is the teineigo conjugation of "da", but the uses of "desu" can be very different from "da". Therefore I follow Tofugu's definition and simply describe "desu" as politeness marker. You already see one difference in this example: "desu" is attached to an i-adjective, which is not possible for "da".

hiragana: おいしかった です
meaning: [It] was tasty. desu: politeness marker According to Tae Kim, Everything that does not end on a verb will become polite by adding "desu" (p. 79). That may be a bit vague, but you'll face "desu" so often that it will become easily clear from context. Technically, it is the teineigo conjugation of "da", but the uses of "desu" can be very different from "da". Therefore I follow Tofugu's definition and simply describe "desu" as politeness marker. You already see one difference in this example: "desu" is attached to an i-adjective, which is not possible for "da".

hiragana: わるくない です ね
meaning: [That's] not bad. desu: politeness marker According to Tae Kim, Everything that does not end on a verb will become polite by adding "desu" (p. 79). That may be a bit vague, but you'll face "desu" so often that it will become easily clear from context. Technically, it is the teineigo conjugation of "da", but the uses of "desu" can be very different from "da". Therefore I follow Tofugu's definition and simply describe "desu" as politeness marker. You already see one difference in this example: "desu" is attached to an i-adjective, which is not possible for "da".
source: Ouran High School Host Club (jp eng)

hiragana: わるくない です よ
meaning: [You're] not to blame / don't worry, it's not bad. desu: politeness marker According to Tae Kim, Everything that does not end on a verb will become polite by adding "desu" (p. 79). That may be a bit vague, but you'll face "desu" so often that it will become easily clear from context. Technically, it is the teineigo conjugation of "da", but the uses of "desu" can be very different from "da". Therefore I follow Tofugu's definition and simply describe "desu" as politeness marker. You already see one difference in this example: "desu" is attached to an i-adjective, which is not possible for "da".
source: さよなら絶望先生 (Sayonara, Zetsubou-Sensei)

kanji: あれ怖くなかったですか
hiragana: あれ こわくなかった です か
meaning: Eh, wasn't [that] scary? desu: politeness marker are: huh?, eh? According to Tae Kim, Everything that does not end on a verb will become polite by adding "desu" (p. 79). That may be a bit vague, but you'll face "desu" so often that it will become easily clear from context. Technically, it is the teineigo conjugation of "da", but the uses of "desu" can be very different from "da". Therefore I follow Tofugu's definition and simply describe "desu" as politeness marker. You already see one difference in this example: "desu" is attached to an i-adjective, which is not possible for "da".

hiragana: かわいい です よ ね
meaning: It's cute, isn't it?

kanji: とても楽しかったです
hiragana: とても たのしかった です
meaning: [Something] was very enjoyable / fun. totemo: very

hiragana: きょう は いい てんき だ ね
romaji: kyou ha ii tenki da ne
meaning: As for today, weather is good, isn't it. tenki: weather

hiragana: うみ たのしかった です ね
meaning: [Going to] the sea was fun, wasn't it

hiragana: おもしろく ありません
meaning: omoshiroi (interesting) in this example becomes omoshiroku arimasen (not interesting). This is the grammatically correct way for a polite negative i-adjective. In practice, you'll encounter "omoshirokunai desu" more often though.
source: さよなら絶望先生 (Sayonara, Zetsubou-Sensei)

kanji: おおいしくありませんでしたか
hiragana: お おいしく ありません でした か
meaning: oishii (yummy) in this example becomes oishiku arimasen deshita (was not yummy). This is the grammatically correct way for a polite past negative i-adjective. In practice, you'll encounter "oishikunakatta desu" more often though.

hiragana: さむくない です か
meaning: Isn't [it] cold [over there]? samui: cold (e.g. weather)​

hiragana: しずか だ
meaning: [It] is quiet. shizuka: quiet; silent

hiragana: とても しずか です
meaning: [It] is very quiet.

hiragana: ‪ きれい でした ね ‬
meaning: [Something] was pretty / lovely.

hiragana: にんげん です よ
meaning: [He's] a human being [not an alien].

hiragana: わたし は すき です
meaning: As for me, [I] like [it].

kanji: 相手が悪かったですね
hiragana: あいて が わるかった です ね
meaning: [Your] partner was at fault, wasn't he? aite: "other party" or "the other", this can mean either opponent or partner / ally. This is a bit confusing, but usually clear from context, read more about this here.
source: BOFURI - Itai no wa Iya nano de Bougyoryoku ni Kyokufuri Shitai to Omoimasu (ep 1-12 w_en)

hiragana: おそい です よ
meaning: [You're] late!

hiragana: おもしろい いもうとさん です ね
meaning: [Your] sister is interesting, isn't she (sounds like she did something weird).

hiragana: せんせい も すき です よ
meaning: [I, the teacher] like [that] too... The speaker refers to herself in 3rd person. Depending on the context however, this can also mean that someone else talks about something the teacher likes. Don't worry about those details, from context this is usually clear (updated in v14).

hiragana: じょうだん です よ
meaning: [Something said before] is a joke.

hiragana: じょうだん じゃない です よ
meaning: This is not a joke [I am serious]!

hiragana: たのしみ です
meaning: [Something] is enjoyment / anticipation. When you're looking forward to something, you can say "tanoshimi" or "tanoshimi desu".

kanji: 買い物早かったですね
hiragana: かいもの はやかった です ね
meaning: Shopping was fast, wasn't it.

kanji: 本当の私じゃないです
hiragana: ほんとう の わたし じゃない です
meaning: [This] is not the real me. This refers e.g. to the picture someone might have in mind about the speaker or to something the speaker did. hontou: truth; reality; actuality; fact

hiragana: かぜ じゃない です
meaning: kaze: (common) cold; influenza

hiragana: うみ です ね
meaning: It's the sea, isn't it. This can be the answer to several questions: What is his favorite vacation destination? What is on this unclear picture? etc.

hiragana: ちゅうがくせい
meaning: The speaker is asking: [Are you] junior high school student? (continues on next card) chuugakusei: junior high school student

hiragana: なんで こども が いる の
meaning: [Are you] junior high school student (previous card)? Why [is] a kid here? nande: why?; what for? kodomo: kid, child We already learned a word for "why": naze, which is slightly more formal than "nande".

hiragana: こども じゃない です
meaning: [I] am not a kid! kodomo: kid, child The older one is using plain, the younger one polite speech.

hiragana: ぼく の いえ です よ
meaning: [This] is my house!
source: Ore no Imouto ga konna ni Kawaii Wake ga Nai_

hiragana: きれい でした
meaning: [Something] was pretty; lovely; beautiful, wasn't it?
source: Terrace House-Boys x Girls Next Door

kanji: 考えたこともなかったです
hiragana: かんがえた こと も なかった です
meaning: Thinking matter wasn't even there -> [I] didn't even think about [this]. Note that "mo" does not mean "too" here, but "even". Especially in negative sentences, "mo" is often used like this, more examples follow later. nakatta: negative past of aru

hiragana: わたし は ずっと しあわせ です
meaning: As for me, [I]'ve been happy the whole time [since I learned about this].

hiragana: ひろしま へ かえります
meaning: [I] return to Hiroshima. hiroshima: city in Japan

hiragana: いい じゃない です か
meaning: Isn't [this idea] good -> isn't this a good idea?

kanji: すみません大丈夫ですか
hiragana: すみません だいじょうぶ です か
meaning: Excuse me, are [you] ok?

kanji: ここにいるじゃないですか
hiragana: ここ に いる じゃない です か
romaji: koko ni iru janai desu ka
meaning: Isn't [someone supposed to be] here?! [Should] not [someone] be here?! It's always amazing how much information is packed into context in Japanese: The entire "supposed to be" or "should be" is completely transmitted by the intonation.

hiragana: わたし も よく しる おとこ です
romaji: watashi mo yoku shiru otoko desu
meaning: [He's] a guy I know well myself Or less literal: I know this guy well myself.

hiragana: ばか で は ありません
meaning: [Someone] is not an idiot (expressed in a polite way :D). "de ha arimasen" is the grammatically correct way to express polite negative state of being. In practice, you'll encounter "janai desu" more often.
source: JoJos Bizzare Adventure スターダストクルセイダース

hiragana: うそ で は ありません
meaning: uso: lie [Something said before] is not a lie. "de ha arimasen" is the grammatically correct way to express polite negative state of being. In practice, you'll encounter "janai desu" more often.

hiragana: じょうだん じゃ ありません
meaning: [Something said before] is not a joke. "ja arimasen" is slightly less formal than "de ha arimasen", refer to this question for details.

kanji: 全然大丈夫じゃありませんでしたよ
hiragana: ぜんぜん だいじょうぶ じゃ ありません でした よ
romaji: zenzen daijoubu ja arimasen deshita yo
meaning: [Someone or something done] was totally not ok. "ja arimasen" is slightly less formal than "de ha arimasen", refer to this question for details.

hiragana: ただいま
meaning: tadaima: Here I am; I'm home! (Phrase people say when returning home)

hiragana: おかえり
meaning: okaeri: welcome home (informal)

hiragana: おかえりなさい
meaning: okaerinasai: welcome home (more formal / polite than okaeri)

hiragana: おじゃまします
meaning: ojamashimasu: Excuse me for disturbing (interrupting) you; greeting used when entering someone's home

hiragana: うみ に いきます
meaning: [I] go to the sea.

hiragana: ただ の にく じゃねえ
meaning: Isn't [this] just ordinary meat? -> The conversation revolves around a piece of meat that is considered special, but looks ordinary to the speaker, so he asks this question. The ending "janee" here is a slurred, casual form of "janai". It's not the empathic sentence ending particle "ne/ね". tada: ordinary; common; usual​ Internal remark: gintama s5 e15 15:00 - and yes, it's ordinary meat

hiragana: おれ の けいたい
meaning: keitai: Abbreviation for mobile telephone; cellular telephone

hiragana: そして わたし の ねがい だ
meaning: ...and this is my wish. negai: desire; wish; hope

kanji: 気づくことができなかったんだ
hiragana: きづく こと が できなかった ん だ
romaji: kidzuku koto ga dekinakatta n da
meaning: [I] wasn't able to notice [this]. kidsuku: to notice dekinakatta: past negative of dekiru (to be able to do) I added only few examples for the plain negative past tense so far, I'll add a few more in the following. Quick reminder: Build the negative form (dekinai) and replace the "i" with "katta".

hiragana: きづかなかった か
meaning: kidzukanakatta: negative past of kidzuku (to notice) I added only few examples for the plain negative past tense so far, I'll add a few more in the following. Quick reminder: Build the negative form (kidzukanai) and replace the "i" with "katta".

hiragana: さけ のみます か
meaning: [Do you like to] drink alcohol/wine? If the conversation already revolves around drinking some alcoholic beverage, this is a perfectly valid way of asking, if someone likes to drink it (i.e. without all the "do you like"). Remark: In western languages, "sake" refers to Japanese rice wine. In Japanese, sake is a broader category that refers to any type of alcoholic beverage, no matter where it comes from. The Japanese rice wine is called nihonshuu/日本酒 in Japanese.

kanji: でもお酒飲まなかった
hiragana: でも おさけ のまなかった
meaning: ...but [person known from context] didn't drink alcohol. demo: but; however; though; nomanakatta: past negative of nomu (to drink) The context is usually important. Depending on the conversation, this sentence can express: [We went out] but [I] didn't drink sake. Or: [He wanted to have a drink at the bar] but [he] didn't drink sake [in the end]. I sometimes put a specific context into the square brackets or a more general one as in this case. I hope you're not confused by this!
source: Terrace House-Boys x Girls Next Door

hiragana: たいが みなかった
meaning: Didn't [you] see taiga? minakatta: negative past of miru (to see)

hiragana: きづかなかった の か
meaning: [You] didn't notice? remember: no in the end of a sentence adds an explanatory tone. Together with the question marker "ka" this indicates that the speaker is looking for an explanation.
source: JoJos Bizzare Adventure スターダストクルセイダース

hiragana: でも わたし は おもう の
meaning: ... but as for me, [i] believe [it / think this way]. The "no" adds an explanatory tone. A less literal translation would be: [that's] what I think / believe. omou: to think; to consider; to believe

hiragana: わたし は おもわない
meaning: As for me, [I] don't believe [something clear from context]. omowanai: negative of omou (to think; to consider; to believe)

hiragana: おもわなかった
meaning: omowanakatta: negative past of omou (to think; to consider; to believe)

hiragana: おいしい です か
meaning: Is [it] tasty?

hiragana: たのしかった です ね
meaning: [It] was enjoyable/fun, wasn't it?

kanji: 今日は学校は楽しかったですか
hiragana: きょう は がっこう は たのしかった です か
romaji: kyou ha gakkou ha tanoshikatta desu ka
meaning: Was school fun today? Note the two "ha" in this sentence, the topic is both today and the school. This is rather rare though.

kanji: おはようございますお父さん
hiragana: おはよう ございます おとうさん
meaning: otousan: father (polite) otousan is the polite word for father. In this example, the speaker uses it to address her own father. She's also using the more polite version of "good morning".

hiragana: ちち は しらなかった
meaning: chichi: father chichi is a less formal word for "father". It's not rude, but usually used to refer to one's own father when talking to others. So this sentence means: As for [my] father [he] didn't know.

hiragana: おとうさん どこ いく の
meaning: Father, where [do you] go? otousan: father otousan is the polite word for father. In this example, the speaker uses it to address her own father. Note, that she further says "doko iku no" (colloquial) and not "doko ni ikimasu no ka". So don't worry about when to use which forms together, just listen to many more examples. As far as I know, most families in Japan speak plain Japanese at home, but "otousan" is used to address ones own father directly or someone else's father. When talking about one's own father to others, "chichi" is used instead, but I think "otousan" can be used as well.
source: 今からあなたを脅迫します

kanji: でお父さんは何してるの
hiragana: で おとうさん は なに してる の
romaji: de otousan ha nani shiteru no
meaning: The speaker talks about someone else's father and asks: As for [your] father, what is [he] doing (at the moment)? The "de" is an informal conjuction (shortened "sorede"). You often hear in conversations, it means: so; therefore; and; (and) then

hiragana: わたし の ちち です
meaning: This can be the answer to the question: Who did it? [It was] my father.

hiragana: だいじょうぶ です おかあさん
meaning: [I'm] ok, mother! okaasan: mother (polite)

hiragana: おかあさん も いない
meaning: Mother is not there either. You often find "mo" in negative sentences, I'll cover that in more detail later.

hiragana: わたし の はは です
meaning: [This] is my mother. haha: mother okaasan and haha follow the same rules as otousan and chichi: Use the polite version when referring to someone else's father or talking to your own father. Use the casual version, when talking to someone about your own father. It's not too strict in practice though...

hiragana: かぞく です
meaning: [This] is [my] family. kazoku: family

kanji: お酒を買うこともできませんし
hiragana: おさけ を かう こと も できません し
romaji: osake wo kau koto mo dekimasen shi
meaning: [The conversation revolves around the question of why the people are drinking at one of the guy's home. One (among other) reasons is that outside we] can't buy any alcoholic beverages. Remember sake (alcoholic beverage)? The prefix "o" makes it more polite. This prefix can't be added to any noun though. Remark: "xxx koto ga dekiru" is one out of several ways to express the ability to do something. This is covered later in more detail. In negative sentences, "ga" is sometimes replaced by "mo" to add emphasis. "mo" translates to something like "even" in this case. I.e. we can't even buy alcohol. Have a look at the reference.

kanji: すみません注文いいですか
hiragana: すみません ちゅうもん いい です か
meaning: Excuse me, [is] order ok? -> Can I order something? chuumon: order (in a restaurant)

hiragana: ごちゅうもん なん に します か
meaning: What [do you want to] order? The prefix "go" makes chuumon more polite in this example. "o" and "go" are the only two prefixes used like this. I can't exactly tell you all the rules of when to use what and as always recommend to consume lots of materials. I will add good resources towards the end of the course. Remark 1: In many cases, you can translate "ni suru" as "to decide on", see https://jlptsensei.com/learn-japanese-grammar/%E3%81%AB%E3%81%99%E3%82%8B-ni-suru-meaning/. Remark 2: Here, we have "何にしますか/nan ni shimasu ka" and NOT "何しますか/nani shimasu ka" - note the different spelling of "nan", the pronunciation is also slightly different. In the first one, key grammar is nan ni suru - what do you decide on, in the second one, the grammar is nani wo suru with a dropped "wo"-particle - what do you want to do. Don't worry about the details of Remark 2, "ni suru" is covered in more detail later.

hiragana: どこ に たべ に いく
meaning: Where do [you] go to eat? tabe: stem of taberu (to eat) Remember: The stem is retrieved by removing the "-masu" or teineigo ending. For a technically more correct way, refer to Tae Kim p. 76 or this website. Verb stems (= special nouns) are mostly used together with "ni" or "he" + motion verb. I.e. the verb stem is the target of the motion verb. This can be translated as "to go (in order) to".

hiragana: きょう どこ み に いく
meaning: Today, where [do we] go to see [something, maybe a movie]? Caution, this is a casual sentence, some particles are missing here. Verb stems (= special nouns) are mostly used together with "ni" or "he" + motion verb. I.e. the verb stem is the target of the motion verb. This can be translated as "to go (in order) to".
source: JoJos Bizzare Adventure スターダストクルセイダース

hiragana: ぜったい み に いく ね
meaning: Definitely go to see [it]. mi: stem of miru (to see)

hiragana: み に いきません か
meaning: Shouldn't [we] go to see [something together]?

hiragana: なに し に いく の
meaning: shi: stem of suru (to do) This sentence is super interesting, because it's very hard to translate to English directly: "shi ni iku" means: "to go to do" or "to go in order to do". The speaker combines it with "nani/what" to ask something like: "what are you going to do"? A more literal translation would be: [you] go in order to do what? There's a show on Japanese TV called "you ha nani shi ni nihon he", which roughly translates to "why did you come to Japan?" It uses the same construction: As for you (you ha), came in order to do what?

hiragana: よび に いく
meaning: [He] goes [there] to call [someone]? yobi: stem of yobu (to call)
source: ももへの手紙(A Letter to Momo)

hiragana: ‪こんど はなし に いく ‬
meaning: Next time [I] go to talk / have a conversation. kondo: next time hanashi: stem of hanasu (to talk)

hiragana: きょう のみ に いかない
meaning: As for today (particle missing), don't [we] go in order to drink? -> Let's go out for a drink. nomi: stem of nomu (to drink)

hiragana: あそび に いく の
meaning: [Do you] go to to visit [them] or just: Do you visit them? asobi: verb stem of asobu (to play) Literally, the sentence means: [Do you] go to play (with a desire for explanation due to "no"). However, the term "asobi ni iku" also means: "To go out on a trip" or "to go out to visit". Have a look at the dictionary if you like.

kanji: 今日はどこに遊びに行くかな
hiragana: きょう は どこ に あそび に いく か な
romaji: kyou ha doko ni asobi ni iku ka na
meaning: As for today, [I] wonder where [I] should go out on a trip / go out to visit? doko: where; what place "ka na" can be translated as "I wonder".
source: Ore no Imouto ga konna ni Kawaii Wake ga Nai_

hiragana: なに を し に きた
meaning: [You] came [here] to do what? In English, you'd rather just say: Why did you come here? shi: stem of suru shi ni kuru: to come in order to do. Remark: "nani wo shi ni kita" is past tense. It's used when person A already arrived and B wants to know what A came to do for. "nani wo shi ni kuru" is present tense. Since Japanese has no dedicated future, this is also used when A wants to come tomorrow, then B asks: Oh, you come tomorrow for doing what...?

kanji: 私ね今日謝りに来たの
hiragana: わたし ね きょう あやまり に きた の
romaji: watashi ne kyou ayamari ni kita no
meaning: I today came to apologize. ayamari: stem of ayamaru (to apologize) Note that the "ne/ね" after watashi makes the sentence sound more feminine. Refer to this article for more details. I'll probably add more elaborate information on gender specific language later.

kanji: 私と友達にならないか
hiragana: わたし と ともだち に ならない か
romaji: watashi to tomodachi ni naranai ka
meaning: Don't [you] become friend with me?
source: JoJos Bizzare Adventure スターダストクルセイダース

hiragana: いま どこ に いる
meaning: Where is [he] now? ima: now; the present time

hiragana: また おなじ ゆめ
meaning: Again, [the] same dream. onaji: same; identical; equal

hiragana: わたし も がんばる
meaning: I too do [my] best. ganbaru: to do one's best; to persist; to keep at it; to hang on

kanji: 頑張ることができたから
hiragana: がんばる こと が できた から
meaning: As usual, a little bit of context is missing here, e.g. [I succeeded] because I could manage to do my best / keep at it. ganbaru: to do one's best; to persist; to keep at it; to hang on Note that Tae Kim covers "kara" later. It usually connects two sentences in the following fashion: Reason kara result, meaning: because of reason, result happened. If the result is clear from context, it is often omitted, just as in this example. I'll pick this up in more detail later.
source: Toaru Kagaku no Railgun S (Railgun S02, JP only)

hiragana: もんだい ありません ね
meaning: There is no problem [with something clear from context]. mondai: problem (e.g. societal, political); question; issue

hiragana: しごと の じかん だ
meaning: It's the hour/time of work -> It's time for work. shigoto: work; job; business

hiragana: おれ に も なまえ が ある
romaji: ore ni mo namae ga aru
meaning: I also have a name (maybe someone didn't call the speaker by his name). namae: name Remark: The key grammar point here is: x ni y ga aru. Or, as Tae Kim explained it: "ni" sets the preceding word as target of something (namae ga aru in this case). In casual Japanese, you could omit the "ni". I wasn't sure of this, but a native speaker confirmed this.

hiragana: こんど は わたし が たすける
meaning: Next time I will help you. tasukeru: to save; to rescue / to help; to assist Remark: "kondo" can mean both next time and this time, which I found a bit confusing. See ref.

hiragana: おれ は はずかしい よ
meaning: hazukashii: embarrassing; embarrassed

kanji: 全然恥ずかしいことじゃないですよ
hiragana: ぜんぜん はずかしい こと じゃない です よ
romaji: zenzen hazukashii koto janai desu yo
meaning: [Something] is totally not an embarassing thing.
source: 下ネタという概念が存在しない退屈な世界 (uncensored)

hiragana: おかね は ある
meaning: [Do you] have money? Literally: As for money, is it there? okane: money Here's the teneigo prefix again: "o". In this case I think it became more common to say "okane" instead of just "kane".

hiragana: おかね なくなった
meaning: [I] used up [my / the] money. Note again that this is informal speech, there's a particle missing (e.g. a "ga" after okane). nakunaru: to be used up; to be missing

hiragana: めいわく な はなし だ
meaning: [This] is an annoying conversation. meiwaku: trouble; bother; annoyance

hiragana: まいにち み に くる ん だ
romaji: mainichi mi ni kuru n da
meaning: [I] come daily to watch (in an explanatory tone). mainichi: daily
source: Higurashi no Naku Koro ni S1 (JP Eng)

hiragana: いえ は ちかい の
meaning: As for [your] house [is it] close? chikai: near; close; short (distance & in time)

hiragana: それ が わたし の ゆめ
meaning: that [it] my dream [hitting my resignment right in the face of my boss]. sore: that; it (indicates closeness to the listener and may refer to almost everything: Object, person or something on the listener's mind) Note the similarity to socchi/sochira, which referred to a direction. Remark: the "ga" sounds very much like "ha" here, don't worry about it. If you want to check the context: Aggretsuko, S1, E2, 13:30

hiragana: それ は わたし も おなじ です
romaji: sore ha watashi mo onaji desu
meaning: As for that [on your mind], same here -> I agree with you and think the same about it. sore: that; it (indicates closeness to the listener and may refer to almost everything: Object, person or something on the listener's mind)

hiragana: それ は なに
meaning: As for that [close to listener], what? -> What is that? sore: that; it (indicates closeness to the listener and may refer to almost everything: Object, person or something on the listener's mind)
source: Boku no Hero Academia S2 (ep 1-25 jp_en)

hiragana: わたし は それ を うしなった
meaning: As for me, [I] lost it. What was lost can be an item the listener still has or for example faith (they seem to be in space, after all).

hiragana: これ は なに
meaning: Note the similarity to kocchi/kochira, which referred to a direction. kore: this; it (indicates closeness to the speaker and may refer to almost everything: Object, person or something on the speaker's mind)

hiragana: これ は おれ の もんだい
meaning: As for this, [it is] my problem / task to solve.

hiragana: これ は おれ の もの だ
romaji: kore ha ore no mono da
meaning: As for this, [it is] my thing/object/item.

hiragana: あれ は なに
meaning: In this sentence, the two might be talking about strange behavior of someone else: "What's that supposed to mean?" are: that; that thing (indicates distance to both speaker and listener and may refer to almost everything: Object, person or something on someone's mind)

hiragana: あれ は いもうと
meaning: That over there, [your] younger sister? -> Is that your sister over there? Remark: Here, the guy is really talking about someone else's sister. Most resources teach that you'd rather use "imoutosan" here, but this is a casual conversation among friends and anime, after all.

hiragana: あれ は いぬ
meaning: As for that over there, a dog?!

hiragana: せんせい の おかげ です
meaning: [Something] is the teacher's help / influence. -> This means that e.g. something worked out well thanks to the teacher's help. okage: assistance; help / effect, influence

kanji: さあごはんできましたよ
hiragana: さあ ごはん できました よ
meaning: Food is ready. gohan: cooked rice, meal -> cooked rice is so important in Japanese, that the word for it is used for describing an entire meal dekiru: besides to do / to be able to / to be ready

hiragana: おみまい に きた よ
meaning: omimai: calling on / visiting someone who is ill

kanji: 皆さんこっちに来ましたよ
hiragana: みなさん こっち に きました よ
meaning: Everybody came over here (towards the speaker).

hiragana: なんで ここ に きた の
meaning: Why did [you] come here?

kanji: 大丈夫ですか佐藤先生
hiragana: だいじょうぶ です か さとう せんせい
meaning: Are [you] ok, satou-sensei? sensei (teacher) is an example for referring to someone by their title or position. It can be used to "just" refer to a teacher - just as in English. In Japanese however, you can use it to directly address your teacher in a polite way. It acknowledges the teacher's (higher) position. In this example, the speaker directly addresses his teacher with the name (satou), sensei is used as suffix.

hiragana: せんせい は おうえん します
meaning: The teacher helps / supports [us]. ouen: aid; assistance; help. Also: to cheer someone up. Here's the true context (which is a bit harder to understand than the above translation): [Please don't join the demons. Let's start over again together] I will help you [the speaker is the teacher and she is referring to herself in 3rd person. This is covered in more detail throughout the deck, don't worry if you don't get it right away]. As usual in Japanese, it depends on the context ;).

hiragana: あの たかはし せんせい は
meaning: ano: say; well (filler word) This sentence is again ambiguous without context. Just as in the last example, the speaker could be directly addressing her teacher with the name (takahashi) + suffix, meaning: As for you, takahashi-sensei... what are you doing tonight? However, she can also use this to talk about takahashi sensei with someone else in a polite way.

hiragana: ひさしぶり だ な せんせい
meaning: It's been a while, teacher! hisashiburi: a long time (since the last time. Mostly used as phrase when meeting someone not seen for a while, e.g. "long time no see"). Here, the teacher ist directly addressed without using the name.

kanji: 高橋先生いい人だったな
hiragana: たかはし せんせい いい ひと だった な
romaji: takahashi sensei ii hito datta na
meaning: Takahashi-sensei was a good person, wasn't he?

kanji: 私が部長だから私が書く
hiragana: わたし が ぶちょう だ から わたし が かく
romaji: watashi ga buchou da kara watashi ga kaku
meaning: Because I am the head of the club, I write [it] down. (They are talking about the sheet of paper on the image. It's a "bukatsu shinsei youshi" - application form for extracurricular activities, and the head of the club wants to fill it out herself for some reason. buchou: head of a (school) club; it also means "head (chief, director) of a section or department", but in school anime, you'll hear this sometimes.

kanji: はいはっ失礼します部長
hiragana: はい はっしつれい します ぶちょう
meaning: "shitsurei shimasu" in this sentence is a polite way to say goodbye to his boss (buchou), in this case probably because the speaker leaves work earlier than the others. It can also mean "excuse me". shitsurei: discourtesy; impoliteness​
source: JoJos Bizzare Adventure ダイヤモンドは砕けない

hiragana: ふじみや さん
meaning: -san: Suffix for mostly names adding politeness. It's similar to addressing someone with mr. or mrs. in English, but not the same. Here, the guy e.g. talks to a girl in school - you'd rather not address her with mrs. in English. An interesting explanation is found on quora (see reference link).

hiragana: みなさん こんにちは
meaning: -san can also be added to other words than just names. In this case to "minna" to address everyone in a polite way.

kanji: 大丈夫お父さん怖くないぞ
hiragana: だいじょうぶ おとうさん こわくない ぞ
meaning: It's ok, [I] am not scared. -> The father is referring to himself in third person. He's dissecting a fish to prepare it for a meal in front of his very young daughter, and he is reassuring her that she shouldn't be afraid because he is not. But actually, he is! Note that "kowai" is an adjective, but it means both scary and scared. Have a look at the reference.

hiragana: ひめ は しんだ
meaning: As for the princess, [she] died. hime: princess

hiragana: だいじょうぶ です か ひめさま
meaning: Are [you] ok, princess? -sama: a politer version of "-san", more on this (honorific) language later. I wanted to add this here, because you'll hear versions of this every once in a while in anime.

hiragana: きれい な おひめさま
meaning: A pretty princess. ohimesama: an even more respectful / honorific way to address the princess. All three versions (hime, himesama, ohimesama) are also found in the dictionary. Interestingly, this version also ironically refers to a spoiled girl ;).

hiragana: きょう は つかれた
meaning: tsukareru: to get tired; to tire; to get fatigued; to become exhausted

kanji: 休憩疲れましたね疲れた
hiragana: きゅうけい つかれました ね つかれた
meaning: Break! I got tired. kyuukei: break, rest These two seem to be tired from playing table tennis. Do you remember the verb stem? Just omit the "-masu/-mashita" part and you'll get a noun to be used for some specific cases. Do it for tsukareru/tsukaremashita now and then have a look at the next cards.

hiragana: おつかれ
meaning: otsukare: goodbye (especially after some work was done together, casual) BUT ALSO: A casual "hi" --> check the answers on japanese stackexchange. wasabi-jpn writes: "Since it cannot be translated because of the wide context, people consider it very difficult". I'd say most of the time, this is means "goodbye" after some joint effort, but is also used as greeting. This will be covered again later in videos by native speakers, so try not to worry too much for now. The origin is interesting: It's the verb stem plus "o"-prefix of "tsukareru - to become tired". I have no idea how to translate this into English, a literal translation would be: "The honored tiredness" or something.

hiragana: おつかれさま です
meaning: Thank you for your efforts (phrase often used as goodbye at the office) "otsukare / sama" is complicated, check the answers on japanese stackexchange. wasabi-jpn writes: "Since it cannot be translated because of the wide context, people consider it very difficult". I'd say most of the time, this is means "goodbye" after some joint effort, but is also used as greeting. This will be covered again later in videos by native speakers, so try not to worry too much for now.

hiragana: ぱんだ くん
meaning: -kun: Usually used for addressing males of equal or lower status. You'll hear this a lot in school anime. Wikipedia however states, that it "is generally used by people of senior status addressing or referring to those of junior status". The panda in this example sentence is always hanging out at the polar bear's cafe and the person speaking belongs to the staff. I'd highly recommend this anime (Shirokuma cafe) for Japanese learners by the way, it's easier to understand than others.

kanji: 香織ちゃんこんにちは
hiragana: かおり ちゃん こんにちは
meaning: -chan: cute suffix for a familiar person, sounds a bit girlish "kaori" is the first name of the girl with the red hair. In this series, the small girl usually addresses her in a familiar and cute way. I also found this anime quite easy to understand by the way.

hiragana: はい ひろえ せんぱい
meaning: -senpai: used to address or refer to one's older or more senior colleagues in a school, workplace, dojo or sports club. Teachers are not senpai, but sensei (from wikipedia).

hiragana: あなた の おかげ です
meaning: [Something good] is [thanks to] your assistance, help. anata: you So finally, after 500+ cards, a word for "you". It is important to realize that this is used in a very different way than the English "you" and can easily sound rude. By now you should be aware of the fact that pronouns are usually omitted in Japanese. The entire thing with pronouns being rude is explained in more detail here. Note that it's not automatically rude to use "anata", but explaining this is beyond the scope of this course. As always: Listen to many examples!

hiragana: きみ に はなし が ある
meaning: [I] need to talk to you! kimi: another word for "you", mostly used by men toward people of lower status. You'll hear this a lot in anime. I think it's rarely used in real life.

hiragana: きみ の あいて は ぼく だ
romaji: kimi no aite ha boku da
meaning: [I] am your ally / partner. Explanation by a Japanese person from the discussion on quora: "Usually bosses can call lower rank person "kimi" or family name with "-kun" to male employees" - just as in this example...

kanji: お前はなぜ来なかった
hiragana: おまえ は なぜ こなかった
meaning: As for you, why didn't [you] come? omae: very casual, rough way to say "you". naze: why You'll hear this in anime a lot, it's not automatically rude, but more casual than "anata". You'd better avoid using this in a conversation unless you're really sure what you're saying.

hiragana: てめえ の せい だ
meaning: [Everything is] your fault! temee: derogatory "you". Again, you'll sometimes hear this in anime, but never use it in a conversation - it's unfriendly by definition and rather used to cause trouble or insult someone.

hiragana: きさま なに を する
meaning: What are you doing, you bastard! kisama: you; you bastard; you son of a bitch Another very unfriendly "you", you'll sometimes hear this in anime.

kanji: 春原妹さんから電話よ
hiragana: すのはら いもうとさん から でんわ よ
meaning: "Sunohara, call from [your] younger sister". imouto: younger sister (+ san here)

kanji: でも私はいい姉じゃなかった
hiragana: でも わたし は いい あね じゃなかった
romaji: demo watashi ha ii ane janakatta
meaning: ...but as for me, [I] wasn't [a] good older sister. ane: older sister

kanji: 今日はありがとうお姉さん
hiragana: きょう は ありがとう おねえさん
meaning: oneesan: more polite way to refer to one's older sister. It also means "young lady" or "miss", which might sound confusing sometimes.

hiragana: ぼく の あに だ よ
meaning: [Who is this person over there?] It's my older brother. ani: older brother

hiragana: わたし の あに です よ
meaning: [Who is this over there?] It's my older brother.

hiragana: せんせい の おにいさん
meaning: oniisan: more polite way for one's older brother
source: さよなら絶望先生 (Sayonara, Zetsubou-Sensei)

hiragana: おれ の おとうと は にんげん だ
romaji: ore no otouto ha ningen da
meaning: My younger brother is a human [the younger brother lost his body, and his soul is bound to a piece of armor, so he does not seem "human"]. otouto: younger brother

kanji: ハニー先輩の弟さんだよ
hiragana: はにー せんぱい の おとうとさん だ よ
romaji: hani- senpai no otoutosan da yo
meaning: otoutosan: younger brother (polite)
source: Ouran High School Host Club (jp eng)

hiragana: かれ は すごい な
meaning: He's great, I tell you! kare: he It's also possible to refer to others in third person, but as you might have guessed already: It's rather uncommon. Just as the other pronouns (I, you), "he" and "she" are almost never used like they are used in English. Most of the time, they are omitted. Only if it is not clear who's being talked about, they are sometimes used. So if you omit "kare ha" in this sentence for example, the remaining "sugoi na" just means that something is great. However, the speaker might refer to the person standing behind him, doesn't know his name and thus adds "kare ha".

hiragana: かれ を ころす の
meaning: [You want to] kill him? (with a tone asking for explanation).

hiragana: かのじょ は いない です ね
meaning: kanojo: she (or girlfriend) We already had the female counterpart to "kare" on earlier cards, it's "kanojo" and in this sentence, "she is not here".

hiragana: かのじょ は かわしま あみ
meaning: The speaker introduces the person accompanying him as "kawashima ami". Note that ami is her first name, in Japanese the names are often mentioned or introduced lastname-first. This also matches the way to address people: If you would address ami directly, you'd probably say "kawashima-san".

hiragana: かれし は います か
meaning: [Do you] have a boyfriend? kareshi: boyfriend The same way kanojo means "she" and "girlfriend", kare means "he" and "boyfriend". However, "kareshi" is used as word for boyfriend more often. This sentence means: Do [you] have a boyfriend? Literally: As for boyfriend, is [he] there?
source: Terrace House- Boys & Girls in the City

kanji: でも会うのは今日が最後だ
hiragana: でも あう の は きょう が さいご だ
romaji: demo au no ha kyou ga saigo da
meaning: But as for meeting [him], today is last time. au: to meet; to encounter; to see saigo: end, conclusion (from previous card) and also last; final (this card).

kanji: そして僕は彼女の息子に会った
hiragana: そして ぼく は かのじょ の むすこ に あった
romaji: soshite boku ha kanojo no musuko ni atta
meaning: And as for me, [I] met her son. musuko: son atta: past tense of au (to meet; to encounter; to see). Remark: "atta" is also the past of "aru". In written Japanese they are easily distinguished by the kanji, but in spoken Japanese it's the context that will help you.

kanji: 息子さんの仕事仲間です
hiragana: むすこさん の しごと なかま です
meaning: [Someone] is the work comrade of [someone's] son. Even though you don't know the context here, the use of "san" tells you that the speaker is most likely referring to someone else's son. Interesting is also the use of "shigoto nakama". In Japanese, you can chain nouns together without particle, if they form one logical entity. The same thing is possible e.g. in German, but in Japanese it is not used that often. The explanation for this is well hidden in Tae Kim's book: P. 59 or this section. Keep in mind, that Japanese has no whitespaces, so "shigoto nakama" is actually one word.

hiragana: むすめ を たのむ
meaning: [Please] take care of [my] daughter. Or more literally: "I commend my daughter to you". This is the real context here (FMA brotherhood, episode 30, 3:20). Depending on the context, this can also mean: Ask [my / someone's] daughter (in order to do something, not to answer a question. Asking a question requires a different word introduced after about 200 cards). If this is too weird, only try to remember "musume"! musume: daughter tanomu: to entrust to (in addition to to request; to beg; to ask)

kanji: その意味がよく分かりました
hiragana: その いみ が よく わかりました
meaning: [I] well understood that meaning or less literal: I understood the significance [of something] well. sono: that; the (distant from the speaker, close to the listener, follows the same pattern as sore/socchi/sochira)

hiragana: その りす かわいい ね
meaning: risu: squirrel sono: that; the (distant from the speaker, close to the listener, follows the same pattern as sore/socchi/sochira)

hiragana: その おとこ の なまえ よ
meaning: [This is] the name of that guy. sono: that; the (distant from the speaker, close to the listener, follows the same pattern as sore/socchi/sochira)

hiragana: その はなし を し に きた
romaji: sono hanashi wo shi ni kita
meaning: I came to talk about that (topic the listener would like to talk about) or more literal: [I] came to do that conversation. sono: that; the (distant from the speaker, close to the listener, follows the same pattern as sore/socchi/sochira)

kanji: この学校は好きですか
hiragana: この がっこう は すき です か
romaji: kono gakkou ha suki desu ka
meaning: As for this school [do you] like it? The listener probably transferred from a different school to the speaker's and the speaker wants to know if the listener likes it. kono: this (close to the speaker, distant to the listener, follows the same pattern as kore/kocchi/kochira)

hiragana: なに この ねこ
meaning: What's up with this cat? kono: this (close to the speaker, distant to the listener, follows the same pattern as kore/kocchi/kochira)

hiragana: この もんだい わかる ひと
meaning: Another nice example for a clause: The teacher is asking for people, who understand this problem (i.e. "kono mondai (wo) wakaru" is a clause describing "hito"). They should probably come to the board and write down the answer. kono: this (close to the speaker, distant to the listener, follows the same pattern as kore/kocchi/kochira)

kanji: あのマンションですね
hiragana: あの まんしょん です ね
meaning: [A: Where does he live? B: ] It's that apartment building [over there]. While a "mansion" is a large, luxurious house in English, "manshon" means apartment building in Japanese.

kanji: この時間がとても好き
hiragana: この じかん が とても すき
meaning: As for this hour/time of the day, [I] like it very much.

hiragana: あの こと は わすれない
meaning: As for that thing/matter, don't forget. ano: that (distant to both speaker and listener, follows the same pattern as are/acchi/achira) We already had "ano" as filler, meaning "say; well; um; er" at the beginning of a sentence.

kanji: あの男は人間じゃない
hiragana: あの おとこ は にんげん じゃない
meaning: As for that guy over there, [he] is not human. ano: that (distant to both speaker and listener, follows the same pattern as are/acchi/achira)

hiragana: あの ゆめ は それ か
meaning: As for that dream [I had a while ago], is it that [what you just explained]? That's an interesting sentence using both ano and sore, if it doesn't make sense without context, just skip it.

kanji: 私あの勝負に勝ちましたの
hiragana: わたくし あの しょうぶ に かちました の
romaji: watakushi ano shoubu ni kachimashita no
meaning: I won that battle/competition (in an explanatory tone). E.g. why are you so happy? Because I won that competition. kachimashita: polite past tense of katsu - to win. shoubu: battle / competition watakushi: slightly more formal and feminine version of "watashi"
source: 下ネタという概念が存在しない退屈な世界 (uncensored)

hiragana: あの ね うえはら くん
meaning: It's a colloquial phase you'll hear quite often. -kun fits here too as it's used to address males of rather lower status. I just added this because of the "ano"-context here ;). ano ne; look here; I say; well (familiar language)

hiragana: わたし もう いきます ね
meaning: I go now. mou: now; soon; shortly

kanji: 俺はもう家に帰るんだから
hiragana: おれ は もう いえ に かえる ん だ から
romaji: ore ha mou ie ni kaeru n da kara
meaning: The speaker doesn't want the kids to follow him and gives the reason: "[Don't follow me] because as for me, [I] now/soon return home". mou: now; soon; shortly Note that Tae Kim covers "kara" later. It usually connects two sentences in the following fashion: Reason kara result, meaning: because of reason, result happened. If the result is clear from context, it is often omitted, just as in this example. I'll pick this up in more detail later.

hiragana: これ は もう みました
meaning: As for this [I] already saw it. mou also means: already; yet

hiragana: いつも おなじ ゆめ を みる
meaning: [I] always dream the same dream. itsumo: always; usually; every time The "ru" is cut off unfortunately, This happens sometimes due to inaccurate timings of the subtitles use for creating the deck.

hiragana: ぱんだ くん いつも の
meaning: The speaker works at the polarbear's cafe and asks the panda (regular guest): "The same as always"? itsumo: always; usually; every time

kanji: お前はいつも強くない
hiragana: おまえ は いつも つよくない
meaning: As for you (rough) [you are] never strong. Literally, this reads: always not strong, but in English you'd say "never strong". itsumo: never (with negative verb)

hiragana: とうきょう の だいがく に いく
meaning: [I] go to Tokyo university. daigaku: university; college

hiragana: ぼく の だいがく の ともだち です
romaji: boku no daigaku no tomodachi desu
meaning: [These people] are my college friends. daigaku: university; college Note the chain of two "no" here, it's quite common to do this.

hiragana: とくべつ な ともだち
meaning: [Someone] is a special friend. tokubetsu: special; particular; extraordinary

hiragana: とくべつ な としょかん
meaning: [This is] a special library. tokubetsu: special; particular; extraordinary

kanji: それは僕にはできない特別なことだ
hiragana: それ は ぼく に は できない とくべつ な こと だ
romaji: sore ha boku ni ha dekinai tokubetsu na koto da
meaning: As for that, it's a special thing I'm not able to do. The sentence is a bit more difficult, "boku ni ha dekinai" is a clause describing "tokubetsu na koto". The "ni ha" emphasizes, that "boku" is the one not being able to do the "tokubetsu na koto", have a look at the references. However, you can also just ignore it for now ;).

hiragana: しつもん が あります
meaning: Question is there -> I have a question. shitsumon: question

hiragana: でも かのじょ は うつくしい
meaning: utsukushii: beautiful; pretty; lovely

hiragana: じぶん の せい だ ね
meaning: jibun: myself; yourself; oneself The dictionary definition of jibun might read weird, but I found it always easy to understand from context what it refers to. It always means "someone self", the someone can be anyone clear from context. So in this sentence: [something] is [someone's] own fault.

kanji: お前と戦うつもりはない
hiragana: おまえ と たたかう つもり は ない
romaji: omae to tatakau tsumori ha nai
meaning: tsumori: intention; plan "tsumori" is a noun very often used together with a relative clause, just as in this sentence: As for "fight-with-you"-intention, not there. Or less literal: I don't have the intention to fight with you.

kanji: 分かるかはい分かるつもりです
hiragana: わかる か はい わかる つもり です
romaji: wakaru ka hai wakaru tsumori desu
meaning: Person A: [Do you] understand? Person B: Yes, [I] assume/think [I] understand. So obviously, B doesn't yet understand it. tsumori: intention; plan; but also: belief, assumtion, thus "I assume/think".
source: Legend of the Galactic Heroes (JP Eng) (Media Added)

kanji: 今度は何するつもりですか
hiragana: こんど は なに する つもり です か
romaji: kondo ha nani suru tsumori desu ka
meaning: What are [we] going to do this time? Or literally: As for this time, what-do intention is it? kondo: this time; now OR next time (I always found kondo a bit weird because of this ambiguous definition, but it's usually clear from context what it means).
source: 下ネタという概念が存在しない退屈な世界 (uncensored)

kanji: 何をするつもりですの
hiragana: なに を する つもり です の
romaji: nani wo suru tsumori desu no
meaning: The speaker wants to know what the others are up to and asks literally: "what-do intention is it" in a tone looking for explanation.
source: Toaru Kagaku no Railgun S (Railgun S02, JP only)

hiragana: わたし に は むり ね
meaning: [Something] is impossible for me. muri: impossible; unreasonable
source: The World God Only Knows S3 (jp eng)

hiragana: むり な もの は むり よ
romaji: muri na mono ha muri yo
meaning: An impossible thing is, well... impossible (it seems like the guy wants to do something the girl considers hard or unreasonable).

kanji: そして僕はもうあの夢を見ることもなくなった
hiragana: そして ぼく は もう あの ゆめ を みる こと も なくなった
romaji: soshite boku ha mou ano yume wo miru koto mo nakunatta
meaning: ...and as for me, [I] already stopped having that dream. Reminder: In Japanese, dreaming is expressed as "seeing a dream".

hiragana: いつ まで いる ん だ
meaning: Until when are [you] there? itsu: when; at what time; how soon

hiragana: いつ から なくなった
meaning: Since when did [your glasses] disappear [the listener has lost his glasses and the speaker wants to know when he lost them]? itsu: when; at what time; how soon

hiragana: いつ から いく の
meaning: Since when [do you] go [somewhere]? itsu: when; at what time; how soon Somewhere can again be almost everything: Work, a language class, etc.
source: Terrace House-Boys x Girls Next Door

hiragana: なに が すき だ
meaning: What [do you] like? nani/nan/何: what (pronunciation depends a bit on the context)

hiragana: な なん です か
meaning: What is it? (Maybe the guy was staring at the girl). nani/nan/何: what Note that the question word for "what" is spelled "何" in native Japanese. The pronunciation is ambiguous, sometimes it's "nani", sometimes it's "nan".

hiragana: だれ の せい だ だれ が わるい
romaji: dare no sei da dare ga warui
meaning: Whose fault is [it], who [is] at fault dare: who Note that the adjective "warui" generally means "bad", but can also mean "at fault".

hiragana: どこ に いく つもり だ
meaning: Where do [you] intend to go? doko: where Again, a nice example for a verb clause: "doko ni iku" describes "tsumori", so literally: Where go-intention it is?

hiragana: どれ が いい
meaning: Which [one] is good? (E.g. when choosing something at the supermarket). dore: which
source: Sakurasou no Pet na Kanojo (jp eng)

kanji: どれくらい大きいんだ
hiragana: どれ くらい おおきい ん だ
meaning: How big is [it] approximately? kurai: approximately; about (note that this also means "dark, gloomy"). In some cases, it is spelled "gurai". You'll face this "softening" of characters often, I'll cover this in more detail on another card. Maybe a monster or something. Remark: "dore" means "which". But especially when used together with "gurai", it rather translates to "how" (long/far/big...), have a look at the reference.

hiragana: いくら だ
meaning: How much [is it / something]? ikura: how much

hiragana: いくら です か
meaning: How much [is it / something], a bit more polite. ikura: how much

kanji: 買いますおいくらですか
hiragana: かいます お いくら です か
meaning: [I] buy [it]. How much is [it]? Notice the politeness prefix "o" here.
source: 今からあなたを脅迫します

hiragana: これ どう おもいます
meaning: As for this, how do [you] think? dou: how; in what way; how about​

hiragana: どう だった きょう は
meaning: How was [it]? Today [I mean].

hiragana: どう します か
meaning: How should [we] do [it]? What should we do? The English equivalent is: What should we do? But in Japanese, this is expressed using "dou - how / in what way should we do [it]".

hiragana: おかえり どう だった
meaning: Welcome back! How was [it]?
source: BOFURI - Itai no wa Iya nano de Bougyoryoku ni Kyokufuri Shitai to Omoimasu (ep 1-12 w_en)

hiragana: おまえ は どう おもう
meaning: As for you, how / in what way [do you] think?

hiragana: どうして
meaning: doushite: why, for what reason? This is slightly more polite than "nande".

hiragana: おかあさん どうして
meaning: Mother, why [did you say this]?

hiragana: かなしい はなし だ
meaning: [Something] is a sad story. The speaker however sounds like he's not serious, also the music is not very sad ;). kanashii: sad; miserable

hiragana: こわい えいが じゃない よ
meaning: [Something] is not a scary movie. eiga: movie

hiragana: げんいん なに です
meaning: Cause - what is it? gen'in: cause; origin; source
source: Boku no Hero Academia S3 (ep 1-25 jp_en)

hiragana: きょう たんじょうび だ よ ね
meaning: Today is [your] birthday, isn't it? tanjoubi: birthday

kanji: 先生お誕生日おめでとうございます
hiragana: せんせい おたんじょうび おめでとう ございます
meaning: A polite way to congratulate someone to his birthday. omedetou: congratulations!; well done!; best wishes!; all the best! This word is used e.g. for congratulating someone to their birthday, but also for wishing a happy new year and others.
source: 今からあなたを脅迫します

kanji: お誕生日 おめでとう
hiragana: おたんじょうび おめでとう
meaning: A more casual way to congratulate someone.
source: 私に天使が舞い降りた! (wataten)

hiragana: だれか いる の
meaning: Is someone there? dareka: someone (it's dare + ka, but I spell it together, because it's also found like this in the dictionary. Remember: Japanese has no whitespaces, so don't worry about this).

hiragana: だれか いない の か
meaning: Isn't someone there? dareka: someone (it's dare + ka, but I spell it together, because it's also found like this in the dictionary. Remember: Japanese has no whitespaces, so don't worry about this).

hiragana: だれ か いない か な
meaning: Isn't someone there? dareka: someone (it's dare + ka, but I spell it together, because it's also found like this in the dictionary. Remember: Japanese has no whitespaces, so don't worry about this).

hiragana: だれか きた
meaning: Oh, someone came!

kanji: 誰かこっちに来ますあ
hiragana: だれか こっち に きます あ
meaning: Someone comes over here (towards the speaker)!

kanji: すみません誰かいませんか
hiragana: すみません だれか いません か
meaning: Excuse me! Isn't someone here?!

hiragana: なにか あった の
meaning: Literally, this translates to: Was something there? It's the Japanese way to ask: Did something happen? Was there something that bothered you? nanika: something (it's nani + ka, but I spell it together, because it's also found like this in the dictionary. Remember: Japanese has no whitespaces, so don't worry about this).

hiragana: なにか ありました か
meaning: Literally, this translates to: Was something there? It's the Japanese way to ask: Did something happen? Was there something that bothered you? The same as before, just a little more polite. nanika: something (it's nani + ka, but I spell it together, because it's also found like this in the dictionary. Remember: Japanese has no whitespaces, so don't worry about this).

hiragana: おれ に なにか した の か
romaji: ore ni nanika shita no ka
meaning: Did [you] do something to me? nanika: something (it's nani + ka, but I spell it together, because it's also found like this in the dictionary. Remember: Japanese has no whitespaces, so don't worry about this).

hiragana: おれ が なにか した か
meaning: Did I do something [wrong]?

hiragana: ひと は いつか しぬ
meaning: As for humans, [they] die someday. itsuka: someday

hiragana: いつか み に きて
meaning: Someday come to see.
source: Terrace House-Boys x Girls Next Door

kanji: でもいつか知るんだし
hiragana: でも いつか しる ん だ し
romaji: demo itsuka shiru n da shi
meaning: ...but someday [you] will know.

kanji: どこかに遊びに行かない
hiragana: どこか に あそび に いかない
meaning: [Why] don't [we] go somewhere on a trip / go to visit? dokoka: somewhere (Refresher: "asobi ni iku" means: to go on a trip / to go to visit someone, it's a set phrase).
source: The World God Only Knows S3 (jp eng)

kanji: それがこの町のどこかにある
hiragana: それ が この まち の どこか に ある
romaji: sore ga kono machi no dokoka ni aru
meaning: That thing (on the listener's mind) is somewhere in this city. Note the interesting way to express "somewhere in this city" using the "no"-particle (city no somewhere). Remark: "sore" does not only mean that something is physically close to the listener, but the meaning is rather figurative. It's indicating an item or person near the listener, the action of the listener, or something on their mind.

kanji: どこかにいるはずだ絶対にいる
hiragana: どこか に いる はず だ ぜったい に いる
romaji: dokoka ni iru hazu da zettai ni iru
meaning: [He] should be somewhere! [He should] absolutely be there! hazu: should (be) -> this will be covered in more detail later.
source: JoJos Bizarre Adventure 黄金の風 (1-25)

hiragana: だれも いない
meaning: Nobody here? daremo: nobody (in negative sentence), everybody (in positive sentence, rare though)
source: BOFURI - Itai no wa Iya nano de Bougyoryoku ni Kyokufuri Shitai to Omoimasu (ep 1-12 w_en)

hiragana: いま は だれも いません
meaning: As for now, [there's] noone there.

hiragana: だれも がんばってる
meaning: Everybody is doing [their] best. As a rule of thumb, "daremo" is more often used in negative sentences, where it means "noone". It can, however, also be used in positive sentences like this one. Remember that we already had "minna" to express "everybody", which is used more often.

hiragana: だれも こない な
meaning: Noone comes.

hiragana: ここ は だれも こない し
meaning: As for here, noone comes -> nobody comes to this place. We already had "shi" on an earlier card, it marks an incomplete list of of reasons in this case and will be covered again later. For this sentence, the speaker maybe tries to convince someone that this is a good place: Noone comes and sees what we're doing here (among other reasons).
source: Higurashi no Naku Koro ni S1 (JP Eng)

kanji: 君は悪くない誰も悪くない
hiragana: きみ は わるくない だれも わるくない
meaning: As for you, [you are] not at fault. Noone's at fault.

kanji: 誰も知るはずがありません
hiragana: だれも しる はず が ありません
meaning: Noone should be supposed to know. hazu: should (be) We have a clause (daremo shiru), which describes "hazu", "ga arimasen" then states that this is not there. For westerners this sounds weird, we're simply not used to express stuff this way. But you'll face many more sentences like this. If it's too difficult for now, just delete the card, it doesn't introduce anything new.
source: JoJos Bizarre Adventure 黄金の風 (1-25)

kanji: あそこには俺がいるはずだったのに｡
hiragana: あそこ に は おれ が いる はず だった のに ｡
romaji: asoko ni ha ore ga iru hazu datta noni ｡
meaning: [I didn't go] even though [I] should have been there. hazu: should (be) noni: even though (this is introduced in more detail later)

kanji: 勝てない勝てるはずがない
hiragana: かてない かてる はず が ない
meaning: [They] can't win. [It] shouldn't be possible [for them] to win. hazu: should (be) Remark: "katenai" is the negative potential form and means "can't win". The negative is "katanai". The potential form is covered later, so please don't worry about this now. The point of this card is to remember "hazu". I didn't notice this when adding the card, this was corrected In v14.

hiragana: できる はず が ない
meaning: [You] shouldn't be able to do [this].

kanji: 悲しいはずはないだろ
hiragana: かなしい はず は ない だろ
meaning: [This] shouldn't be sad/sorrowful. darou: seems; I think; I guess; sometimes also used to seek agreement: right?; don't you agree?

kanji: 誰もいない恐ろしい世界で
hiragana: だれも いない おそろしい せかい で
meaning: It's a scary world where nobody lives [and we have to live in it now]. Literally: It's a "noone-there-scary-world..." [and we have to live in it now]. Again, if it's too weird or you don't get it, just delete this card.

hiragana: なにも できない
meaning: [Someone] can't do anything. nanimo: nothing, (not) anything In contrast to daremo, nanimo is exclusively used in negative sentences. It always means "nothing" or "(not) anything". Just in case you're wondering how to express "everything" in Japanese: We already had one example (subete), I'll add more on separate cards soon!

hiragana: おれ は なにも しらない
meaning: As for me, [I] don't know anything. nanimo: nothing, (not) anything In contrast to daremo, nanimo is exclusively used in negative sentences. It always means "nothing" or "(not) anything". Just in case you're wondering how to express "everything" in Japanese: We already had one example (subete), I'll add more on separate cards soon!

kanji: 僕は君のこと何も知らないんだな
hiragana: ぼく は きみ の こと なにも しらない ん だ な
romaji: boku ha kimi no koto nanimo shiranai n da na
meaning: As for me, [I] don't know anything about you (in an explanatory tone). The "about you" is not explicitly stated here. There are words for this in Japanese, but expressing it like this is perfectly fine.

kanji: 私バカだから自分のこと何も知らなかった
hiragana: わたし ばか だ から じぶん の こと なにも しらなかった
romaji: watashi baka da kara jibun no koto nanimo shiranakatta
meaning: Because I am an idiot, [I] didn't know anything [about] me. Sounds a bit weird without context. The speaker is surprised about not having noticed something and is pondering about the reasons. Just delete this sentence if it's too difficult or doesn't make sense, it doesn't add anything new.

hiragana: でも なにも みなかった
meaning: ...but [I] didn't see anything.

hiragana: なにも たべない の
meaning: [You] don't eat anything (in tone asking for explanation)?

kanji: ごめんなさい何もない
hiragana: ごめんなさい なにも ない
meaning: "nanimo nai" literally means "nothing is there". The speaker says: Sorry, [it's] nothing.

hiragana: な なにも ない です
meaning: It's nothing [forget about it]!

hiragana: なにも かいません よ
meaning: The kid wants her robot servant to go somewhere and buy something. She answers: [I] don't buy anything!

kanji: でもあそこには何もないわよ
hiragana: でも あそこ に は なにも ない わ よ
romaji: demo asoko ni ha nanimo nai wa yo
meaning: As for "over there", nothing there. asoko: over there (distant from listener and speaker). This again follows the same "positional" pattern as achira, kochira, sochira.
source: blood c the last dark (jp eng)

hiragana: ぜんぶ あなた の せい
meaning: Everything is your fault! Remember: It's not very common and sometimes rude to address someone directly with "anata - you". But the speaker is pointing a gun at the people here, so he probably doesn't care anyways... ;). zenbu: everything; all; entire; whole; altogether

kanji: ごめんなさい私が全部悪いです
hiragana: ごめんなさい わたし が ぜんぶ わるい です
romaji: gomennasai watashi ga zenbu warui desu
meaning: Sorry, everything is my fault! Note that "zenbu" does not just simply mean "everything". It rather carries the meaning of "something in its completeness", have a look at the dictionary. So while this sentence can be translated like above, a more accurate translation would be: Sorry, I am completely to blame. Don't worry about this, the meaning is pretty much the same and the meaning of "zenbu" is pretty much always clear from context!

kanji: 全部お前のせいじゃないか
hiragana: ぜんぶ おまえ の せい じゃない か
romaji: zenbu omae no sei janai ka
meaning: Everything is your fault, isn't it?! Remark: "omae no sei janai" means: It isn't your fault. When used as a question like in this sentence however, "janai (ka)" often translates to the English "isn't it".
source: Kokoro ga Sakebitagatterunda (Anthem of the Heart)

hiragana: もう みました ぜんぶ
meaning: [I] already saw [it], everything. Or: I've already seen everything.

kanji: この時間が全てじゃない
hiragana: この じかん が すべて じゃない
meaning: This time isn't everything (in a sense: There's more to come). It seems like the two are having a good time.

kanji: 全ての問題は人間の心から来るんだよ
hiragana: すべて の もんだい は にんげん の こころ から くる ん だ よ
romaji: subete no mondai ha ningen no kokoro kara kuru n da yo
meaning: As for all problems, [they] come from the heart of humans. Seems like humans are to blame for something here. If the sentence is too weird, delete it! It didn't add any new points.

hiragana: すべて を うしなう か
meaning: [We] lose everything (profits, achievements, whatever)?
source: 今からあなたを脅迫します

kanji: ええあなたどこも怪我はない
hiragana: ええ あなた どこも けが は ない
romaji: ee anata dokomo kega ha nai
meaning: You are injured nowhere -> literally: You, injury nowhere present. dokomo: everywhere or nowhere (in negative sentence) kega: injury, hurt

kanji: 海の匂いってどこも同じね
hiragana: うみ の におい って どこも おなじ ね
romaji: umi no nioi tte dokomo onaji ne
meaning: As for the smell of the sea, it's the same everywhere, isn't it. tte: casual topic marker nioi: smell

kanji: いつものことじゃないですか
hiragana: いつも の こと じゃない です か
romaji: itsumo no koto janai desu ka
meaning: Isn't [it] the same thing as always? We already had itsu + mo on a previous card: It almost always means "always" and pretty much never means "never". Some more words on how to say "never" follow soon.

hiragana: いつも ありがとう
meaning: Always thank you.

kanji: ここいつもの図書館だ
hiragana: ここ いつも の としょかん だ
meaning: As for here, [it] is the same library as always. Note the interesting way for expressing "same xxx as always" using the "no"-particle.

kanji: 男の人はいつもずるい
hiragana: おとこ の ひと は いつも ずるい
romaji: otoko no hito ha itsumo zurui
meaning: Guys are always sly/dishonest. Maybe someone cheated on her. zurui: sly; cunning; sneaky; crafty; unfair; dishonest

hiragana: いつも の あさ です
meaning: It's the same morning as always (I guess the speaker refers to some morning routine, which is always the same). asa: morning

kanji: 今まで全然気付かなかった
hiragana: いま まで ぜんぜん きづかなかった
meaning: Until now [I] totally did not notice (or never noticed). zenzen: (not) at all / totally (not) (in negative sentence) In Japanese you can use "zenzen" + negative sentence to express "never" - just in case you've been wondering. This pattern is quite common, we already had it in the context of question words a few cards ago.

kanji: 友達も全然いないみたい
hiragana: ともだち も ぜんぜん いない みたい
meaning: Friends totally not exist, it seems - or less literal: It seems like [he] does not have any friends. mitai: seems like -> this will be covered in more detail again later. Moreover, ignore the "mo" for now: It's often used in negative sentences like this.

hiragana: ぜんぜん うれしくない よ
meaning: [Something] is totally not happy; glad; joyful.

hiragana: ぜんぜん だめ
meaning: [Something is] totally not good, maybe something that was suggested or done by someone. In Japanese, you can also use this to express that something is not possible or to refuse to do something. dame: no good

hiragana: ぜんぜん かまいません
meaning: [I] totally don't mind. kamau: to mind

hiragana: だれ でも いい よ
meaning: Anyone is ok, anyone can do this job. dare demo: anyone / whoever

kanji: パンダくん誰でもいいの
hiragana: ぱんだ くん だれ でも いい の
romaji: panda kun dare demo ii no
meaning: The panda in this anime is a totally lazy bum. In this episode hovever, he'd like to become an apprentice in order to learn something. The waitress asks: Panda, is anyone ok [as teacher]?

hiragana: だれ でも できる し
meaning: Anyone can do this, among other reasons. shi: one reason out of many
source: 私に天使が舞い降りた! (wataten)

hiragana: だれ でも いい です か
meaning: The conversation is revolving around kissing and the question, if you'd kiss anyone. The speaker asks: Is anyone [really] ok?

kanji: いつでも相手になるよ
hiragana: いつ でも あいて に なる よ
romaji: itsu demo aite ni naru yo
meaning: [Let's] become partners any time. itsudemo: any time

kanji: ええっていつでも飲みに来てな
hiragana: ええ って いつ でも のみ に きて な
romaji: ee tte itsu demo nomi ni kite na
meaning: [A: Thank you for so many cups of tea! B:] It's ok, come to drink whenever [you like]. itsudemo: any time Remark: "ee tte" is kansai dialect and means "ii yo".

hiragana: いつ でも いい よ
meaning: Any time is ok. itsudemo: any time
source: Terrace House- Boys & Girls in the City

hiragana: どこ でも いい よ
meaning: Anywhere [is] ok. dokodemo: anywhere / wereever
source: Terrace House- Boys & Girls in the City

hiragana: どこ でも いく ぞ
meaning: [Let's] go anywhere! A weird sentence, but it looks like these people are about to fight and ready to go anywhere.

kanji: 俺よく分からないからどこでもいいよ
hiragana: おれ よく わからない から どこ でも いい よ
romaji: ore yoku wakaranai kara doko demo ii yo
meaning: Looks like they want to go out in order to do something, but haven't decided where to go yet. The speaker says: Because I don't know anything [about it], anywhere is ok.
source: Wotakoi Otaku ni Koi ha Muzukashii

kanji: 別にどこでもいいじゃないですか
hiragana: べつに どこ でも いい じゃない です か
romaji: betsuni doko demo ii janai desu ka
meaning: Isn't anywhere ok?

kanji: どこでもいいです私は
hiragana: どこ でも いい です わたし は
romaji: doko demo ii desu watashi ha
meaning: As for me, anywhere is ok.

hiragana: かんたん な こと だ よ
meaning: [Something] is an easy thing [to do]. kantan: simple; easy; uncomplicated

hiragana: おかしい です よ ね
meaning: [It's] strange, isn't it! okashii: strange; odd

hiragana: つぎ は ぼく だ
meaning: As for next, it's me -> It's my turn now. tsugi: next; following; subsequent

hiragana: わたし は げんき です
