meaning: As for me, I'm good! genki: healthy; well; fit Translating this to English literally sounds a bit weird: "I'm healthy". It's a common way to say: I'm good!

hiragana: きょう は あたたかい な
meaning: As for today, it's warm (in a pleasant way), isn't it. atatakai: warm; mild; (pleasantly) hot

hiragana: きょう も あつい ね
meaning: Today's hot too, isn't it. atsui: hot (temperature, not in a too pleasant way)

kanji: 今日はとても暑いですね
hiragana: きょう は とても あつい です ね
romaji: kyou ha totemo atsui desu ne
meaning: As for today, [it] is extremely hot, isn't it?

hiragana: とても つめたい ひと です
meaning: [Someone] is a cold person. tsumetai: (emotionally) cold "tsumetai" also refers to temperature.
source: ぼくたちは勉強ができない

kanji: 友達が最近冷たいんだ
hiragana: ともだち が さいきん つめたい ん だ
romaji: tomodachi ga saikin tsumetai n da
meaning: [My] friends are cold recently. saikin: recently

hiragana: あいかわらず つめたい ね
meaning: [She is] cold as usual, isn't [she]. aikawarazu: as ever; as usual

kanji: はいちょっと冷たいですよ
hiragana: はい ちょっと つめたい です よ
meaning: The doctor is touching the patient with something cold and wants to express: It's getting cold now... tsumetai: cold (to the touch) chotto: a little; a bit; slightly​ You can't use "tsumetai" for the temperature outside, see next card!

hiragana: さむい です
meaning: It's cold! samui: cold (e.g. weather)

hiragana: さむい よ ここ は さむい よ
romaji: samui yo koko ha samui yo
meaning: It's cold! As for this place (close to the speaker), it's cold!

kanji: さすがにちょっと寒いですね
hiragana: さすが に ちょっと さむい です ね
romaji: sasuga ni chotto samui desu ne
meaning: As you'd expect, it is a bit cold [here]. sasuga: as one would expect; just as you'd expect If you wonder about the difference to "tashika ni", have a look at the reference. If you don't know this word yet: It's covered in about 2000 cards, you'll find the reference again then.

hiragana: ぶしつ は さむい から な
meaning: [It's uncomfortable in here] because the club room is cold. bushitsu: club room "butshitsu" might sound like an unusual word, but if you like school-related anime, you'll definitely hear this, because extracurricular activities are very common in Japan. Moreover, "bu" means "club" and "shitsu" means room (do you remember the word for bedroom from an earlier card?). Note that "shitsu" is used in compound words like this and rather not as standalone word for room. I'll add this a few cards later. Note that Tae Kim covers "kara" later. It usually connects two sentences in the following fashion: Reason kara result, meaning: because of reason, result happened. If the result is clear from context, it is often omitted, just as in this example. I'll pick this up in more detail later.

kanji: 毎日こんなに寒いのか
hiragana: まいにち こんなに さむい の か
meaning: Every day [it's] cold like this?! konnani: like this; in this way (focused on the speaker's opinion) The intonation together with "no ka" makes the sentence sound like: "Is it really this cold every day [here]"?! Or, depending on the context: "Does it really have to be this cold every day"?!

kanji: こんなに寒いのが悪いんだ
hiragana: こんなに さむい の が わるい ん だ
romaji: konnani samui no ga warui n da
meaning: As for this cold / coldness like this, [it's] bad (in an explanatory tone). konnani: like this; in this way (focused on the speaker's opinion) Remember that "no" can also be used to nominalize adjectives (samui) in order to append noun-related particles.

hiragana: さむい わ この へや
meaning: [It's] cold, this room [I mean]. heya: room Remarks: heya is a more general word for "room" and used to refer to rooms in general. The "shitsu" from previous cards is rather not used like this, it usually occurs as suffix. The "wa" in here is the feminine sentence ending particle. It's in the middle, because the speaker seems to have forgotten the context: Note the pause after "samui wa". Have a look at the references for a repetition.

hiragana: そんなに うれしい か
meaning: [Are you] really that happy? sonnani: so much; so; like that (focused on the listener's opinion)

hiragana: そんなに たいせつ な もの
meaning: [Is it really] such an important thing? sonnani: so much; so; like that (focused on the listener's opinion)

hiragana: そんなに つよい の か
meaning: [Is it (drink, opponent, whatever) really] that strong?

kanji: そんなに長くなかったね
hiragana: そんなに ながくなかった ね
meaning: [Something] was not that long, was it?

kanji: よく食べるなそんなにうまいか
hiragana: よく たべる な そんなに うまい か
romaji: yoku taberu na sonnani umai ka
meaning: [You] eat [this] frequently, [is it] that tasty? yoku: properly, well / frequently, often Remember: "yoku" is the irregular conjugation of the adjective "ii - good, excellent, fine" to an adverb (i.e. it describes a verb in this case). Note that it can also be translated to "frequently, often", which fits in this case. umai: tasty - same meaning as "oishii".

kanji: 実はそんなに長くない
hiragana: じつ は そんなに ながくない
meaning: Actually, [it] is not that long. jitsu: truth, reality. Note that this dictionary definition of "jitsu" is a bit technical. This word occurs together with the "ha" particle most of the time and almost always translates to "actually", "in fact" or "to tell you the truth". Therefore, "jitsu ha" also has its own dictionary entry.
source: Boku no Hero Academia S2 (ep 1-25 jp_en)

hiragana: あんなにかんたん に
meaning: In this example, the speaker seems to watch something happening at a certain distance. E.g. someone is doing something without much effort. Then he states: [did he really do it] that easily? annani: to that extent; to that degree; so much; so konnani, sonnani and annani follow the usual pattern of kore, sore and are. I.e. they refer to something related to the speaker, the listener or something unrelated. The actual verb is omitted here, which is common in conversations. Just imagine a "shimashita" in the end.

hiragana: まけた の か
meaning: [You were] defeated? makeru: to lose; to be defeated

hiragana: あんなに はやい あいて に
meaning: [I was defeated] by an opponent that fast (with "that fast" referring to the opponent). During a natural conversation you often find incomplete sentences like this. Just add the "maketa" from the last card in the end and it makes more sense: The card doesn't add anything new, just delete it if it makes no sense.

hiragana: ちょっと
meaning: chotto not only means "a little; a bit; slightly​" as introduced on an earlier card, but it also means "hey! come on!" In the sense of "wait a minute" or "give me a break".

hiragana: ほんとう だ よ
meaning: It's the truth! hontou: truth; reality; actuality; fact What's the difference between "jitsu" and "hontou"? As already mentioned a few cards before, "jitsu" is usually used like the English "actually" or "in fact". hontou is used in a very similar way, but emphasizes "truth without lying" a bit more. Have a look at this question for more details. As usual, don't focus on speaking yourself yet. It's usually very easy to get the meaning from context by just listening to many examples!

hiragana: ほんとう です か
meaning: Truth?! -> Is [this really] true? hontou: truth; reality; actuality; fact

hiragana: ほんとう です こまります
meaning: Is [this] true? [Now we're] in trouble! komaru: to be troubled; to have difficulty

hiragana: ほんとうに ごめん ね
meaning: I'm really sorry! hontouni: really, truly As a rule of thumb, "hontou" = truth, reality and "hontouni" = really. I never actually thought about the grammar of "hontou + ni", which I think is "na-adjective + ni = adverb", but this phrase often describes non-verbs, too. Just stick to the rule of thumb, it's usually very easy to understand. If you're really into grammar, I added two links to Japanese stackexchange below, but the answers there are not very sharp either. Don't worry and keep going :).

hiragana: ほんとうに ありがとう
meaning: Thank you [I am really grateful].

hiragana: ほんとうに うまかった よ
meaning: [It] was really tasty.

meaning: Thank you [I am really grateful].

kanji: よく頑張ったよ本当に

meaning: [You] well hung in there. Really! [You] well did your best. Really! Or less literal: You really did your best!

kanji: 本当に恐ろしかったんだ
hiragana: ほんとうに おそろしかった ん だ
meaning: [It] was really scary.
source: JoJos Bizzare Adventure スターダストクルセイダース

kanji: 困ります本当に困ります
hiragana: こまります ほんとうに こまります
meaning: [We are] in trouble. Really in trouble.

hiragana: ほんとうに あつくない
meaning: [Is it] really not hot? atsui/暑い: hot (weather) atsui/熱い: hot (to the touch) Note that "atsui" refers to both weather and touching things. In kanji however, the words are spelled differently. Here, the speaker (i.e. the child kneeling on the floor) was trying to touch the flame of a candle and asked if it was really OK to touch it.

hiragana: なんで わらう
meaning: Why [do you] laugh? warau: to laugh

hiragana: ほんとうに わらわない
meaning: [You] really don't laugh [if I tell you]?

kanji: 誰か見ませんでしたか
hiragana: だれ か みません でした か
meaning: Didn't [you] see someone? Refresher: "mimasen deshita" is the grammatically correct teineigo-past of "miru". In spoken Japanese, you'd probably rather hear: "dareka minakatta desu"?

kanji: お父さんが誰かと来たの
hiragana: おとうさん が だれ か と きた の
romaji: otousan ga dare ka to kita no
meaning: Did [your] father come together with someone?

kanji: かわいくてすてきです
hiragana: かわいくて すてき です
meaning: [Something] is cute and lovely. You can connect an i-adjective (or a sentence ending on an i-adjective) "x" to another sentence "y" by replacing -i with -kute. The meaning becomes "x and y". This grammar part is commonly referred to as "te-form".

hiragana: くらくて あぶない から
meaning: [Don't go in there] because it is dark and dangerous. You can connect an i-adjective (or a sentence ending on an i-adjective) "x" to another sentence "y" by replacing -i with -kute. The meaning becomes "x and y". This grammar part is commonly referred to as "te-form". Remark: abunai is not a negative word, it means: dangerous.

kanji: 温かくて本当によかった
hiragana: あたたかくて ほんとうに よかった
meaning: The guy is talking about his hand. For some reason, [it] is warm and [this] was great -> He's glad that his hand is warm. You can connect an i-adjective (or a sentence ending on an i-adjective) "x" to another sentence "y" by replacing -i with -kute. The meaning becomes "x and y". This grammar part is commonly referred to as "te-form".

kanji: すごい冷たくて甘いですよこれ
hiragana: すごい つめたくて あまい です よ これ
romaji: sugoi tsumetakute amai desu yo kore
meaning: Amazing, [it, judging from the picture maybe ice cream] is cold and sweet. amai: sweet You can connect an i-adjective (or a sentence ending on an i-adjective) "x" to another sentence "y" by replacing -i with -kute. The meaning becomes "x and y". This grammar part is commonly referred to as "te-form".

kanji: 天気がよくて気持ちいいね
hiragana: てんき が よくて きもちいい ね
meaning: The weather is great and [this is] feeling good. kimochiii: good feeling; feeling good (from kimochi - feeling, sensation + ii - good) You can connect an i-adjective (or a sentence ending on an i-adjective) "x" to another sentence "y" by replacing -i with -kute. The meaning becomes "x and y". This grammar part is commonly referred to as "te-form".

kanji: 優しくてすてきな人だなあって
hiragana: やさしくて すてき な ひと だ なあ って
romaji: yasashikute suteki na hito da naa tte
meaning: [He] is a kind and lovely person, isn't he. yasashii: tender; kind; gentle You can connect an i-adjective (or a sentence ending on an i-adjective) "x" to another sentence "y" by replacing -i with -kute. The meaning becomes "x and y". This grammar part is commonly referred to as "te-form".

kanji: ん甘くておいしいです
hiragana: ん あまくて おいしい です
meaning: [It] is sweet and tasty. You can connect an i-adjective (or a sentence ending on an i-adjective) "x" to another sentence "y" by replacing -i with -kute. The meaning becomes "x and y". This grammar part is commonly referred to as "te-form".

hiragana: あまくて うまい ぞ
meaning: [It] is sweet and delicious. umai and oishii can both refer to delicious food. umai also can mean "skillfull, clever", see next card.

hiragana: うまい よ わたし
meaning: Skilled! Me, I mean. -> I'm skilled! I guess it's clear that she's not saying: "I'm tasty" here ;). The "umai" sounds a little bit like "komai", but it is indeed "umai". Sometimes, this is caused by background noise, music or others speaking, don't worry about this. The card is from mitsuboshi colors, ep. 8 around 11:50 if you want to check yourself.

hiragana: せまくて わるい ね
meaning: [This place] is small and bad, isn't it. semai: narrow; confined; small

hiragana: おおきくて おもい
meaning: [It] is big and heavy. This anime revolves around music in a school orchestra, so I guess they are talking about an instrument. omoi: heavy

kanji: やっぱりすごく嬉しくて
hiragana: やっぱり すごく うれしくて
meaning: After all, [you] are very happy (and then the speaker gets doubts: Aren't you?) yappari: as expected, after all Note, that "sugoi" as a matter of expressing "very" is casual, a more proper way would be to use "totemo". Reminder: Replacing "i" of an i-adjective with "ku" makes it an adverb, which allows to describe a verb. By now I guess you got the pattern: All of the previous -kute examples could be translated to "x and y". Due to this "and"-nature, you'll often find the -te form at the end of an incomplete sentence (like in this example), indicating that the speaker is unsure or might want to add something else. Especially in this sentence, this is also clear from the intonation.

hiragana: しろくて つめたくて
meaning: [It's] white, cold and (...maybe something else will be added due to the ending -te). shiroi: white

kanji: 静かで悪くない部屋だ
hiragana: しずか で わるくない へや だ
meaning: [This] room is quiet and not so bad. The same chaining that we had for sentences ending on an i-adjective can be done for na-adjectives and nouns by appending "de" (to "shizuka" in this case):

kanji: キレイで優しいさわ子先生はどこに
hiragana: きれい で やさしい さわこ せんせい は どこ に
romaji: kirei de yasashii sawako sensei ha doko ni
meaning: As for the lovely and kind sawako sensei, where [is she / did she go]? This refers to the character of the teacher, it seems like the teacher somehow changed, the speaker sounds pretty disappointed. yasashii: tender; kind; gentle The same chaining that we had for sentences ending on an i-adjective can be done for na-adjectives and nouns by appending "de". Reminder: Even though "kirei" ends on an i, it is still a na-adjective.

kanji: きれいで楽しくてカッコよくて
hiragana: きれい で たのしくて かっこよくて
meaning: [Someone seems to be] lovely, cheerful and stylish. kakkoii: attractive; good-looking; stylish; cool (conjugated like ii) Here we have a chain of both na- and i-adjectives.

kanji: 髪が長くてキレイで優しい
hiragana: かみ が ながくて きれい で やさしい
romaji: kami ga nagakute kirei de yasashii
meaning: [Her] hair is long, lovely and tender. kami: hair

kanji: 朝ごはん食べて学校いくよ
hiragana: あさごはん たべて がっこう いく よ
meaning: [I] eat breakfast and go to school. asagohan: breakfast (it's "asa - morning" + "gohan - meal") The te-form also exists for verbs: Conjugate the verb to past tense (e.g. taberu -> tabeta) and replace "ta" by "te". The meaning is the same as for the adjective examples here: The -te form connects the first sentence (asagohan (wo) tabete) to the second one (gakkou (ni) iku) by means of "and". Note that some particles are missing here.

kanji: 朝ごはん食べてこなかったの
hiragana: あさごはん たべて こなかった の
meaning: [You] ate breakfast and did not come? (maybe she missed the first lesson at school). asagohan: breakfast The te-form also exists for verbs: Conjugate the verb to past tense (e.g. taberu -> tabeta) and replace "ta" by "te".

hiragana: ごはん たべて のんで
meaning: [I go there and] eat a meal and drink [...and maybe have a dessert]. gohan: meal The te-form also exists for verbs: Conjugate the verb to past tense (e.g. nomu -> nonda) and replace "da" by "de". When the past ends on "da" instead of "ta", you attach "de" instead of "te".
source: Terrace House- Boys & Girls in the City

hiragana: たべなくて よかった
meaning: [I] didn't eat [it] and this was good -> I'm happy that I didn't eat it. The -te form also exists for negative verbs and is built in a similar way as for the adjectives: Take the negative verb (taberu -> tabenai) and replace "i" with "kute". Or: Replace the "nai" of the negative form with "nakute". The -te form does not have a past tense. The tense is determined by the last verb, see ref.

kanji: 今日はもう疲れたから帰って寝る
hiragana: きょう は もう つかれた から かえって ねる
romaji: kyou ha mou tsukareta kara kaette neru
meaning: As for today, because [I am] already tired, [I] go home and sleep. kara: because; it can connect two sentences in the following sense: reason kara result, the meaning always is: Because of reason, result happens. Note that the result may be omitted, if it's clear from context. Note that we already had "kara" on previous cards in different roles: To state a relative time (asa kara - since morning) or a direction (gakkou kara - from school).

kanji: 疲れたから私は寝るぞ
hiragana: つかれた から わたし は ねる ぞ
romaji: tsukareta kara watashi ha neru zo
meaning: Because [I] became tired, [I] sleep. kara: because; it can connect two sentences in the following sense: reason kara result, the meaning always is: Because of reason, result happens. Note that the result may be omitted, if it's clear from context. In English, this can also translate to "so": I became tired, so I sleep.

kanji: 食べたことないから楽しみだね
hiragana: たべた こと ない から たのしみ だ ね
romaji: tabeta koto nai kara tanoshimi da ne
meaning: Very interesting sentence, it means: I'm excited to eat this, because I never ate it before. "tabeta koto nai" -> [I] ate [it]-thing not there -> I never ate this. "tanoshimi da" -> excitement is there -> I'm excited. "kara" links the first as reason to the second. Reminder: "koto" is a very generic sort of placeholder noun used to refer to a "thing" or "matter". The matter is usually described by a clause, just as in this example. Some more "koto"-examples follow soon.

kanji: ちょっと疲れたから休憩
hiragana: ちょっと つかれた から きゅうけい
meaning: [Let's] take a break because [I] became a bit tired. Maybe you noticed an interesting pattern: In English, you'd rather say: I do x because of y. In Japanese, this is usually expressed vice versa. You'll notice this many times, Jay Rubin's book "Making Sense of Japanese" has an entire chapter dedicated to this. This book is totally worth reading, but not for beginners. I'll recommend it again at the end of this course.

hiragana: あぶない から
meaning: [Don't go there] because it is dangerous. In this sentence, the result of our pattern "reason kara result" is omitted, because it seems to be clear from context.

hiragana: なかま だ から な
meaning: [It's no problem] because [he] is [my] comrade. Note that if the reason for something ends on a noun, you usually add "da" before "kara": Without the "da", this might sound like kara in the role of "from", i.e. I received something from my comrade.

hiragana: ともだち だ から だ よ
meaning: [It's no problem] because [I] am [your] friend. Note that if the reason for something ends on a noun, you usually add "da" before "kara": Without the "da", this might sound like kara in the role of "from", i.e. I received something from my comrade.

hiragana: しごと だ から な
meaning: [I can't go] because of work. Note that if the reason for something ends on a noun, you usually add "da" before "kara": Without the "da", this might sound like kara in the role of "from", i.e. I received something from my comrade.
source: JoJos Bizarre Adventure 黄金の風 (26-39)

hiragana: いい から いい から
meaning: ii kara: never mind that; don't worry about that Note that in some cases, "kara" is used to express sympathy and can't be directly translated to "because / from / since".

hiragana: たき いま いくいく から
meaning: Taki [character name], I['ll] go now, I go [there now to rescue you]. Note that in some cases, "kara" is used to express sympathy and can't be directly translated to "because / from / since". An example is this sentence, the guy is hurrying to save taki from an evil spirit.

kanji: 映画で見たことがある
hiragana: えいが で みた こと が ある
romaji: eiga de mita koto ga aru
meaning: [I] saw [it] in a movie-thing is there -> I saw it in a movie. Reminder: "koto" is a very generic sort of placeholder noun used to refer to a "thing" or "matter". The matter is usually described by a clause, just as in this example. Tae Kim covers this much later, but it's very easy useful.
source: JoJos Bizarre Adventure 黄金の風 (1-25)

kanji: 会ったことがあるのか
hiragana: あった こと が ある の か
romaji: atta koto ga aru no ka
meaning: Met-thing exists? -> Did you meet him? Reminder: "koto" is a very generic sort of placeholder noun used to refer to a "thing" or "matter". The matter is usually described by a clause, just as in this example. Tae Kim covers this much later, but it's very easy useful.

kanji: テレビで見たことがあるぞ
hiragana: てれび で みた こと が ある ぞ
romaji: terebi de mita koto ga aru zo
meaning: Saw on tv-thing exists -> I already saw it on TV. terebi: television

kanji: この道来たことがあるな
hiragana: この みち きた こと が ある な
romaji: kono michi kita koto ga aru na
meaning: Came to this street-thing exists -> I've already been to this street before. michi: road; path; street Pay attention to the past tense of "kuru - to come, to visit" here (kita) and keep this in mind for the next card.

hiragana: きいた こと が ある
meaning: Heard-thing exists -> I've heard that before. kiku: to hear, to listen to something The past tense of kuru and kiku sound very similar and are sometimes hard to distinguish. The "i" is pronounced longer for "kiku".
source: JoJos Bizzare Adventure スターダストクルセイダース

hiragana: きいた こと が ある か
meaning: Did you [already] hear about this?

kanji: うんそれは俺も聞いたことがある
hiragana: うん それ は おれ も きいた こと が ある
romaji: un sore ha ore mo kiita koto ga aru
meaning: As for this, I also heard-thing is there -> I've also heard of this.
source: Legend of the Galactic Heroes (JP Eng) (Media Added)

kanji: 一度聞いたことがある
hiragana: いちど きいた こと が ある
meaning: Once heard-thing is there -> I heard about this once. ichido: once; one time; on one occasion

kanji: そっちの２人は見たことがあるな
hiragana: そっち の ふたり は みた こと が ある な
romaji: socchi no futari ha mita koto ga aru na
meaning: As for those two over there (close to the listener), [I] saw-matter exists -> I've already seen these two over there. futari: two persons, two people, couple

kanji: 味わったことがあるのか
hiragana: あじわった こと が ある の か
romaji: ajiwatta koto ga aru no ka
meaning: Tasted-thing exists? -> Have you tasted this (food) before? ajiwau: to taste; to savor I hope you get the pattern by now, some more "koto" sentences follow and then we'll continue with compound sentences.

kanji: その目は見たことがある
hiragana: その め は みた こと が ある
romaji: sono me ha mita koto ga aru
meaning: As for those eyes, I've already seen them. me: eye, eyes

kanji: 一度だけ見たことがある
hiragana: いちど だけ みた こと が ある
romaji: ichido dake mita koto ga aru
meaning: Saw only once-thing is there -> I've seen this only once. dake: only I think Tae Kim covers "dake" in more detail later, but this sentence fits in here well.

kanji: 綾野さんのおばあさんの
hiragana: あやの さん の おばあさん の
meaning: [This item] is ayano's grandmother's? obaasan: grandmother Remark: The trailing "no" here is not the explanatory one, this is something I forgot to explain. If the explanatory "no" follows a noun or a na-adjective, there's a "na" added in between to distinguish it from the "no" used for linking a property. Don't worry about this for now, more examples are added soon. Tae Kim explains this here.

kanji: おばあちゃんから聞いたことがあるの
hiragana: おばあちゃん から きいた こと が ある の
romaji: obaachan kara kiita koto ga aru no
meaning: [I] heard [this] from grandma-matter exists -> I heard this from grandma (in an explanatory tone). obaachan: cute / familiar way to refer to a grandmother

hiragana: あるばいと
meaning: arubaito: part time job This word is derived from the German word "Arbeit", which means "work, job". While this refers to a full-time job in German, it's just a part time job in Japanese. Japanese people are known to work hard, after all ;).

hiragana: ばいと
meaning: baito: short for arubaito (part time job) This abbreviation is more common.

hiragana: きょう も ばいと
meaning: Work today, too? -> You're also working today (part time)?
source: Higurashi no Naku Koro ni S1 (JP Eng)

hiragana: おふろ に も いません
meaning: [He] is not in the bathroom either. ofuro: bath, room where people take a bath

kanji: 私とごはんを食べませんか
hiragana: わたし と ごはん を たべません か
romaji: watashi to gohan wo tabemasen ka
meaning: Don't you want to eat with me?

kanji: とても強いので注意を
hiragana: とても つよい ので ちゅうい を
meaning: Because [it / someone] is very strong, be careful. chuui: caution; being careful; attention "node/ので" can be used to indicate a reason in the same way as "kara/から": reason node result -> because of "reason", "result" happened. There are subtile difference between "kara" and "node": First, "kara" is more casual than "node". Second, ので puts emphasis on the reason, whereas から puts emphasis on the result. For casual listening comprehension, it's totally fine to just ignore this - have a look at the references if you want to know more.

hiragana: なまえ を つけた か
meaning: Did you attach a name [to someone] -> did you already name it? E.g. your new pet. tsukeru: to attach namae wo tsukeru: to name "tsukeru" has a lot of different meanings, just have a look at the dictionary. It is used in many different contexts, which confused me in the beginning.

kanji: 名前は俺が付けました
hiragana: なまえ は おれ が つけました
meaning: As for name, I attached it -> I named [something]. tsukeru: to attach namae wo tsukeru: to name

kanji: 名前がなかったので私がつけた
hiragana: なまえ が なかった ので わたし が つけた
romaji: namae ga nakatta node watashi ga tsuketa
meaning: Because there was no name, I attached one -> Because something didn't have a name, I named it. "node/ので" can be used to indicate a reason in the same way as "kara/から": reason node result -> because of "reason", "result" happened. There are subtile difference between "kara" and "node": First, "kara" is more casual than "node". Second, ので puts emphasis on the reason, whereas から puts emphasis on the result. For casual listening comprehension, it's totally fine to just ignore this - have a look at the references if you want to know more.

hiragana: すぐ に わすれる ので
meaning: [I write it down] because I soon will forget. Just as for "kara", the result of something may be omitted for "node", if it is clear from context:

kanji: 私はかまいませんので
hiragana: わたし は かまいません ので
meaning: [Don't worry] because I don't mind. Just as for "kara", the result of something may be omitted for "node", if it is clear from context:

hiragana: き を つける みんな
meaning: Attach you mind, everybody -> The Japanese way to say: Be careful! ki: spirit; mind; heart​
source: Boku no Hero Academia_ Futari no Hero

hiragana: なぜ うそ を つく
meaning: Why do you lie? uso: lie, sometimes also joke (noun); this is often used together with "tsuku": uso wo tsuku: to tell a lie

hiragana: うそ つかない
meaning: [You're] not lying?

hiragana: うそつき

kanji: 大きい願いはダメなの
hiragana: おおきい ねがい は だめ な の
romaji: ookii negai ha dame na no
meaning: As for a large wish/favor, is it no good / not allowed? The panda in this series is not only super lazy, but also quite demanding and wants to have a big wish granted by someone. We had "negai" as "wish, hope" before. It can also mean "favor". dame: no good, not allowed, not possible

hiragana: めーる の あいて だれ な の
romaji: me-ru no aite dare na no
meaning: As for mail partner, who [is it]? me-ru: email

kanji: その気持ちは分かります
hiragana: その きもち は わかります
meaning: As for that feeling [I] understand [it]. kimochi: feeling; sensation; mood; state of mind Remember kimochiii from an earlier card? Now you know where it comes from: kimochi + ii = good feeling / mood.

hiragana: こっち に も みち が
meaning: They seem to be walking a road that's maybe not in good condition and seem to have talked about this. Then the speaker notes: "Here too road is [bad]".

kanji: わ私はなぜここにいる
hiragana: わ わたし は なぜ ここ に いる
romaji: wa watashi ha naze koko ni iru
meaning: As for me, why am I here?

hiragana: かんたん な ので いい よ
meaning: Because it's easy, it's ok -> maybe the guy was asked for a favor and answers: Ok, I do it, but only because it's easy. If "no" is used in the explanatory role after a noun or na-adjective, there's usually a "na" in front of it. Tae Kim explains the reason on p. 67 or here. Without the "na", it sounds like you'd link the noun to another thing clear from context.

kanji: 時間なので失礼します
hiragana: じかん な ので しつれいします
meaning: Because [it is] time, I go now, bye. shitsurei: discourtesy; impoliteness​ Reminder: "shitsurei shimasu" is a polite way to say goodbye. If "no" is used in the explanatory role after a noun or na-adjective, there's usually a "na" in front of it. Tae Kim explains the reason on p. 67 or here. Without the "na", it sounds like you'd link the noun to another thing clear from context.

hiragana: むかし から の ともだち な ので
romaji: mukashi kara no tomodachi na node
meaning: Because [he is] a friend from long ago [I'm looking forward to meet him]. If "no" is used in the explanatory role after a noun or na-adjective, there's usually a "na" in front of it. Tae Kim explains the reason on p. 67 or here. Without the "na", it sounds like you'd link the noun to another thing clear from context.

hiragana: なあ ほんとうに やる の か
meaning: [Do we] really do it [physical action]? yaru: to do; to undertake; to perform (for physical actions). "yaru" and "suru" have a similar meaning, but you can't just attach "yaru" to nouns the same way as "suru". It is used for physical actions only, read Tae Kim's blog post for more details. Also keep in mind that "yaru" can sound quite rude in certain contexts, this will be explained later.

hiragana: これ いつ まで やる の
meaning: This, until when do [we do] it? yaru: to do; to undertake; to perform (for physical actions). "yaru" and "suru" have a similar meaning, but you can't just attach "yaru" to nouns the same way as "suru". It is used for physical actions only, read Tae Kim's blog post for more details. Also keep in mind that "yaru" can sound quite rude in certain contexts, this will be explained later.

hiragana: あつい のに よく やる な
meaning: Even though [it is] hot, [he] does well [physical action]. noni: even though, despite. It can connect two sentences: "sentence 1" noni "sentence 2", the meaning always is: even though "sentence 1", "sentence 2" happened. The same rules as for "node" apply, see following cards.

kanji: こんなに熱いのにお茶って
hiragana: こんなに あつい のに おちゃ って
meaning: Even though [it is] this hot, tea? noni: even though, despite. It can connect two sentences: "sentence 1" noni "sentence 2", the meaning always is: even though "sentence 1", "sentence 2" happened. The same rules as for "node" apply, see following cards. ocha: tea, usually green Ignore the "tte" here, it means: "you/someone said" It will be covered later in more detail.

kanji: みんなで頑張ったのに悔しいよ
hiragana: みんな で がんばった のに くやしい よ
romaji: minna de ganbatta noni kuyashii yo
meaning: Even though [we] did our best with everybody (i.e. the whole team), it's frustrating. Maybe they lost a match. noni: even though, despite. It can connect two sentences: "sentence 1" noni "sentence 2", the meaning always is: even though "sentence 1", "sentence 2" happened. The same rules as for "node" apply, see following cards. kuyashii: annoying; frustrating

kanji: あんなに大きいのに迷子ですって
hiragana: あんなに おおきい のに まいご です って
romaji: annani ookii noni maigo desu tte
meaning: Even though [he] is that big, [he is] a lost child? -> The person that got lost is actually grown up and his friends pranked him in a department store. The speaker is seeing this person and wonders: Is he really a lost child? noni: even though, despite. It can connect two sentences: "sentence 1" noni "sentence 2", the meaning always is: even though "sentence 1", "sentence 2" happened. The same rules as for "node" apply, see following cards. maigo: lost child, lost person, stray child Ignore the "tte" here, it means: "they said"? It will be covered later in more detail.
source: Ouran High School Host Club (jp eng)

kanji: 負けたのに偉そうだニャ
hiragana: まけた のに えらそう だ にゃ
meaning: Even though [he] was defeated, [he] looks / seems to feel self-important. noni: even though, despite. It can connect two sentences: "sentence 1" noni "sentence 2", the meaning always is: even though "sentence 1", "sentence 2" happened. erasou: self-important Ignore the "nya" part.

kanji: こんなに近くにいるのにキスもできないよ
hiragana: こんなに ちかく に いる のに きす も できない よ
romaji: konnani chikaku ni iru noni kisu mo dekinai yo
meaning: Even though [they are] that close, [they] can't kiss / don't kiss. noni: even though, despite. It can connect two sentences: "sentence 1" noni "sentence 2", the meaning always is: even though "sentence 1", "sentence 2" happened. chikaku: closeness, neighborhood Ignore the "mo" for now, it's often used in negative sentences like this. It translates to something like "even", I'll add more details later.

hiragana: せっかく きた のに
meaning: [Noone is here], even though we made an effort and came. "sekkaku" usually means to make some kind of effort. I find this quite hard to translate, it's a weird word ;). Just as for "node", the result that happened "despite something" can be omitted if clear from context. sekkaku: with trouble; at great pains; specially

hiragana: うみ が ちかく に ある のに
romaji: umi ga chikaku ni aru noni
meaning: [You don't go surfing] even though the sea is close? Just as for "node", the result that happened "despite something" can be omitted if clear from context.

hiragana: おかね ない のに
meaning: [You want to buy it] even though money is not there [i.e. even though you have no money]? Just as for "node", the result that happened "despite something" can be omitted if clear from context.

hiragana: やくそく した のに
meaning: [He didn't come] even though [he] promised. Just as for "node", the result that happened "despite something" can be omitted if clear from context.

hiragana: じかん が ない のに
meaning: [Why do you complain?! I do it] even though time is not there [even though I don't have time]. Just as for "node", the result that happened "despite something" can be omitted if clear from context.

hiragana: たいせつ な もの な のに
meaning: [You lost it] even though it is an important thing? If the word before "noni" is a noun or na-adjective, there usually is a "na" in between. Don't worry about the rules too much here.

hiragana: がんばった のに
meaning: [I lost] even though [I] tried hard / did my best.

hiragana: うまい のに
meaning: [You don't want to eat this] even though [it is] tasty?

kanji: よく分からないけど全然いいよ
hiragana: よく わからない けど ぜんぜん いい よ
romaji: yoku wakaranai kedo zenzen ii yo
meaning: [I] don't understand well, but [it] is totally ok. kedo: but; it connects two sentences to indicate a contradiction.
source: Erased - 僕だけがいない街

kanji: 怖かったけど本当に優しかった
hiragana: こわかった けど ほんとうに やさしかった
meaning: [he looked] scary, but was really gentle / kind. kedo: but; it connects two sentences to indicate a contradiction.
source: Fate Stay Night Unlimited Blade Works S02 (JP Eng)

kanji: 熱はあるけど大丈夫だよ
hiragana: ねつ は ある けど だいじょうぶ だ よ
romaji: netsu ha aru kedo daijoubu da yo
meaning: As for temperature / fever, [it] is there, but [this is] ok -> He has temperature, but he's ok. Maybe they're also talking about the cow :D. kedo: but; it connects two sentences to indicate a contradiction.

kanji: 疲れたけど気持ちいいな
hiragana: つかれた けど きもちいい な
meaning: [I] became tired but [it / something] feels good / is a good feeling. kedo: but; it connects two sentences to indicate a contradiction.

kanji: 疲れたけど楽しかったね
hiragana: つかれた けど たのしかった ね
meaning: [I] became tired but it was enjoyable. kedo: but; it connects two sentences to indicate a contradiction.

kanji: ちょっと遅いけど朝ご飯
hiragana: ちょっと おそい けど あさごはん
meaning: [It is] a bit late, but [here's] breakfast.

hiragana: たべます けど
meaning: [I don't like this meal] but I eat. If the reason is clear from context, it can be omitted as usual.

hiragana: なまえ は おなじ だ けど
meaning: [It looks different] but as for name, [it is] the same. If the reason is clear from context, it can be omitted as usual. If "kedo" follows a noun or na-adjective, there's usually a "da" in between. This construction is often taught as standalone word (dakedo = but). However, the "but" comes from "kedo" only.

kanji: あっこれ私のだけど飲む
hiragana: あっこれ わたし の だ けど のむ
romaji: akkore watashi no da kedo nomu
meaning: This is mine [i.e. my drink] but [do you want to] drink [it]? If "kedo" follows a noun or na-adjective, there's usually a "da" in between. This construction is often taught as standalone word (dakedo = but). However, the "but" comes from "kedo" only. Here, the actual noun is omitted (i.e. watashi no drink), but the "da" is still required. If this card is too confusing, just suspend and ignore it. The "want to" is a consequence of the intonation (this sentence is a question without marker). There are dedicated ways to express "want to", covered later.

hiragana: だ けど ここ に いる
meaning: [He said he'd go out ] ...but [he] is here! "da kedo" can also be used to start a sentence: It just means "but" and refers to something said before.

hiragana: だ から ごめんなさい
meaning: ...so [I am] sorry. Just as "da kedo", "da kara" can also be used to start a sentence: It just means "because" and refers to something said before. Note that this is often taught as standalone word "dakara", but it's in fact da + kara.

hiragana: わたし は たのしかった けど
meaning: [The others didn't like it] but as for me, [it] was enjoyable / fun. If the reason is clear from context, it can be omitted as usual.

hiragana: おちついた
meaning: Did [you] calm down? ochitsuku: to calm down

kanji: 気持ちは分かりますが落ち着いて
hiragana: きもち は わかります が おちついて
meaning: As for [your] feelings [I] understand, but please calm down -> I understand how you feel, but calm down. Instead of "kedo", you may also use "ga" to express "but". It means exactly the same, but is slightly more polite. As a rule of thumb, "ga" is used with teineigo (i.e. -masu forms), while "kedo" is used with plain Japanese. Don't mix this up with the noun-related "ga", it simply means "but" in this case. "ochitsuite" is the te-form of ochitsuku - to calm down. It is used as imperative here, this will be covered soon.

kanji: 時間はありませんが落ち着いて
hiragana: じかん は ありません が おちついて
meaning: [We] don't have time, but calm down -> please calm down, even though we have no time (maybe they're in trouble and have to escape). Instead of "kedo", you may also use "ga" to express "but". It means exactly the same, but is slightly more polite. As a rule of thumb, "ga" is used with teineigo (i.e. -masu forms), while "kedo" is used with plain Japanese. Don't mix this up with the noun-related "ga", it simply means "but" in this case. "ochitsuite" is the te-form of ochitsuku - to calm down. It is used as imperative here, this will be covered soon.

kanji: かまいませんが大丈夫ですか
hiragana: かまいません が だいじょうぶ です か
meaning: [I] don't [mean to] interfere, but [are you] ok? (Maybe the speaker saw some stranger on the street who looks like he could need some help). Instead of "kedo", you may also use "ga" to express "but". It means exactly the same, but is slightly more polite. As a rule of thumb, "ga" is used with teineigo (i.e. -masu forms), while "kedo" is used with plain Japanese. Don't mix this up with the noun-related "ga", it simply means "but" in this case. kamau: to interfere with, to meddle with (it has multiple meanings, it was introduced as "means to mind, to care about").

kanji: はい私は大丈夫ですが
hiragana: はい わたし は だいじょうぶ です が
romaji: hai watashi ha daijoubu desu ga
meaning: Yes, [I] am ok, but.... [something is still bothering me]. Instead of "kedo", you may also use "ga" to express "but". If clear from context, a sentence part may be omitted:

kanji: でもあの子は友達じゃない
hiragana: でも あの こ は ともだち じゃない
romaji: demo ano ko ha tomodachi janai
meaning: ...but as for that kid, [it] is not friend. ko: kid, child (it's short for kodomo, we already had this before).

kanji: 私は構いませんがあの子たちは
hiragana: わたし は かまいません が あの こたち は
romaji: watashi ha kamaimasen ga ano kotachi ha
meaning: As for me [I] don't [mean to] interfere, but as for these kids... [should they really be doing this?!] The "ga" is hard to notice here.

hiragana: きれい だ し やさしい し
meaning: [I like her] because [she's] pretty and kind [among other things]. When you want to provide an (incomplete) list of reasons for something, you can use "shi". Simply append it to the sentence / relative clause. If the clause ends on a noun or na-adjective, there's usually a "da" before the "shi". We already this on earlier cards, Tae Kim officially introduces it in the "compound sentences"-chapter. Since the list of reasons is usually incomplete, I use "among other things" in the translation. Remark: Quite often, "shi" is appended to every relative clause in the list of incomplete reasons, just as in this example. As we will see however, this is not always the case.

kanji: 暑いしそれに疲れたわよ
hiragana: あつい し それ に つかれた わ よ
romaji: atsui shi sore ni tsukareta wa yo
meaning: [I don't like it here in this forest, because it's] hot among other things... and besides this [I] became tired. soreni: besides, in addition When you want to list multiple reasons for something, you can append "shi" to (each) sentence/clause. Note that this usually is an incomplete list of reasons, hence the "among other things" in the translation. Remark: The additional "sore ni" here caused some confusion, because it adds another reason why the speaker wants to leave the forest. Tae Kim and other resources however, point out that the "shi" must be added after every reason (which is wrong). Here, you could interpret this as two distinct sentences, joined together by "sore ni" - this is just what it does: The "atsui shi" is one out of a few reasons the speaker does not being in the forest. And then, in addition to this, she became tired. It's from Hyouka, ep. 8 around 8:00, if you want to check.

kanji: 嘘もつかないし悪いこともしない
hiragana: うそ も つかない し わるい こと も しない
romaji: uso mo tsukanai shi warui koto mo shinai
meaning: [You're a good person because you] not only do not lie, but [you] also do not do any bad things. If "shi" is used like this, it can also be translated as "not only x, but also y". Have a look at the references, they are more exhaustive as Tae Kim's guide in this case. Note that the general meaning of an incomplete list of reasons also applies here, but the "shi" is not appended to every sentence as explained in some resources.

kanji: それは私の問題だしさ
hiragana: それ は わたし の もんだい だ し さ
romaji: sore ha watashi no mondai da shi sa
meaning: [You don't need to help / do this, because it's] my problem [among other things]. When you want to list multiple reasons for something, you can append "shi" to every sentence. Again, Tae Kim's explanation of this topic is a bit superficial, if you want to know more, have a look at the refs. "sa" is a sentence ending particle that indicates assertion. It already appeared on an earlier card, where I recommended to ignore it, which you can also do here. However, it's usually easy to understand, read more here if you are interested.

kanji: 今日は天気もいいし楽しいよさあ
hiragana: きょう は てんき も いい し たのしい よ さあ
romaji: kyou ha tenki mo ii shi tanoshii yo saa
meaning: [Let's go to the sea because] as for today, not only the weather is good, but it's also fun! My translations of "shi" focused a bit too hard on Tae Kim's explanation (one out of many reasons). If used like this, I'd rather translate it as "not only X, but also Y" - see additional refs.
source: Saiki Kusuo no Psi Nan S1 (斉木楠雄のΨ難 第1期)

hiragana: うまい し はやい し
meaning: [He's] skilled and fast [among other things]. shi: marks incomplete list of reasons for something. Here, it's appended to every reason, but this is not always the case.

hiragana: だれも いない し さむい し
meaning: [I want to go home because] noone is here and it is cold [among other things]. shi: marks incomplete list of reasons for something. Here, it's appended to every reason, but this is not always the case.
source: The World God Only Knows S3 (jp eng)

kanji: 怖いし寂しいし悲しいわ
hiragana: こわい し さびしい し かなしい わ
romaji: kowai shi sabishii shi kanashii wa
meaning: [I want to go home because it's] scary, lonely and miserable [here]. sabishii: lonely; lonesome; solitary kanashii: sad; miserable shi: marks incomplete list of reasons for something. Here, it's appended to every reason, but this is not always the case.

hiragana: あかるい し おもしろい よ ね
meaning: [I like her because she's] not only cheerful but also interesting. akarui: cheerful, bright (of a colour) shi: marks incomplete list of reasons for something. Here, it's used for emphasis (not only, but also).

kanji: あなた美人だしとても好きよ
hiragana: あなた びじん だ し とても すき よ
romaji: anata bijin da shi totemo suki yo
meaning: I like you very much [because you're a] beautiful woman [among other things]. bijin: beautiful woman shi: marks incomplete list of reasons for something. Here, only one out of several reasons is given.

kanji: ねえ暑いし何か飲まない
hiragana: ねえ あつい し なにか のまない
meaning: It's hot [among other things], [why] don't we drink something? shi: marks incomplete list of reasons for something. Here, only one out of several reasons is given.
source: JoJos Bizarre Adventure 黄金の風 (26-39)

hiragana: でも おれ じゅく ある し な
romaji: demo ore juku aru shi na
meaning: [I can't go because among other things] cram school is there -> I have to go to cram school. juku: cram school; private tutoring school. The wikipedia article on Japanese cram schools is interesting, they are very common in Japan. shi: marks incomplete list of reasons for something. Here, only one out of several reasons is given.
source: Kokoro ga Sakebitagatterunda (Anthem of the Heart)

kanji: 僕はお前を許さないしお前は僕を許さない
hiragana: ぼく は おまえ を ゆるさない し おまえ は ぼく を ゆるさない
romaji: boku ha omae wo yurusanai shi omae ha boku wo yurusanai
meaning: [We'll continue to fight because] I don't forgive you and you don't forgive me [among other things]. yurusu: to forgive; to pardon

hiragana: ここ きもちいい し さ
meaning: [I like this place. The view is great and] it feels good [here, among other things].

kanji: 全然嬉しくないし楽しくない
hiragana: ぜんぜん うれしくない し たのしくない
meaning: [Something was] totally not joyful and fun. ureshii: happy; glad; joyful tanoshii: enjoyable; fun

kanji: 知らないし興味もないよ
hiragana: しらない し きょうみ も ない よ
romaji: shiranai shi kyoumi mo nai yo
meaning: [I can't help you because I] not only don't know anything [about it] but also have no interest [in this]. kyoumi: interest in something, curiosity

kanji: でももう飽きたし眠いわ
hiragana: でも もう あきた し ねむい わ
romaji: demo mou akita shi nemui wa
meaning: [You really want to continue?] But [I] not only lost interest already but also am sleepy. akiru: to get tired of; to lose interest in The "wa" in the end is a female sentence ending particle. The use varies around regions and is a bit hard to explain - just ignore it or read the ref. Here's Tofugu's summary: "わ usually follows a statement that expresses your realization of something, reflecting your view or attitude toward a situation or event. It indicates that you came to a conclusion, felt a certain way, or are making a sudden observation based on personal experience."

hiragana: くさい し ね
meaning: [I don't like this place] it's stinky, among other things. kusai: stinking; smelly

hiragana: なに し に きた の
meaning: Do you remember this sentence? Reminder: The "shi" here has a different meaning, it's the nominalized form of "suru - to do" and means: What did you come here for? You get the nominalization of a verb by omitting the "masu" part in teineigo.

hiragana: ないた か
meaning: [You] cried? naku: to cry

hiragana: はい なきません
meaning: Yes, [I] don't cry. naku: to cry The guy told the girl not to cry. Sounds like a weird conversation, but I need the word "naku" for one of the next cards...

hiragana: こい する の
meaning: [You] fell in love? koi: romantic love koi suru: to fall in love (not: to make love!)

hiragana: さいご に わらう の は
meaning: As for the one who laughs last [it's probably the speaker].

hiragana: しっぱい した
meaning: [I] failed / made a mistake. shippai: failure; mistake

kanji: この仕事に失敗は許されない
hiragana: この しごと に しっぱい は ゆるされない
romaji: kono shigoto ni shippai ha yurusarenai
meaning: This job does not forgive mistakes (looks like they are working on a dangerous construction site).

hiragana: なんで わらう の
meaning: Why [do you] laugh? The "nande" is hard to understand. If you didn't use headphones up to this point, now is probably a good time to try, they make listening comprehension much easier...

hiragana: わたし しっぱい した か な
meaning: I failed / made a mistake, didn't I?

kanji: 皆さんは最近失敗をしましたか
hiragana: みなさん は さいきん しっぱい を しました か
romaji: minasan ha saikin shippai wo shimashita ka
meaning: As for everybody [you, the audience], recently made a mistake / failed? -> How about you? Did you recently make a mistake?

hiragana: なぜ にげる
meaning: Why [do you] run away? nigeru: to escape; to run away

hiragana: にげる の よ ふたり で
meaning: [We] escape! With the two of you.

kanji: でもその子も私から逃げた
hiragana: でも その こ も わたし から にげた
romaji: demo sono ko mo watashi kara nigeta
meaning: [A long time ago I had a single friend] but that kid also ran away from me.

kanji: みんなたぶん逃げたよね
hiragana: みんな たぶん にげた よ ね
meaning: [They] all escaped, maybe.

kanji: もちろん逃げますよね
hiragana: もちろん にげます よ ね
meaning: [We] escape, of course. mochiron: of course; certainly; naturally

kanji: 笑ったり泣いたり恋したりするの
hiragana: わらったり ないたり こいしたり する の
meaning: [I want to return to earth] because [there I can] do things like laughing, crying and falling in love [just like other girls]. You can connect a list multiple actions / verbs among a potentially larger list using the pattern "-tari + suru": Put the verb to past tense, attach "ri" and end the sentence with suru (and maybe a sentence ending particle like in this example). The meaning becomes: I did this, that and a few other things. The tense is determined by the last "suru". The difference to the te-form is, that the "-tari + suru"-pattern lists multiple things among others in no particular order. If you said: "waratte naite koi suru", you'd to these things in exactly this order. The difference to "shi" is that "-tari suru" applies only to verbs and not necessarily states reasons.

kanji: 一度失敗して泣いたり逃げたりすると
hiragana: いちど しっぱい して ないたり にげたり する と
romaji: ichido shippai shite naitari nigetari suru to
meaning: This is a nice example of multiple "compound constructors" in one sentence (-te form and -tari suru), it means: If you fail once and cry and run away (among other things)...[it's ok]. You can connect a list multiple actions / verbs among a potentially larger list using the pattern "-tari + suru": Put the verb to past tense, attach "ri" and end the sentence with suru (and maybe a sentence ending particle like in this example). The meaning becomes: I did this, that and a few other things.

kanji: 僕は彼女が泣いたり困ったりするのが好きじゃない
hiragana: ぼく は かのじょ が ないたり こまったり する の が すき じゃない
romaji: boku ha kanojo ga naitari komattari suru no ga suki janai
meaning: As for me, I don't like it if she cries and is in trouble (among other things). You can connect a list multiple actions / verbs among a potentially larger list using the pattern "-tari + suru": Put the verb to past tense, attach "ri" and end the sentence with suru (and maybe a sentence ending particle like in this example). The meaning becomes: I did this, that and a few other things.

kanji: おいしいお店があったりする
hiragana: おいしい おみせ が あったり する
meaning: [I like to go there, because there's a] tasty shop there [among other things] -> It means a store offering tasty food. mise: store; shop (with polite o-prefix) The "-tari suru"-construction does not need multiple verbs in this form as in the previous examples. You'll often have sentences like this with just one verb ending on -tari. This adds the meaning of "among other things" or "...and the like". It's imply a single thing out of many more. Remark: Here, we have the -tari suru form of "aru", which means: to be there, among other things.

kanji: 何か予定あったりするの
hiragana: なんか よてい あったり する の
meaning: Do you have any kind of plans [and maybe other things in mind]? yotei: plans; arrangement; schedule nanka: something like ...; things like (casual of nanika) The "-tari suru"-construction does not need multiple verbs in this form as in the previous examples. You'll often have sentences like this with just one verb ending on -tari. This adds the meaning of "among other things" or "...and the like". It's imply a single thing out of many more.

hiragana: かるく なったり する
meaning: [Something] becomes light [among other things]. karui: light, not heavy The "-tari suru"-construction does not need multiple verbs in this form as in the previous examples. You'll often have sentences like this with just one verb ending on -tari. This adds the meaning of "among other things" or "...and the like". It's imply a single thing out of many more.
source: ダンベル何キロ持てる (dumbbell) 1-6

hiragana: ねぼう したり する
meaning: [I am often late because I] oversleep [among other things]. nebou: oversleeping (noun) Note the interesting noun-suru-suru construction here: nebou suru = to oversleep conjugated to -tari suru.

kanji: 私明日いなかったりする
hiragana: わたし あした いなかったり する
meaning: I am not there tomorrow [among other things - they are talking about going to a party. Terrace house boys x girls next door, S7 after 19:30]. ashita: tomorrow The "suru" in the end sounds like a "s". Remark: We don't have past tense here, it's -tari suru - incomplete listing.
source: Terrace House-Boys x Girls Next Door

kanji: お家を忘れたりしませんよね
hiragana: おうち を わすれたり しません よ ね
romaji: ouchi wo wasuretari shimasen yo ne
meaning: [I] won't forget my home. uchi: one's house; one's home; one's family (with polite o-prefix) In this example you see how the conjugations work for "-tari suru"-constructions: The last suru is inflected.

kanji: 私たちは逃げたりしません
hiragana: わたしたち は にげたり しません
meaning: As for us, [we] don't run away. In this example you see how the conjugations work for "-tari suru"-constructions: The last suru is inflected.

hiragana: これ たべたり
meaning: [I] eat this [among other things]. The "suru" is often omitted in casual conversations. The speaker lists stuff she's doing at the moment.

hiragana: びーる のん だり
meaning: [I] drink beer [and so on / and do other things]. The "suru" is often omitted in casual conversations. The speaker lists stuff she's doing at the moment.

hiragana: きょう は たのしかった な
meaning: As for today, [it] was fun.

hiragana: でも ひょっとして
meaning: But maybe... hyottoshite: by any chance; by some chance; maybe

hiragana: また ゆめ だったり とか
meaning: ...[it] was a dream again [and the like...] The "-tari suru"-form also works for the state of being (da), with exactly the same rules, it's da -> datta (past) -> dattari. However, the "suru" is again missing here.

hiragana: ゆめ じゃない
meaning: The first word is supposed to mean "atsui", sounds like she's taking a hot shower and finally realizes, that she's not dreaming.

kanji: それは友達だったり好きな人だったり
hiragana: それ は ともだち だったり すき な ひと だったり
romaji: sore ha tomodachi dattari suki na hito dattari
meaning: As for that... [he's] a friend, a person [I] like [among other things]. The "-tari suru"-form also works for the state of being (da), with exactly the same rules, it's da -> datta (past) -> dattari. The "suru" is again missing here.

kanji: かかわいかったりするの
hiragana: か かわいかったり する の
meaning: [You think it/someone is] cute and all that? -> Answer see next card. "-tari suru" also works for i-adjectives, even though this is less common than for verbs.

hiragana: はい かわいい です が
meaning: Yes, cute but... (the "but" comes from "ga", just as we learned before).

hiragana: だめ だめ わたし を ころして
meaning: 'No! Don't [go away]. Kill me!' Here, the speaker is telling the other person in the image to kill her.

hiragana: だめ です よ おさけ は
meaning: No good, alcoholic beverage [I mean].

kanji: それはダメなことなのか
hiragana: それ は だめ な こと な の か
romaji: sore ha dame na koto na no ka
meaning: As for that, [is it a] no good-thing? -> It this something [someone] shouldn't do? "dame" is used within a broad context to express that something is not good and maybe should not be done. We'll learn some more important use cases later.

kanji: ダメです兄は渡しません
hiragana: だめ です あに は わたしません
meaning: No good! As for [my] older brother, [I] don't hand [him] over. watasu: to hand over Note again that the thing to be handed over is clear from context. Seems like the red haired girl wants to go out with the guy and the black haired girl is holding him (older brother) back. Depending on the context it could also mean that they're talking about some item and the girl explains: Brother doesn't hand it over.

kanji: ダメだ全然集中できない
hiragana: だめ だ ぜんぜん しゅうちゅう できない
meaning: No good / impossible, [I] totally can't concentrate. shuuchuu: concentration, focusing

hiragana: もも うそ は だめ よ
meaning: Momo, as for a lie, [it's] no good -> don't lie, Momo!
source: ももへの手紙(A Letter to Momo)

kanji: ダメこの恋は叶わない
hiragana: だめ この こい は かなわない
meaning: No good, as for this love, [it] doesn't come true (maybe someone doesn't love her back). kanau: to come true (of a wish, prayer, etc.); to be realized; to be fulfilled
source: さよなら絶望先生 (Sayonara, Zetsubou-Sensei)

kanji: ごめん甘い物ダメだった俺
hiragana: ごめん あまいもの だめ だった おれ
meaning: Sorry, sweets were no good (for me). Maybe he spat them out and apologizes for that. amaimono (amai + mono): sweet things, sweets
source: The Daily Lives of High School Boys (EP 1-12)

kanji: 駄目だ私にはできない
hiragana: だめ だ わたし に は できない
romaji: dame da watashi ni ha dekinai
meaning: It's no good, [it's something] I can't do. Note the "ni + ha" particle combination. We already had this on a separate card before, the sentence was "bokutachi ni ha wakaru". Technically, it marks "watashi" as target of "dekiru". This means, that "not being able to do something" is limited to "watashi" in this case. They're talking about marrying someone here and the speaker can't do that for whatever reason. Read more on this here.

hiragana: おかし おいしい
meaning: okashi: sweets, confections, candy This is a different word for sweets, it's more specific than the "amaimono" of the last card. Note that particles are missing again (e.g. okashi ha/ga).

kanji: あのね私は先生なのよ
hiragana: あの ね わたし は せんせい な の よ
romaji: ano ne watashi ha sensei na no yo
meaning: Well, as for me, [I am your] teacher. (conversation continues on next card) The speaker is the teacher of some kids, who invited her to join their all girls gossip meeting. She wants to refuse and gives the reason here. Remember: The explanatory "no" requires a "na" before it, if it's used together with a noun, otherwise it would imply there's an attribute / possession linked to the teacher, that's clear from context and thus omitted.

kanji: ねえ少しだけお菓子もありますよ
hiragana: ねえ すこし だけ おかし も あります よ
romaji: nee sukoshi dake okashi mo arimasu yo
meaning: Come on [teacher], only a little bit, sweets are there, too! dake: only

kanji: 何のことだか分からない
hiragana: なん の こと だ か わからない
romaji: nan no koto da ka wakaranai
meaning: I have no idea what [you are talking] about. -> Here, the conversation revolves around the question of what a certain thing or matter actually is. The speaker doesn't understand and says: I don't understand the question of "what matter is it?". A relative clause (i.e. a subsentence embedded into a larger sentence) ending on "ka" allows to talk about a certain question. Relative clause: "nan no koto da ka - what matter is it?" "Main" sentence: "wakaranai - I don't understand". Note that "wakaru" means to understand or comprehend something. To just "know" something is "shiru" in Japanese, keep this in mind for the following examples.

kanji: どこに行ったか分かります
hiragana: どこ に いった か わかります
meaning: Here, the conversation revolves around the question of where someone went, the speaker asks: Do you understand where he went? A relative clause (i.e. a subsentence embedded into a larger sentence) ending on "ka" allows to talk about a certain question. Relative clause: "doko ni itta ka - where did [he] go?" "Main" sentence: "wakarimasu - do you know?" (Listen to the intonation, it's a question). Note that "wakaru" means to understand or comprehend something. To just "know" something is "shiru" in Japanese, keep this in mind for the following examples.

kanji: 今はどこにいるか分かんねぇけど
hiragana: いま は どこ に いる か わかんねぇ けど
romaji: ima ha doko ni iru ka wakannee kedo
meaning: Here, the conversation revolves around the question of where someone is. The speaker says: [I know where he was yesterday] but I don't understand where he is now. A relative clause (i.e. a subsentence embedded into a larger sentence) ending on "ka" allows to talk about a certain question. Relative clause: "ima ha doko ni iru ka - as for now, where is [he]?" "Main" sentence: "wakaranai kedo - but I don't understand".

kanji: 何をしたか分かりますか
hiragana: なに を した か わかります か
romaji: nani wo shita ka wakarimasu ka
meaning: Here, the conversation revolves around the question of what someone did. The speaker wants to understand and asks: Do you understand what [he] did? Maybe someone did a complicated task. A relative clause (i.e. a subsentence embedded into a larger sentence) ending on "ka" allows to talk about a certain question. Relative clause: "nani wo shita ka - what did [he] do?" "Main" sentence: "wakarimasu ka - do you know?" Do you get the pattern? The essence is this: When you want to talk about a certain question, you explicitly include it as relative clause (i.e. subsentence). I add more sentences, but keep the explanations shorter on the next cards. If you need more explanations, please drop me a message using the question links.

kanji: 何があったか分かるよな
hiragana: なに が あった か わかる よ な
romaji: nani ga atta ka wakaru yo na
meaning: You understand what happened, don't you?! Relative clause: "nani ga atta ka - what was there? what happened?" "Main" sentence: "wakaru yo na - you know, don't you!?"

kanji: 俺が誰だか分かったか
hiragana: おれ が だれ だ か わかった か
romaji: ore ga dare da ka wakatta ka
meaning: Did [you] understand who I am?

kanji: どうしていいのか分からない
hiragana: どうして いい の か わからない
meaning: I don't understand why [that] is ok.

kanji: どこにいるか分かるか
hiragana: どこ に いる か わかる か
romaji: doko ni iru ka wakaru ka
meaning: Do [you] understand where [we] are? Sounds like they are in some special place.

kanji: どこに向かうのか分からないけど
hiragana: どこ に むかう の か わからない けど
romaji: doko ni mukau no ka wakaranai kedo
meaning: [I know where he is now], but [I] don't understand where [he] heads towards. mukau: to go towards; to head towards

kanji: 自分が何をするか分からないかな
hiragana: じぶん が なに を する か わからない か な
romaji: jibun ga nani wo suru ka wakaranai ka na
meaning: [I just] don't understand what [I] would do myself [if they were dating]. We already had "jibun" on earlier cards, it has a funny dictionary definition: "myself; yourself; oneself; himself; herself". It refers to "someone self" in general. Ignore the "ka na" ending for now.

kanji: 何があったか知らないけどさあ
hiragana: なに が あった か しらない けど さあ
romaji: nani ga atta ka shiranai kedo saa
meaning: [She behaves weird, ] but [I] don't know what happened. A sentence with "shiru - to know":

kanji: 何で興味持ったのか知らないけど
hiragana: なんで きょうみ もった の か しらない けど
romaji: nande kyoumi motta no ka shiranai kedo
meaning: ... but I don't know why [he] had interest [in something]. kyoumi: interest motsu: to carry kyoumi wo motsu: to have interest in something

kanji: みんなどこに行ったか知らないかな
hiragana: みんな どこ に いった か しらない か な
romaji: minna doko ni itta ka shiranai ka na
meaning: [You] don't know where the others went, do you?

kanji: いつだったか忘れたけど
hiragana: いつ だった か わすれた けど
meaning: [I know what happened] but [I] forgot when it was.

hiragana: なに を かんがえて いる の か
romaji: nani wo kangaete iru no ka
meaning: What are [you] thinking?! Here, we have kangaete (from kangaeru: to think) + iru (to be, to exist). This combination does not translate to "I think and I am", but is used to express an enduring state or action (I am thinking), so the sentence means:

hiragana: なに を して いる
meaning: What are [you] doing? verb in te-form + iru: Enduring state or action, similar to the English "-ing" form. It is used for both animate and inanimate things.

hiragana: ここ で なに を して いる
romaji: koko de nani wo shite iru
meaning: What are [you] doing here? verb in te-form + iru: Enduring state or action, similar to the English "-ing" form. It is used for both animate and inanimate things.

kanji: お前は強いしよくやっているさ
hiragana: おまえ は つよい し よく やって いる さ
romaji: omae ha tsuyoi shi yoku yatte iru sa
meaning: As for you, you are strong [among other things] and are doing well (physical action, because "yaru" is used here. The speaker is referring to the listener's fighting skills). verb in te-form + iru: Enduring state or action, similar to the English "-ing" form. It is used for both animate and inanimate things. Friendly reminder: "omae" is super often used in anime but most likely will sound rude in "real" Japanese.

hiragana: きいて いる
meaning: [I] am listening. verb in te-form + iru: Enduring state or action, similar to the English "-ing" form. It is used for both animate and inanimate things. Note that "kiku" can mean "to listen" and "to ask". It's a bit confusing sometimes.

kanji: 質問をしているのはこっちだ
hiragana: しつもん を して いる の は こっち だ
romaji: shitsumon wo shite iru no ha kocchi da
meaning: As for asking of questions, this direction (towards the speaker) -> I am the one who's asking questions. verb in te-form + iru: Enduring state or action, similar to the English "-ing" form. It is used for both animate and inanimate things.

hiragana: どうして ないて いる
meaning: Why are [you] crying? verb in te-form + iru: Enduring state or action, similar to the English "-ing" form. It is used for both animate and inanimate things.

kanji: 私はいつも君を見ている
hiragana: わたし は いつも きみ を みて いる
romaji: watashi ha itsumo kimi wo mite iru
meaning: As for me, [I'm] always watching you. verb in te-form + iru: Enduring state or action, similar to the English "-ing" form. It is used for both animate and inanimate things.

hiragana: かれ は ぼく を まって いる
romaji: kare ha boku wo matte iru
meaning: As for him, [he's] waiting for me.
source: Erased - 僕だけがいない街

hiragana: なに を はなして いる
meaning: What [are you] saying?

hiragana: ゆめ を みて いる
meaning: [I'm] dreaming (see next card).

hiragana: だれか を まって いる ゆめ
meaning: [It's a] waiting-for-someone-dream.

kanji: 私の家で何をしている
hiragana: わたし の いえ で なに を して いる
romaji: watashi no ie de nani wo shite iru
meaning: What [are you] doing in my house?

kanji: 誰かが俺を呼んでいる
hiragana: だれ か が おれ を よんで いる
romaji: dare ka ga ore wo yonde iru
meaning: Someone is calling me.

hiragana: なに を たくらんで いる
meaning: What [are you] planning? (Not in a sense of "planning for tomorrow", rather in a mischievous way). takuramu: to scheme; to plan; to play a trick

hiragana: いま まで なに を して いた
romaji: ima made nani wo shite ita
meaning: Until now, what were [you] doing? The "-te iru" construct can be conjugated by conjugating "iru". Here, "ita" is past tense, which refers to an ongoing action or state in the past.

hiragana: ずっと かんがえて いた
meaning: [I] was thinking the whole time.

kanji: 自分に何ができるかをずっと考えていた
hiragana: じぶん に なに が できる か を ずっと かんがえて いた
romaji: jibun ni nani ga dekiru ka wo zutto kangaete ita
meaning: [I] was thinking about what [I] can do myself the whole time (note the relative clause ending on "ka" here).

hiragana: かのじょ は わらって いた
meaning: As for her, [she] was laughing.

kanji: 彼女はいつも笑っていた
hiragana: かのじょ は いつも わらって いた
meaning: As for her, [she] was always laughing.

kanji: この男何を考えている
hiragana: この おとこ なに を かんがえて いる
romaji: kono otoko nani wo kangaete iru
meaning: As for this guy, what is [he] thinking?

hiragana: わたし が おもって いた こと
meaning: The thing that [I] was thinking [was this:...]. Here, the speaker is referring to something she has just said out loud to a larger audience. She's explaining why she said this by saying: The thing that [I] thought [while saying what I said was this: ...] kakegurui, s1e9 - 16:50

kanji: 今は東京の大学で頑張っています
hiragana: いま は とうきょう の だいがく で がんばって います
romaji: ima ha toukyou no daigaku de ganbatte imasu
meaning: As for now, [someone] is doing his best at Tokyo university. To get teineigo, just conjugate "iru".

kanji: 私はいつでもあなたを待っています
hiragana: わたし は いつ でも あなた を まって います
romaji: watashi ha itsu demo anata wo matte imasu
meaning: As for me, [I] am always waiting for you. To get teineigo, just conjugate "iru". Remark: itsumo and itsu demo both mean "always", but you can also translate "itsu demo" as "anytime". Check out the refs if you want to know more.

kanji: 部屋からなくなっていました
hiragana: へや から なくなって いました
meaning: [Something] was missing from the room. To get teineigo, just conjugate "iru". Remark: "iru" means to be there, to exist for animate/living things. However, "-te iru" in its role of describing an ongoing state is also used for inanimate things. Therefore, it is not necessarily a person that has disappeared from the room.
source: 今からあなたを脅迫します

hiragana: あの うみ を みて いない
meaning: [He] didn't see that ocean over there? There's also a negative "-te iru". It's all pretty easy, just conjugate the "iru". Remark: Confusing is the tense here: In English, you'd use past tense, but here not seeing the ocean in the past is expressed by "mite inai" in this case. It's from Fate/Zero, Ep 13, around 18:00 if you want to check yourself. If this bothers you, just translate the sentence as "he's not seeing the ocean over there" - Judging from the image, it's foggy there after all ;).

hiragana: わたし は なにも して いない
meaning: As for me, [I am] not doing anything [about it].
source: blood c the last dark (jp eng)

hiragana: これ を しって いる か
meaning: [Do you] know this? It's important to keep in mind that "-te iru" describes not only ongoing actions, but also ongoing states. States often do not directly translate to the English progressive forms. This is covered on the following cards, also refer to Tae Kim's explanation. "To know" refers to the ongoing state of knowing something. So in Japanese, the term "shitte iru" is quite common, while in English you'd rather not say "I'm knowing this". Note how similar the te-forms of suru - shite and shiru - shitte sound, it's easy to mix them up when listening to something.

hiragana: なぜ わたし を しって いる
meaning: Why [do you] know me? It's important to keep in mind that "-te iru" describes not only ongoing actions, but also ongoing states. States often do not directly translate to the English progressive forms. This is covered on the following cards, also refer to Tae Kim's explanation. "To know" refers to the ongoing state of knowing something. So in Japanese, the term "shitte iru" is quite common, while in English you'd rather not say "I'm knowing this". Note how similar the te-forms of suru - shite and shiru - shitte sound, it's easy to mix them up when listening to something.
source: blood c the last dark (jp eng)

kanji: その答えは君が知っている
hiragana: その こたえ は きみ が しって いる
romaji: sono kotae ha kimi ga shitte iru
meaning: As for that answer, you know it! It's important to keep in mind that "-te iru" describes not only ongoing actions, but also ongoing states. States often do not directly translate to the English progressive forms. This is covered on the following cards, also refer to Tae Kim's explanation. "To know" refers to the ongoing state of knowing something. So in Japanese, the term "shitte iru" is quite common, while in English you'd rather not say "I'm knowing this". Note how similar the te-forms of suru - shite and shiru - shitte sound, it's easy to mix them up when listening to something.

kanji: それは分かっています
hiragana: それ は わかって います
meaning: As for that, [I] got it -> literally: I'm understanding it, but this doesn't make sense in English. The sentence refers to a continuing state of understanding. wakaru - to understand also refers to an ongoing state. Refer to Tae Kim's short remark on shiru vs. wakaru here.

kanji: どうなるか分かっているな
hiragana: どう なる か わかって いる な
romaji: dou naru ka wakatte iru na
meaning: [You] understand what will happen, don't you.

hiragana: ついた
meaning: [I] arrived. tsuku: to arrive (other tsuku / uso)

kanji: もうすぐマンション着きますからね
hiragana: もうすぐ まんしょん つきます から ね
meaning: [Don't worry] because [we] soon arrive at the apartment building. Maybe it's raining...
source: ぼくたちは勉強ができない

kanji: 勝負はもうついていた
hiragana: しょうぶ は もう ついて いた
meaning: The fight had already been settled / decided -> Here, the speaker is supposed to kill someone to settle a fight, but he refuses and declares that he has already won. shoubu: match; contest; victory or defeat tsuku: This has many meanings, in this case it means to be settled; to be resolved; to be decided

hiragana: つかれて いました の ね
meaning: [Oh, they are in bed already? I guess it's because they] had become tired.

hiragana: きづいて いない の か
meaning: [You] are not noticing it?

kanji: でもあなたは残っている
hiragana: でも あなた は のこって いる
meaning: But as for you, you are being left behind. nokoru: to remain; to be left

kanji: でも僕は気付いていなかった
hiragana: でも ぼく は きづいて いなかった

source: Boku no Hero Academia S3 (ep 1-25 jp_en)

hiragana: きてる
meaning: [He's] coming. kiteru: contraction of kite iru. In spoken Japanese, the "i" of the iru is often omitted, especially in casual speech. This confused me a lot, because the resulting words almost look like standalone verbs. This is from "kuru", press r to play the audio again and remember the pronunciation for the next card.
source: Higurashi no Naku Koro ni S1 (JP Eng)

hiragana: きいてる
meaning: [Are you] listening? kiiteru: contraction of kiite iru. In spoken Japanese, the "i" of the iru is often omitted, especially in casual speech. This confused me a lot, because the resulting words almost look like standalone verbs. kuru (to come) -> kite iru kiku (to hear, to ask) -> kiite iru The te-forms almost sound the same.

hiragana: ひと の はなし きいてる
meaning: [Are you] listening to the conversation of the people? In spoken Japanese, the "i" of the iru is often omitted, especially in casual speech. This confused me a lot, because the resulting words almost look like standalone verbs.

hiragana: わらってる
