kanji: ダメだ何考えてるのか分からねえ
hiragana: だめ だ なに かんがえてる の か わからねえ
romaji: dame da nani kangaeteru no ka wakaranee
meaning: [I] don't understand what [she] is thinking. wakaranee - slang for wakaranai. [It's no good]. [I] don't understand what [you're] thinking.

kanji: みんな私のことどう思ってるんだろう
hiragana: みんな わたし の こと どう おもってる ん だろう
romaji: minna watashi no koto dou omotteru n darou
meaning: [I] wonder what everyone is thinking about me. darou: I wonder -> covered in more detail later.

kanji: ケガしてるじゃないか
hiragana: けが してる じゃない か
meaning: [You] are wounded, aren't you? kega: wound, injury

kanji: バイトのことご両親は知ってるの
hiragana: ばいと の こと ごりょうしん は しってる の
romaji: baito no koto goryoushin ha shitteru no
meaning: As for part time job thing, do [your] parents know? goryoushin: teineigo for parents (ryoushin)

hiragana: おまえ も きてた の か
meaning: You also came [and were there afterwards]? kiteta: contraction of kite ita. Unfortunately, omitting the "i" works for all possible conjugations ;).

kanji: 聞いてたけど意味分かんないです
hiragana: きいてた けど いみ わかんない です
meaning: [I] had heard [it] but don't understand. wakannai is a slangy written form for wakaranai. kiiteta: contraction of kiite ita. Unfortunately, omitting the "i" works for all possible conjugations ;).

kanji: 本当みんな頑張ってたわね
hiragana: ほんとう みんな がんばってた わ ね
meaning: Really, everybody was doing [their] best. ganbatteta: contraction of ganbatte ita. Unfortunately, omitting the "i" works for all possible conjugations ;).

kanji: 俺全部分かってますみたいな
hiragana: おれ ぜんぶ わかってます みたい な
meaning: As for me, [I] completely understand. mitai: seems like -> covered again later. wakattemasu: contraction of wakatte imasu. Unfortunately, omitting the "i" works for all possible conjugations ;).

hiragana: てがみ を かいて いた
meaning: [Someone] was writing a letter. (Keep this sentence in mind for the next cards)

hiragana: なに かいて いる の
meaning: What [are you] drawing / writing? (Keep this sentence in mind for the next cards) Remark: "kaku" means both writing and painting / drawing.
source: Sakurasou no Pet na Kanojo (jp eng)

hiragana: ここ に かいて ある
meaning: [Something] is written here [the process of writing is completed and now the everything stays to be written down]. Here, we have kaite (from kaku: to write) + aru. This combination describes the state after a certain action was completed, not the ongoing action itself. The sentence means: Using "te iru" instead (koko ni kaite imasu) the sentence would mean: The writing is ongoing at the moment, someone "is writing". Something I found a bit confusing here is the fact that both "-te iru" and "-te aru" describe states. The difference is that "-te aru" describes the state after an action completed and usually translates to the English passive voice (writing vs. was written).

kanji: ここに書いてあるじゃないか
hiragana: ここ に かいて ある じゃない か
romaji: koko ni kaite aru janai ka
meaning: Isn't [the solution] written down here? -te form + aru: Resulting state after an action completed (not the ongoing action itself). Something I found a bit confusing here is the fact that both "-te iru" and "-te aru" describe states. The difference is that "-te aru" describes the state after an action completed and usually translates to the English passive voice (writing vs. was written).

hiragana: のみもの は かって ある
meaning: As for beverage, did you buy some? Meaning: Do we have drinks here (after they were bought), i.e. "katte aru" refers to the state after the buying was completed. -te form + aru: Resulting state after an action completed (not the ongoing action itself). Tae Kim writes: "Usually, this expression is used to explain that something is in a state of completion. The completed action also carries a nuance of being completed in preparation for something else."

hiragana: はって ある
meaning: [A poster] has been glued [to the window]. haru: to stick; to paste; to affix​ -te form + aru: Resulting state after an action completed (not the ongoing action itself).

hiragana: どこ に はって ある
meaning: Where is it glued [the picture these folks are searching]? haru: to stick; to paste; to affix​ -te form + aru: Resulting state after an action completed (not the ongoing action itself).

kanji: それでお姉さん今日のお菓子は何ですか
hiragana: それで おねえさん きょう の おかし は なに です か
romaji: sorede oneesan kyou no okashi ha nani desu ka
meaning: As for today's sweets, what is it? Seems like they're meeting and snacking on a regular basis.
source: 私に天使が舞い降りた! (wataten)

hiragana: つくって ある よ
meaning: It's a bit hard to directly translate this to English and fully capture the meaning of "-te aru": She has sweets available that she had prepared herself earlier, i.e. the sentence refers to the state after the preparation was finished. tsukuru: to make; to produce; to manufacture -te form + aru: Resulting state after an action completed (not the ongoing action itself).
source: 私に天使が舞い降りた! (wataten)

hiragana: ようい は できた か
meaning: Are the preparations completed? youi: preparation; arrangements

kanji: 飲み物すぐ用意するから
hiragana: のみもの すぐ ようい する から
meaning: I immediately prepare beverages. sugu: immediately; at once; right away

hiragana: ようい して ある よ
meaning: The preparations have been completed. You could also say: "youi ha dekita", which just means that some preparations where completed. This sentence puts more emphasis on the resulting state. If this is too hard to understand without context, just keep in mind: -te form + aru = resulting state after an action completed.

kanji: 僕の名前が書いてあります
hiragana: ぼく の なまえ が かいて あります
romaji: boku no namae ga kaite arimasu
meaning: My name is written down [here -> on the thing the kid is handing over]. -te form + aru: resulting state after an action completed, it is conjugated using "aru".

kanji: やっぱりあの手紙に何か書いてあったのかな
hiragana: やっぱり あの てがみ に なにか かいて あった の か な
romaji: yappari ano tegami ni nanika kaite atta no ka na
meaning: I wonder if something was written in that letter. The "I wonder if" is a result of "..no ka na", listen to the intonation. The "no" here is again the explanatory one: Together with the question, this emphasizes that the speaker is looking for an explanation.

hiragana: ここ に おく よ
meaning: [I] place [it] here. oku: to put, to place

hiragana: どこ に おいた っけ
meaning: Where did [I] put [it]?! oku: to put, to place -kke: indicates that the speaker is trying to recall some information

kanji: でも何か考えておくね
hiragana: でも なにか かんがえて おく ね
meaning: ... but [we] have to think [of something, a present in this case]. If "oku" is added to a verb in te-form, the verb is carried out explicitly with the future in mind, e.g. to prepare for something. "-te oku": To do something in preparation of the future.

hiragana: まぁ かんがえて おく よ
meaning: Well, [I] think [about it, an offer made to the guy in this case]. "-te oku": To do something in preparation of the future.

hiragana: うん はなして おく ｡
meaning: Yes, [I] talk [to him, e.g. in order to solve some issue]. "-te oku": To do something in preparation of the future.

kanji: ないしょにしておくね
hiragana: ないしょ に して おく ね
meaning: Keep [this] a secret [such that I'm not in trouble in the future]. naisho: secret "-te oku": To do something in preparation of the future.
source: 私に天使が舞い降りた! (wataten)

hiragana: まぁ かえして おく ぜ
meaning: The guy accidentially found a love letter he wasn't supposed to read in his backpack. He's musing about how to return it without getting in trouble in the future and says: [I] return [it, such that you have it again and nothing happened]. kaesu: to return (something); to restore; to put back "-te oku": To do something in preparation of the future.

hiragana: ごはん あたためて おく か
meaning: A person is leaving while the others are eating. The speaker asks: [Should I] warm dinner / keep dinner warm [such that it is warm when you return]? atatameru: to warm; to heat "-te oku": To do something in preparation of the future.
source: Sakurasou no Pet na Kanojo (jp eng)

kanji: ここに置いておきますね
hiragana: ここ に おいて おきます ね
meaning: [I] put [it] here [for later]. Interestingly, "oku" can be connected to itself using the "te oku"-pattern. The first oku simply means: "To put" and the second one indicates, that this is done in preparation for the future. Note that the second oku is conjugated here.
source: Fate Stay Night Unlimited Blade Works S1 (JP Eng)

kanji: 悪いけどここに置いておくわよ
hiragana: わるい けど ここ に おいて おく わ よ
romaji: warui kedo koko ni oite oku wa yo
meaning: [It's] bad, but [I] put [it] here for later. warui: bad, poor, undesireable, but also: sorry; (my) bad; unforgivable "warui" is an interesting word. It means "bad, poor" most of the time but is also a way for apologizing in Japanese meaning "sorry; (my) bad; unforgivable". Just have a look at the dictionary. Interestingly, "oku" can be connected to itself using the "te oku"-pattern. The first oku here is conjugated to "oite" and simply means "to put", while the second one indicates that this is done in preparation for the future.

hiragana: おちゃ いれます
meaning: [I] make tea. ireru: to put in; to let in; to take in; to bring in Note that in the context of tea of coffee, "ocha/kohii wo ireru" simply means: to make coffee or tea. This is covered in a nice instructional video in about 1000 cards.

hiragana: ごはん いれて おく ね
meaning: [I] put food [into the box for later]. Maybe she's trying to send him somewhere by mail, weird...

hiragana: さがして おく から
meaning: [I] search [for it, such that you have it back later]. "-te oku": To do something in preparation of the future. sagasu: to search

hiragana: よく あやまって おいた が
meaning: [He is still mad] but [I] apologized [in order be good again]. Just an example for "te oku" with oku in past tense. I'll add some more examples in a different context later. The "ga" here is the contrasting one meaning "but / even though".

hiragana: かんがえとく ね
meaning: Think about it [e.g. about accepting an offer]. Sometimes the "e" in "te oku"-constructions is omitted, I found these forms often hard to understand in the beginning. Just as for the omitted "i" in "-te iru", these contractions look like standalone verbs. kangaetoku: contraction of kangaete oku

hiragana: かえしとく ね
meaning: [I] return [it, so that you have it back agan in the future]. Sometimes the "e" in "te oku"-constructions is omitted, I found these forms often hard to understand in the beginning. Just as for the omitted "i" in "-te iru", these contractions look like standalone verbs. kaeshitoku: contraction of kaeshite oku

hiragana: じゃ おいとく わ よ
meaning: Ok, then [I] put it / leave it here [it's better if I keep it at my place in the future]. Sometimes the "e" in "te oku"-constructions is omitted, I found these forms often hard to understand in the beginning. Just as for the omitted "i" in "-te iru", these contractions look like standalone verbs. oitoku: contraction of oite oku ja/じゃ: Then, well

kanji: おお菓子も用意しとくね
hiragana: お おかし も ようい しとく ね
romaji: o okashi mo youi shitoku ne
meaning: Sweets also [should be] prepared [for later]. Sometimes the "e" in "te oku"-constructions is omitted, I found these forms often hard to understand in the beginning. Just as for the omitted "i" in "-te iru", these contractions look like standalone verbs. shitoku: contraction of shite oku

hiragana: いって みる
meaning: [Should we] try to go [in there] or more literal: Go and see? -te form + miru: To try something out in the sense: “To give something a try and see how it goes”. Note that it does not mean "to try hard" in most cases, Japanese has a different expression for that covered later. Reminder: miru = to see
source: BOFURI - Itai no wa Iya nano de Bougyoryoku ni Kyokufuri Shitai to Omoimasu (ep 1-12 w_en)

hiragana: てつだって みる
meaning: [Should I] try to help? Or, depending on the context: [Can you] try to help [me]? -te form + miru: To try something out in the sense: “To give something a try and see how it goes”. Note that it does not mean "to try hard" in most cases, Japanese has a different expression for that covered later.

hiragana: うん がんばって みる よ
meaning: Yes, [I] try to do [my] best. -te form + miru: To try something out in the sense: “To give something a try and see how it goes”. Note that it does not mean "to try hard" in most cases, Japanese has a different expression for that covered later.

hiragana: おれ も がんばって みる
meaning: I also try to do [my] best. -te form + miru: To try something out in the sense: “To give something a try and see how it goes”. Note that it does not mean "to try hard" in most cases, Japanese has a different expression for that covered later.

kanji: お父さんに聞いてみるよ
hiragana: おとうさん に きいて みる よ
meaning: [I don't know, but] try to ask [your] father. -te form + miru: To try something out in the sense: “To give something a try and see how it goes”. Note that it does not mean "to try hard" in most cases, Japanese has a different expression for that covered later. Remark: kiku means both to hear and to ask, have a look at the hinative link if this confuses you.

hiragana: わたし の たべて みる
meaning: [Do you want to] try to eat mine? -> Do you want to try my icecream? -te form + miru: To try something out in the sense: “To give something a try and see how it goes”. Note that it does not mean "to try hard" in most cases, Japanese has a different expression for that covered later.

kanji: 分かったよ帰って考えてみる
hiragana: わかった よ かえって かんがえて みる
meaning: [I] got it. [I] go home and try to think [about it]. -te form + miru: To try something out in the sense: “To give something a try and see how it goes”. Note that it does not mean "to try hard" in most cases, Japanese has a different expression for that covered later. Here we have 3 verbs chained by the te-form: "Go home, think and see".

kanji: どれがおいしかったか聞いてみるの
hiragana: どれ が おいしかった か きいて みる の
romaji: dore ga oishikatta ka kiite miru no
meaning: [I] try to ask which one was tasty -> I try to ask which one they liked. -te form + miru: To try something out in the sense: “To give something a try and see how it goes”. Note that it does not mean "to try hard" in most cases, Japanese has a different expression for that covered later. This also is a nice example for a relative clause ending on "ka". Remember: This allows you to talk about a question, the question of "dore ga oishikatta ka - which one was tasty?" in this case.
source: Honzuki - Ascendance of a Bookworm S1 (JP Only)

hiragana: けんじ に きいて みた
meaning: [I] tried to ask kenji. -te form + miru: To try something out (not: to try hard)

kanji: でも僕は目を閉じて考えてみた
hiragana: でも ぼく は め を とじて かんがえて みた
romaji: demo boku ha me wo tojite kangaete mita
meaning: But as for me, [I] closed my eyes and tried to think [about it]. tojiru: to close (e.g. book, eyes, meeting, etc.); to shut -te form + miru: To try something out (not: to try hard) Note that the past tense of "miru" applies to the entire te-chain.

hiragana: かんがえて みます
meaning: [I] try to think [about it]. -te form + miru: To try something out (not: to try hard)

kanji: 分かりました聞いてみます
hiragana: わかりました きいて みます
meaning: Got it. [I] try to ask. -te form + miru: To try something out (not: to try hard)
source: Midnight Diner Tokyo Stories S1 (jp only)

kanji: 分かりました捜してみます
hiragana: わかりました さがして みます
meaning: Got it. [I] try to search [for it]. -te form + miru: To try something out (not: to try hard)

kanji: 分かりましたもう少し待ってみます
hiragana: わかりました もうすこし まって みます
meaning: [Someone is being late here]. Got it, [I] try to wait a little longer. mousukoshi: a bit more; a bit longer -te form + miru: To try something out (not: to try hard)

kanji: なるほどやってみます
hiragana: なるほど やって みます
meaning: I see, [I] try to do [it, physical action; the conversation revolves around training fighting skills]. naruhodo: I see; that's right; indeed -te form + miru: To try something out (not: to try hard)

hiragana: さがして みました
meaning: [I] tried to search [for it]. -te form + miru: To try something out (not: to try hard)

hiragana: つくって みました
meaning: [I] tried to prepare / make [a set of photobooks in this case, but also e.g. a meal]. -te form + miru: To try something out (not: to try hard)
source: Ouran High School Host Club (jp eng)

kanji: パンダくんに聞いて作ってみました
hiragana: ぱんだ くん に きいて つくって みました
romaji: panda kun ni kiite tsukutte mimashita
meaning: [I] asked Panda [about a weird dish he wanted to eat: Bamboo Parfait] and tried to prepare [it]. -te form + miru: To try something out (not: to try hard)

hiragana: かえって いく ｡
meaning: [I] go home. -te iku: directs the verb in te-form away from a place, persons or a point in time (for example from the present to the future). This is already the dictionary definition of "kaeru", but together with iku it means to leave a certain place, i.e. the action is directed away from e.g. you friend's place. kaette kuru on the other hand means to return home, i.e. the "going home" is directed towards someone's home.

hiragana: かえって きません ねえ
meaning: [You] don't return home, do you? -te kuru: directs the verb in te-form towards a place, persons or a point in time (for example from the past to the present). Here's the "return home" counterpart with conjugated "kuru". The speaker e.g. already is at home and asks this question, i.e. the "returning home" is directed towards the joint home of the two.

hiragana: かさ かって いく か
meaning: [Should I] go out / away [from home] and buy an umbrella? -te iku: directs the verb in te-form away from a place, persons or a point in time (for example from the present to the future). The "should" is a consequence of the "ka" in the end, this is a question the speaker asks himself.
source: Sakurasou no Pet na Kanojo (jp eng)

hiragana: かって くる
meaning: [I] buy [it] and return. -te kuru: directs the verb in te-form towards a place, persons or a point in time (for example from the past to the present). Especially the "-te kuru" construct very often means to do something and then return. I.e. saying "katte kuru" while at home, this means to go out and buy something (you have to go out to do this of course, as you're at home), but then you return. Remember the previous "katte iku"? In this case, the speaker does not return anywhere, he just goes out to buy an umbrella, maybe while on his way somewhere else.

hiragana: かえって いった
meaning: [I] went home (emphasizing that the speaker left some place). -te iku: directs the verb in te-form away from a place, persons or a point in time (for example from the present to the future).

hiragana: かえって きた
meaning: [I] came home (emphasizing that the speaker returned). -te kuru: directs the verb in te-form towards a place, persons or a point in time (for example from the past to the present).
source: Fate Stay Night Unlimited Blade Works S02 (JP Eng)

kanji: それ持って行きますか
hiragana: それ もって いきます か
meaning: [Do you] take this with you [when you go]? -te iku: directs the verb in te-form away from a place, persons or a point in time (for example from the present to the future). motsu (to hold (in one's hand)) is a good example for indicating direction, as it works well for both iku and kuru: Literally, "motte iku" means: to take something and go, i.e. the person leaves a place and takes something along. "motte kuru" means: to take something and come, i.e. to bring something along towards a certain place.

hiragana: てれび もって きた
meaning: [I] brought a television. -te kuru: directs the verb in te-form towards a place, persons or a point in time (for example from the past to the present). motsu (to hold (in one's hand)) is a good example for indicating direction, as it works well for both iku and kuru: Literally, "motte iku" means: to take something and go, i.e. the person leaves a place and takes something along. "motte kuru" means: to take something and come, i.e. to bring something along towards a certain place.

hiragana: きょう もって きた
meaning: [I] brought [it] today. -te kuru: directs the verb in te-form towards a place, persons or a point in time (for example from the past to the present). motsu (to hold (in one's hand)) is a good example for indicating direction, as it works well for both iku and kuru: Literally, "motte iku" means: to take something and go, i.e. the person leaves a place and takes something along. "motte kuru" means: to take something and come, i.e. to bring something along towards a certain place.

kanji: 今度お酒でも持っていきます
hiragana: こんど おさけ でも もって いきます
meaning: Next time [we even] take alcohol (beverage) with us. -te iku: directs the verb in te-form away from a place, persons or a point in time (for example from the present to the future). "demo" means "even" here, just ignore it if that confuses you.

hiragana: にげて いきます よ
meaning: [I] flee [away from this place]. -te iku: directs the verb in te-form away from a place, persons or a point in time (for example from the present to the future). Note that -te iku can also direct an action away from the current point in time. In this case, -te iku refers to starting something - this could also apply here I'd say, see this page for more details.

hiragana: ちから が ぬけて いく
meaning: [My] power is fading. -te iku: directs the verb in te-form away from a place, persons or a point in time (for example from the present to the future). nukeru: to fade, to be missing (this has many more meanings, but together with "chikara" it means this). Note that -te iku can also direct an action away from the current point in time, which is the case here. -te iku emphasizes a continuing change here, see this page for more details.

kanji: 僕の人生は変わっていく
hiragana: ぼく の じんせい は かわって いく
romaji: boku no jinsei ha kawatte iku
meaning: As for my life, [it] is changing. -te iku: directs the verb in te-form away from a place, persons or a point in time (for example from the present to the future). kawaru: to change

kanji: だんだん強くなっていく
hiragana: だんだん つよく なって いく
meaning: [He] gradually becomes stronger. -te iku: directs the verb in te-form away from a place, persons or a point in time (for example from the present to the future). dandan: gradually; by degrees; little by little; more and more I think you could also say "tsuyoku natte iru" to express the continuous state of becoming strong. However, "tsuyoku natte iku" puts more emphasis on the change over time, see this page for more details.

hiragana: れんしゅう して いく
meaning: [I] go out to practice. If the speaker says this to someone who is currently near to him, it would mean: I search something and then come back. Or in other words: "-te kuru" very often means: "I do xxx and come back".

kanji: 飲み物忘れた買ってくる

meaning: [I] forgot [my] drink. [I] go buy one and return. -te kuru: directs the verb in te-form towards a place, persons or a point in time (for example from the past to the present). Especially the "-te kuru" construct very often means to do something and then return. I.e. saying "katte kuru" while at home, this means to go out and buy something (you have to go out to do this of course, as you're at home), but then you return. Remember the previous "katte iku"? In this case, the speaker does not return anywhere, he just goes out to buy an umbrella, maybe while on his way somewhere else.
source: The World God Only Knows S3 (jp eng)

So "world I cannot see" is probably something like the olympics. Interestingly, this sentence could also be translated to "I could see the world I was not able to see", depending on the context. Suspend this card if it's still too difficult, it does not introduce anything new . Together with a relative clause, "xxx-koto ga dekiru" is another way to express the ability to do something: "Ore ga mirarenai sekai wo miru: to see the world I cannot see" is the relative clause in this case. Together with the rest the full sentence then literally means something like: [He] will be able to do the thing of seeing a world I cannot see.

hiragana: みて は だめ よ

In order to express that you must not do something, put the verb in -te form, add "ha/は" and then either "dame", "ikenai" or "naranai" (I'll add examples for each of these starting with dame - no good). In short: The pattern "-te ha dame" is used to express that you must not do something, it means: "doing [something] is no good". Note that the concept of "must not do something" is expressed in a completely different way in Japanese. It requires some time to get used to this, because it is expressed by a negation. Therefore, I'll add the literal translation and the English way to express this next to each other.

kanji: 行きましょうみんなを助けに
hiragana: いきましょう みんな を たすけ に
meaning: Let's go! To rescue everyone! In order to get the polite volitional form, use -mashou instead of -masu. It's the same for all verbs.
source: Boku no Hero Academia_ Futari no Hero

kanji: 医者医者に行きましょう
hiragana: いしゃ いしゃ に いきましょう
meaning: Doctor! Let's go to the doctor! isha: (medical) doctor

kanji: まず今できることをしましょう
hiragana: まず いま できる こと を しましょう
romaji: mazu ima dekiru koto wo shimashou
meaning: First, let's do what-we-can-do-now thing. mazu: first (of all)

hiragana: 「ありがとう」 と いった
meaning: [He] said: "thank you". In order to quote someone, you append "to itta" to the sentence the person said. "itta" is past tense of "iu - to say". Note that the person who said "thank you" is not named here. It is known from context and therefore omitted as usual. If you want to name someone explicitly, you'd say: "tanaka-san ha arigatou to itta - Mr. tanaka said thank you". In Japanese, quotation marks look like this: 「」. In anime subtitles, they're usually not found, but on the following cards I added them for clarity. They have a special role, I'll comment on that again in a few cards.

kanji: 「話を聞きたい」と言ったのに
hiragana: 「はなし を ききたい」 と いった のに
meaning: [Hey, you don't listen] even though [you] said: "[I] want to hear the talk". In order to quote someone, you append "to itta" to the sentence the person said. "itta" is past tense of "iu - to say". Note that the person who said something is not named here. It is known from context and therefore omitted as usual.

hiragana: 「じょうだん」 と いった の すべて じょうだん
meaning: [He] said: "It's a joke". Everything is a joke. In order to quote someone, you append "to itta" to the sentence the person said. "itta" is past tense of "iu - to say". Note that the person who said something is not named here. It is known from context and therefore omitted as usual.
source: Ore no Imouto ga konna ni Kawaii Wake ga Nai_

kanji: いつ私が「あなたを好きだ」と言いましたか
hiragana: いつ わたし が 「あなた を すき だ」 と いいました か
romaji: itsu watashi ga 「anata wo suki da」 to iimashita ka
meaning: When did I say: "I like you"?! -> Here the speaker is given, it's "watashi", so the speaker is quoting herself. In order to quote someone, you append "to itta" to the sentence the person said. "itta" is past tense of "iu - to say". Note that we do not have a direct quote here, because the speaker expresses that he never actually says "I like you". In this case (musing about something or "interpreted quotes" as Tae Kim calls it), the quotation marks are actually not used. I'll leave them on the following cards for clarity.

kanji: 誰が「寝ていい」と言った
hiragana: だれ が 「ねて いい」 と いった
meaning: Who said "it's ok to sleep"?! -> The player is lying on the floor, I guess he's not sleeping, but the trainer seems to be tough and strict. In order to quote someone, you append "to itta" to the sentence the person said. "itta" is past tense of "iu - to say".
source: Saiki Kusuo no Psi Nan S1 (斉木楠雄のΨ難 第1期)

kanji: 「分かっている」と言っただろう
hiragana: 「わかって いる」 と いった だろう
meaning: [I] thought [you] said: "I'm getting it". In order to quote someone, you append "to itta" to the sentence the person said. "itta" is past tense of "iu - to say". Note that we again do not have a direct quote here, because the speaker is not sure if the other person really said something. In this case (musing about something or "interpreted quotes" as Tae Kim calls it), the quotation marks are actually not used. I'll leave them on the following cards for clarity.

kanji: 今日は「帰る」って言ったじゃないですか
hiragana: きょう は 「かえる」 って いった じゃない です か
romaji: kyou ha 「kaeru」 tte itta janai desu ka
meaning: Didn't [you] say that we go home today? The "to" of "to iu / itta" is often abbreviated as "tte". Note that this only applies to this quotation context, not e.g. the conditional "to". We already had a few examples of this on earlier cards. Again, no direct quote but quotation marks for clarity - the 「」-marks are only used for real, direct quotes. Since I practice Japanese pretty much only by listening comprehension myself, I can't tell you more ;).

kanji: 「聞こえない」って言ったじゃないか
hiragana: 「きこえない」 って いった じゃない か
meaning: Person A: Why are you screaming?! Speaker: Didn't [you] say: [I] can't hear [you]? In practice, the "to" of "to iu" is often spelled "tte/って". It's easier pronounced and casual.

hiragana: さびしい って いったら
meaning: If [you] say [you] are lonely, [then we need to do something]. So far, we had direct quotes (someone was quoted 1:1) and indirect quotes (the speaker mused about what someone might have said - the current card is another example for that). By conjugating "iu", you get even more possible meanings ("If you said" in this case). All of these have in common that you talk about what someone (might have) said. In practice, the "to" of "to iu" is often spelled "tte/って". It's easier pronounced and casual.

kanji: 待ってるって言ったのに
hiragana: まってる って いった のに
meaning: [You already left] even though [you] said: [I] am waiting. In practice, the "to" of "to iu" is often spelled "tte/って". It's easier pronounced and casual.

kanji: きれいな名前だなって
hiragana: きれい な なまえ だ な って
romaji: kirei na namae da na tte
meaning: [She] said: "It's a beautiful name". In practice, the "to" of "to iu" is often spelled "tte/って". It's easier pronounced and casual. In case of "tte", the "iu" can be skipped. Again, it's casual!

hiragana: つよい って きいた けど
meaning: [I wanted to drink booze] but [I] heard that it's strong. Or: [I wanted to fight the monster] but I heard that it's strong. Instead of "iu - to say", you can also use other words, for example "kiku - to hear" or "yobu - to call". Again, all of these expressions have in common, that you talk about something that someone said. With "kiku", you express that you heard something.

kanji: 昔私にも先生と呼ぶ人がいたの
hiragana: むかし わたし に も せんせい と よぶ ひと が いた の
romaji: mukashi watashi ni mo sensei to yobu hito ga ita no
meaning: Long time ago, there were people who also called me "sensei". Instead of "iu - to say", you can also use other words, for example "kiku - to hear" or "yobu - to call". Again, all of these expressions have in common, that you talk about something that someone said. With "to yobu", you explain how someone is called. "to yobu" refers to "sensei" here. It's used as clause to describe "hito".

kanji: これからあなたをヒルダと呼ぶことにする
hiragana: これから あなた を ひるだ と よぶ こと に する
romaji: korekara anata wo hiruda to yobu koto ni suru
meaning: From now on, [I] will call you "hiruda". Instead of "iu - to say", you can also use other words, for example "kiku - to hear" or "yobu - to call". Again, all of these expressions have in common, that you talk about something that someone said. With "to yobu", you explain how someone is called. Remark: The "ni suru" at the end of the sentence usually means "to decide on"
source: Legend of the Galactic Heroes (JP Eng) (Media Added)

kanji: 遅くなると思うんだけど
hiragana: おそく なる と おもう ん だ けど
romaji: osoku naru to omou n da kedo
meaning: [I will hurry] but [I] think [I] will be late. "to omou" is another very useful example for talking about a relative clause. It allows to express what you think.

kanji: 私が話すと思うのかい
hiragana: わたし が はなす と おもう の かい
romaji: watashi ga hanasu to omou no kai
meaning: [You] think that I would say [it]? You can also use "to omou" to talk about what others think, but only if you formulate this as question. You don't know what's really on the person's mind! There are other ways to express this, which are covered later.

hiragana: たぶん ねこ だ と おもう
meaning: [I] think [this strange looking thing] is maybe a cat.

kanji: 何か意味があるんだと思う
hiragana: なにか いみ が ある ん だ と おもう
romaji: nanika imi ga aru n da to omou
meaning: [I] think there's some meaning [to this] -> maybe a strange thing is happening here.

kanji: 悪い話ではないと思うが
hiragana: わるい はなし で は ない と おもう が
romaji: warui hanashi de ha nai to omou ga
meaning: [I] don't think this is a bad conversation but... Refreshers: "ga" means "but" here. de ha nai is a negative form of "da".

kanji: ‪多分温かくなると思うけど‬
hiragana: ‪ たぶん あたたかく なる と おもう けど ‬
romaji: ‪ tabun atatakaku naru to omou kedo ‬
meaning: [It is still cold] but [I] think it maybe gets warmer.

kanji: 夢じゃないかと思った
hiragana: ゆめ じゃない か と おもった
meaning: [I] thought: Isn't this a dream?

hiragana: なつめ と いいます
meaning: [I] am called "natsume" or: [You] call me "natsume". I hope it became clear from the previous examples that the person who's actually saying something can be omitted very often and in general can be anybody. Moreover, it's not even necessary, that someone actually said something, which is the case here: There's no real speaker involved, but a generic one. This sentence expresses, that people in general call the guy "natsume".

kanji: 相手はユウスケさんという人です
hiragana: あいて は ゆうすけ さん という ひと です
romaji: aite ha yuusuke san toiu hito desu
meaning: As for [your] opponent, it's a person called yuusuke. Together with "to", "iu" ultimately can become a generic verb that just allows to talk about a complete, "quoted" sentence. As Tae Kim explains, this can be used to describe anything. In many cases, this translates to "a thing called xxx", like in this example, but not always.

kanji: 俺はあなたを食べようとした
hiragana: おれ は あなた を たべよう と した
romaji: ore ha anata wo tabeyou to shita
meaning: As for me, [I] attempted to eat you [which seemed to be hard]. Do you remember "tabete miru" from previous cards? The "-te miru" construct means to try out some action and see how you like it. On this card, we have a similar construction: verb volitional (you/ou-form) + to suru, which means "to attempt to do something". Tae Kim actually explained these forms together, as both mean to try something. While no effort is required for "-te miru", an effort might be required with "verb-volitional to suru".

kanji: 僕はそれをやろうとしてるんだよ
hiragana: ぼく は それ を やろう と してる ん だ よ
romaji: boku ha sore wo yarou to shiteru n da yo
meaning: As for me, I'm attempting to do that [physical action]. This sounds weird in English, but matches the progressive form (-te iru / shiteru). Verb volitional (you/ou-form) + to suru: To attempt to do something.

kanji: でも誰も助けようとしなかったの
hiragana: でも だれも たすけよう と しなかった の
romaji: demo daremo tasukeyou to shinakatta no
meaning: But didn't anyone attempt to save [you]? Verb volitional (you/ou-form) + to suru: To attempt to do something.

kanji: 何を隠そうとしてるの
hiragana: なに を かくそう と してる の
romaji: nani wo kakusou to shiteru no
meaning: What are [you] attempting to hide? Verb volitional (you/ou-form) + to suru: To attempt to do something.

hiragana: にげよう と した のに
meaning: [We're still here], even though [we] attempted to escape. Verb volitional (you/ou-form) + to suru: To attempt to do something.

hiragana: もどろう と して います
meaning: [I] am attempting to go back / return. Verb volitional (you/ou-form) + to suru: To attempt to do something.
source: JoJos Bizarre Adventure 黄金の風 (1-25)

kanji: よく分かったな俺が言おうとしたこと
hiragana: よく わかった な おれ が いおう と した こと
romaji: yoku wakatta na ore ga iou to shita koto
meaning: [You] understood it well, what [I] attempted to say?! Verb volitional (you/ou-form) + to suru: To attempt to do something.

kanji: 仲良くしようとするのも
hiragana: なかよく しよう と する の も
romaji: nakayoku shiyou to suru no mo
meaning: [I] attempt to get along well [with you]. nakayoku: on good terms with; on cordial terms with; getting along well with Verb volitional (you/ou-form) + to suru: To attempt to do something.

kanji: 動きを止めようとしているんだ
hiragana: うごき を とめよう と して いる ん だ
romaji: ugoki wo tomeyou to shite iru n da
meaning: [We] are attempting to stop the motion (maybe they are fighting something strong and are trying to come up with a good strategy). ugoki: movement; move; motion Verb volitional (you/ou-form) + to suru: To attempt to do something.

hiragana: みず を あげよう
meaning: Let's give [them, people distant from speaker] some water. mizu: water [xxx] wo ageru: Speaker or person close to speaker gives something to someone else. Never the other way round!

kanji: 私に勝ったら食べ物をあげる
hiragana: わたし に かったら たべもの を あげる
romaji: watashi ni kattara tabemono wo ageru
meaning: If [you] win against me, [I] give you something to eat. [xxx] wo ageru: Speaker or person close to speaker gives something to someone else. Never the other way round! Remark: "katsu" means to win, "ni" defines "watashi" as target of the verb/katsu, so the meaning is: "If you win against me", which means if you beat me.

kanji: このチケットをあげましょう
hiragana: この ちけっと を あげましょう
meaning: Let's give [them] this ticket. chiketto: ticket (English loan word, the Japanese word follows on the next card) [xxx] wo ageru: Speaker or person close to speaker gives something to someone else. Never the other way round!

hiragana: これ むかし の きっぷ よ ね
romaji: kore mukashi no kippu yo ne
meaning: This is an old ticket / ticket from the past. kippu: ticket

kanji: 頼まれてた切符買ってきたよ
hiragana: たのまれてた きっぷ かって きた よ
meaning: [I] bought the ticket [you] asked for (and returned). tanomareta is past passive tense of tanomu. Don't worry about this for now, this is introduced in about 150 cards. If you're curious, I added two references you can check in advance.

kanji: そっちに行ってあげるわよ
hiragana: そっち に いって あげる わ よ
romaji: socchi ni itte ageru wa yo
meaning: [I] give you the favor of going over there. If used together with the te-form, "ageru" means the speaker (or someone from the speaker's group) does the verb in te-form for someone else. I.e. the favor of doing something is given to someone.

hiragana: いい よ はなして あげる
meaning: [I] give [you] the favor of talking [to someone]. If used together with the te-form, "ageru" means the speaker (or someone from the speaker's group) does the verb in te-form for someone else. I.e. the favor of doing something is given to someone.

hiragana: いい よ ゆるして あげる
meaning: [I] give you the favor of forgiving [you]. If used together with the te-form, "ageru" means the speaker (or someone from the speaker's group) does the verb in te-form for someone else. I.e. the favor of doing something is given to someone.

hiragana: ゆるして あげよう
meaning: Let's give [them] the favor of forgiving them. If used together with the te-form, "ageru" means the speaker (or someone from the speaker's group) does the verb in te-form for someone else. I.e. the favor of doing something is given to someone.

hiragana: はんぶん もって あげる
meaning: [I] give [you] the favor of carrying half [of this heavy load]. If used together with the te-form, "ageru" means the speaker (or someone from the speaker's group) does the verb in te-form for someone else. I.e. the favor of doing something is given to someone.
source: JoJos Bizzare Adventure ダイヤモンドは砕けない

kanji: 何か作ってあげるちょっと待っててね
hiragana: なにか つくって あげる ちょっと まってて ね
romaji: nanika tsukutte ageru chotto mattete ne
meaning: [I] prepare something [food]. Just wait a sec. "-te ageru": The speaker (or someone from the speaker's group) does the verb in te-form for someone else.

kanji: 聞かなかったことにしてあげる
hiragana: きかなかった こと に して あげる
meaning: [I] give [you] the favor of not having heard this. "-te ageru": The speaker (or someone from the speaker's group) does the verb in te-form for someone else.

hiragana: しらべて あげる
meaning: [I] give [you] the favor of checking it out. "-te ageru": The speaker (or someone from the speaker's group) does the verb in te-form for someone else.

hiragana: てつだって あげる ね
meaning: [I] give [you] the favor of helping. "-te ageru": The speaker (or someone from the speaker's group) does the verb in te-form for someone else.
source: Mahoutsukai no Yome (The Ancient Magus Bride) ep 13-24

hiragana: ぼく が いって あげる よ
meaning: [I] give [you] the favor of saying [it for you]. They are talking about the crush of the penguin. He doesn't want to say something to her and the polar bear answers with this (he's not doing him a favor, though ;)). "-te ageru": The speaker (or someone from the speaker's group) does the verb in te-form for someone else.

kanji: みんなに温かいごはんを作ってあげよう
hiragana: みんな に あたたかい ごはん を つくって あげよう
romaji: minna ni atatakai gohan wo tsukutte ageyou
meaning: Let's give the others the favor of preparing some warm food. I on purpose leave "to give" in here, even though it sounds rather weird. "-te ageru": The speaker (or someone from the speaker's group) does the verb in te-form for someone else.

kanji: まず名前をつけてあげないとね
hiragana: まず なまえ を つけて あげない と ね
romaji: mazu namae wo tsukete agenai to ne
meaning: First, [we] must give [it] the favor of attaching a name (naming it). "-te ageru": The speaker (or someone from the speaker's group) does the verb in te-form for someone else.
source: BOFURI - Itai no wa Iya nano de Bougyoryoku ni Kyokufuri Shitai to Omoimasu (ep 1-12 w_en)

kanji: 何をしてあげればいいのか分かりません
hiragana: なに を して あげれば いい の か わかりません
romaji: nani wo shite agereba ii no ka wakarimasen
meaning: [I] don't understand, what [I] could do for [him]. "-te ageru": The speaker (or someone from the speaker's group) does the verb in te-form for someone else.

kanji: 私は何もしてあげられなかった
hiragana: わたし は なにも して あげられなかった
meaning: As for me, [I] could not do anything for them. Here we have the potential past form: ageru -> agerareru (can give/do for) -> agerarenai -> agerarenakatta. It's covered later. "-te ageru": The speaker (or someone from the speaker's group) does the verb in te-form for someone else.

kanji: 案内してあげるからついてきて
hiragana: あんない して あげる から ついて きて
romaji: annai shite ageru kara tsuite kite
meaning: Follow me, because [I] give you the favor of leading the way. annai: guidance; leading (the way) We had several examples already: The te-form is used as soft, casual command/request here, we'll soon cover that in more detail.
source: JoJos Bizzare Adventure ダイヤモンドは砕けない

hiragana: みせて あげる よ
meaning: [I] give [you] the favor of showing [you]. miseru: to show; to display Note that this sentence never means: "show me". It's always the nature of "ageru" to go from speaker to someone else. Just in case you're wondering: It can also be used in third person, which is covered on the next card.
source: JoJos Bizzare Adventure ダイヤモンドは砕けない

kanji: それはお父さんがお母さんに買ってあげた大事なものなんだよ
hiragana: それ は おとうさん が おかあさん に かって あげた だいじ な もの なんだ よ
romaji: sore ha otousan ga okaasan ni katte ageta daiji na mono nanda yo
meaning: As for that, it's a father-bought-it-for-mother-precious item (the "otousan ga okaasan ni katte ageta" describes, how "daiji" the item is: father bought it for mother). This is an example, where the speaker actually is not "-te ageru'ing" herself. Instead, her father is doing something for her mother. In this case, she and her father form a logical group or entity and from that group, something is given to someone else / outside of this group. Of course, she, her father and her mom are a group in terms of being a family, but it's the nature of "-te ageru" to never work towards the speaker, that's why I wrote: They form a "logical group".
source: ももへの手紙(A Letter to Momo)

kanji: お姉さんがしてあげますか
hiragana: おねえさん が して あげます か
meaning: Can [you, older sister] do it for them? Let's assume the younger girl is saying this sentence to her older sister: She is not asking "can you do it for me", because "-te ageru" never works towards the speaker. So you know that something should be done for someone else here. I.e. the two girls form one group and the "-te ageru" acts from the group towards someone outside of this group.

kanji: 絵麻が手伝ってあげたりできないの
hiragana: えま が てつだって あげたり できない の
romaji: ema ga tetsudatte agetari dekinai no
meaning: Aren't [you, ema] able to give [them] the favor of helping [them] out? -> Can't you help them out somehow? The speaker is addressing the listener with her name here. "-te ageru" never works towards the speaker, so this sentence can't mean "can't ema help me"? Instead, imagine two people who are supposed to help someone. One of them does not want to help and says: can't you do it? Takeaway message: "-te ageru" never acts towards the speaker. This has an important influence on what is done for whom and sometimes also on who is doing something. It takes some time to get used to this.

kanji: 僕にちょっと時間をくれませんか
hiragana: ぼく に ちょっと じかん を くれません か
romaji: boku ni chotto jikan wo kuremasen ka
meaning: Can't [you] give me some [of your] time? "kureru" is used when an item or favor is given to the speaker or a person close to the speaker. I.e. it represents the opposite direction of "ageru".

kanji: 手紙をくれたのはお前か
hiragana: てがみ を くれた の は おまえ か
romaji: tegami wo kureta no ha omae ka
meaning: As for the one who gave [me] the letter: Was it you? "kureru" is used when an item or favor is given to the speaker or a person close to the speaker. I.e. it represents the opposite direction of "ageru".
source: Saiki Kusuo no Psi Nan S1 (斉木楠雄のΨ難 第1期)

hiragana: てつだって くれる か
meaning: Can you give [me] the favor of helping? Just as for "ageru", it's much easier to find good example sentences where no real items, but favors are "given". "kureru" is used when an item or favor is given to the speaker or a person close to the speaker. I.e. it represents the opposite direction of "ageru".

kanji: また食べに来てくれる
hiragana: また たべ に きて くれる
meaning: Can [you] give [me] the favor of coming again to eat? "kureru" is used when an item or favor is given to the speaker or a person close to the speaker. I.e. it represents the opposite direction of "ageru".

hiragana: てがみ みて くれた ん だ
meaning: [He] gave me the favor of viewing the letter. "kureru" is used when an item or favor is given to the speaker or a person close to the speaker. I.e. it represents the opposite direction of "ageru".

kanji: 来てくれてありがとう
hiragana: きて くれて ありがとう
meaning: Thank you for giving [me] the favor of coming. "kureru" is used when an item or favor is given to the speaker or a person close to the speaker. I.e. it represents the opposite direction of "ageru".

kanji: 助けに来てくれたんだ
hiragana: たすけ に きて くれた ん だ
romaji: tasuke ni kite kureta n da
meaning: [I'm grateful] because [he] gave [me] the favor of coming to save/help [me]. "kureru" is used when an item or favor is given to the speaker or a person close to the speaker. I.e. it represents the opposite direction of "ageru".

kanji: みんな応援してくれるんだ
hiragana: みんな おうえん して くれる ん だ
romaji: minna ouen shite kureru n da
meaning: [I'm super happy] because everybody is giving [me] the favor of supporting/assisting. "kureru" is used when an item or favor is given to the speaker or a person close to the speaker. I.e. it represents the opposite direction of "ageru".

hiragana: おうえん して くれた ひと
meaning: Someone here is a "gave [me] the favor of supporting"-person. "kureru" is used when an item or favor is given to the speaker or a person close to the speaker. I.e. it represents the opposite direction of "ageru".

kanji: 学校で先生がすごいことしてくれたんだよ

meaning: At school, teacher gave [me / us] the favor of doing a big/amazing thing. "kureru" is used when an item or favor is given to the speaker or a person close to the speaker. I.e. it represents the opposite direction of "ageru".

kanji: でも待ってくれている人がいるから

I.e. it represents the opposite direction of "ageru".

kanji: じゃあ約束してくれますか

kanji: 月が出たらまた会いに来てくれるって

meaning: If the moon comes out, [he] gives [me] the favor of coming again to meet. tsuki: moon "kureru" is used when an item or favor is given to the speaker or a person close to the speaker. I.e. it represents the opposite direction of "ageru".

kanji: 何お母さんに作ってくれたの
hiragana: なに おかあさん に つくって くれた の
romaji: nani okaasan ni tsukutte kureta no
meaning: Here, a mother is talking to her child. She's referring to herself in third person and says: What, you gave [me, mother] the favor of making this? (the kid has made some handcrafted item).

kanji: 今日はお母さんに会いにきてくれたんだよ
hiragana: きょう は おかあさん に あい に きて くれた ん だ よ

meaning: As for today, [he] came to give [me] the favor of meeting you. Here, the speaker is introducing her husband to her passed away mother (they are standing in front of the mother's grave).

kanji: 去年お父さんが作ってくれたの
hiragana: きょねん おとうさん が つくって くれた の

meaning: Last year, father gave [me] the favor of making this. kyonen: last year

kanji: 見送りに来てくれたのか
hiragana: みおくり に きて くれた の か
romaji: miokuri ni kite kureta no ka
meaning: Did [she] come to see [me] off? miokuri: seeing one off; farewell

kanji: わざわざ見送りに来てくれたのか
hiragana: わざわざ みおくり に きて くれた の か
romaji: wazawaza miokuri ni kite kureta no ka
meaning: Did [you] especially come to see [me] off? wazawaza: expressly; especially; taking the trouble (to do)

kanji: おばあちゃんが教えてくれた

meaning: Grandma gave [me] the favor of teaching [this to me]. oshieru: to teach; to instruct

meaning: The adult gave something to the kid and says: [This is] the gratitude/"thank you" for giving me the favor of leading the way. orei: thanks; gratitude​ (teineigo, note the "o"-prefix)

kanji: まあまあそう言わないでくれる
hiragana: まあまあ そう いわないで くれる
meaning: Give [me] the favor of not saying [it] this way. In order to ask someone to not do something, add "de" to the negative verb and add "kureru". Note that this is not the te-form.

kanji: 覚えてないなら無理しないでくれる

meaning: If [you] don't remember, give me the favor of not overdoing it (i.e. don't think too hard if you're not remembering it). In order to ask someone to not do something, add "de" to the negative verb and add "kureru". Note that this is not the te-form. muri: unreasonable, forced muri suru: to try too hard

kanji: 忘れないでくれる私のこと
hiragana: わすれないで くれる わたし の こと
meaning: Give me the favor of not forgetting me. In order to ask someone to not do something, add "de" to the negative verb and add "kureru". Note that this is not the te-form.

kanji: からかわないでくれるかな
hiragana: からかわないで くれる か な
meaning: I wonder if [you] could give [me] the favor of not teasing me. karakau: to tease; to make fun of In order to ask someone to not do something, add "de" to the negative verb and add "kureru". Note that this is not the te-form.

kanji: お母さんが持ってきてくれたんだ
hiragana: おかあさん が もって きて くれた ん だ
romaji: okaasan ga motte kite kureta n da
meaning: [I am happy] because mother was giving me the favor of bringing [this].

kanji: お母さんが持って行ってあげるから
hiragana: おかあさん が もって いって あげる から
romaji: okaasan ga motte itte ageru kara
meaning: Here, the mother is speaking and referring to herself in third person: [You can leave it here] because [I, mother] give you the favor of taking it with me / bringing it [there].

kanji: 俺も応援に来てやったぜ
hiragana: おれ も おうえん に きて やった ぜ
romaji: ore mo ouen ni kite yatta ze
meaning: I also came to support [you, inferior]. Caution, Tae Kim writes: "Usually used for pets, animals, and such, you can substitute yaru for ageru. You would normally never use this type of yaru for people". It's often used in anime though. It's very casual, less polite and usually used to express that the receiver of the item or favor is inferior. Have a look at the references if you're interested. Remark: -te yaru has a second meaning that is less common and usually not found in any textbook. Keep this in mind for now, it's covered in about 700 cards.

kanji: 用意してやったぞさあ来い
hiragana: ようい して やった ぞ さあ こい
romaji: youi shite yatta zo saa koi
meaning: [I] did the preparations for you! Come! (very casual, "koi" is the casual command form of "kuru", covered soon). Caution, Tae Kim writes: "Usually used for pets, animals, and such, you can substitute yaru for ageru. You would normally never use this type of yaru for people". It's often used in anime though. It's very casual, less polite and usually used to express that the receiver of the item or favor is inferior. Have a look at the references if you're interested.

hiragana: てがみ もらった ん だ
meaning: [I'm super happy] because I received a letter! morau: to receive morau can be used as: [item] wo morau. morau implies that something is received by the speaker or someone close to the speaker. If used in third person (e.g. he received), it means that "he" received something from another person, but not from the speaker. In other words, morau never means "he gets from me", so the giver is never the speaker or someone close to the speaker. This is explained very well in the book "making sense of Japanese", p. 54. Remark: This was corrected in v14, sorry for the mistake.

hiragana: へんじ もらった よ
meaning: [I / you] received a reply! morau can be used as: [item] wo morau (the "wo" is dropped here, it's casual speech). morau implies that something is received by the speaker or someone close to the speaker. If used in third person (e.g. he received), it means that "he" received something from another person, but not from the speaker. In other words, morau never means "he gets from me", so the giver is never the speaker or someone close to the speaker. This is explained very well in the book "making sense of Japanese", p. 54. Remark: This was corrected in v14, sorry for the mistake.

kanji: 最後はお母さんに手伝って貰ったの

romaji: saigo ha okaasan ni tetsudatte moratta no
meaning: [I'm not good at this] so in the end, [I] received helping from mother. morau can not only be used for receiving objects, but also for actions by using "-te morau". morau implies that something is received by the speaker or someone close to the speaker. If used in third person (e.g. he received), it means that "he" received something from another person, but not from the speaker. In other words, morau never means "he gets from me", so the giver is never the speaker or someone close to the speaker. This is explained very well in the book "making sense of Japanese", p. 54. Remark: This was corrected in v14, sorry for the mistake. saigo: end; conclusion, also: In the end.

kanji: この問題教えてもらっていいですか

romaji: kono mondai oshiete moratte ii desu ka
meaning: Can [I] receive the explaining of this problem -> Can you explain this problem to me? morau can also used as: -te morau to receive an action that someone does for you. morau implies that something is received by the speaker or someone close to the speaker. If used in third person (e.g. he received), it means that "he" received something from another person, but not from the speaker. In other words, morau never means "he gets from me", so the giver is never the speaker or someone close to the speaker. This is explained very well in the book "making sense of Japanese", p. 54. kanji: 手伝ってもらいたいんだが
hiragana: てつだって もらいたい ん だ が
meaning: [I] want to receive [your] helping / assisting, but... morau can also used as: -te morau to receive an action that someone does for you. morau implies that something is received by the speaker or someone close to the speaker. If used in third person (e.g. he received), it means that "he" received something from another person, but not from the speaker. In other words, morau never means "he gets from me", so the giver is never the speaker or someone close to the speaker. This is explained very well in the book "making sense of Japanese", p. 54. Remark: This was corrected in v14, sorry for the mistake.

kanji: いつか話してもらえるかな
hiragana: いつか はなして もらえる か な
meaning: [I] wonder if [I] can receive talking [from him] someday... This again sounds pretty weird in English, but I try to keep the translations close to Japanese. What the speaker wants to express is: "I wonder if he will talk to me someday".

hiragana: じかん を もらえる か な
meaning: [I] wonder if [I] can receive [some of his] time. Note the potential form: moraeru - can receive. As you can see, "morau" is also useful when you want to ask for a favor. Usually, kureru and moraeru are used for this, Tae Kim covers this in a small section.

kanji: 許してもらえるだろうか
hiragana: ゆるして もらえる だろう か
meaning: [I] wonder if [I] can receive forgiving. Here, forgiving is considered a favor that the speaker receives from someone. As you can see, "morau" is also useful when you want to ask for a favor. Usually, kureru and moraeru are used for this, Tae Kim covers this in a small section.

kanji: 見せてもらえませんか
hiragana: みせて もらえません か
meaning: Can't [I] receive [you] showing [this to me]? The negative form of "-te morau" makes asking for favors a bit more polite. Note that we have the negative potential form here (negative: moraimasen - don't receive, potential: moraeru - can receive). You could also simply ask: "misete?" but that's a lot less polite. "misete moraimasu ka" would be a better option. The negative "morau" then makes this request a bit more indirect and thus more polite.

kanji: 教えてはもらえませんか
hiragana: おしえて は もらえません か
meaning: Can't [I] receive [you] explaining [this to me]? The negative form of "-te morau" makes asking for favors a bit more polite. Note, that we have the negative potential form here (negative: moraimasen - don't receive, potential: moraeru - can receive). As you can see, "morau" is also useful when you want to ask for a favor. Usually, kureru and moraeru are used for this, Tae Kim covers this in a small section.

hiragana: へや かたづける から

kanji: ちょっと待ってください
hiragana: ちょっと まって ください
meaning: Please wait a little bit. -te kudasai: Polite way of making a request (i.e. please to "verb in -te form"). Making a request this way is more direct than asking for a favor with "kureru" or "moraeru".

kanji: 簡単に言わないでください

meaning: Please don't say [this] so easily. To make a negative request, use "negative verb + de kudasai", just as we learned in the context of "morau" and "kureru" before.

hiragana: あの これ ください
meaning: This, please. Just as for "ageru, kureru, morau", you can use "kudasai" for requesting both actions and items.

hiragana: おしえて ください
meaning: Please teach me! -te kudasai: Polite way of making a request (i.e. please to "verb in te form").

kanji: うわあついてこないでください

hiragana: やめて ください

hiragana: すこし じかん を ちょうだい

hiragana: さっさと たべろ おいていく ぞ
meaning: Eat quickly! [I] leave [it, food] here. sassato: quickly (caution: rude!) Here we have the command form (taberu -> tabero). hiragana: のめ よ
meaning: Drink! Here we have the command form (nomu -> nome). According to Tae Kim, it "is quite rude so you should use it with caution (if at all)". For -u verbs, simply replace the -u vowel sound (mu in this case) by an -e vowel sound (me in this case) to get this form. Or the sloppy listening comprehension rule: If a verb ends on ke/け, se/せ, te/て, ne/ね, me/め (or even sloppier*: if it ends on -e) and is not in -te form, you have the command form. *Why sloppier? Because the -e in the end of a verb is an artifact of the romanization and does not exist as single character. The Japanese alphabet does have an "e" character, but this one is not used here - only the ones I listed above.

hiragana: しろ よ
meaning: Do it! shiro: command form of suru (conjugation exception). Rude!

hiragana: いい から すぐ こい よ
