meaning: [I like this book] because [it] is interesting. When [you] return home, try to read [it].

hiragana: すこし ちから を いれて な
meaning: Put a little bit of strength / force / power in. The "na" here is not the negative order "na", listen to the pronunciation.

kanji: 朝ご飯用意できたから早く来てね
hiragana: あさごはん ようい できた から はやく きて ね
romaji: asagohan youi dekita kara hayaku kite ne
meaning: Because [I] finished breakfast preparations, come quickly!

kanji: キスの意味とか考えて
hiragana: きす の いみ とか かんがえて
meaning: Think about the meaning of a kiss!

hiragana: すごい わたし に も みせて
meaning: Amazing, also show [this] to me.

hiragana: かい に いって
meaning: Go [out] to buy [something] and... -> the "and" is from the -te form, the speaker continues.
source: Terrace House- Boys & Girls in the City

kanji: またいつでも遊びに来てね
hiragana: また いつ でも あそび に きて ね
romaji: mata itsu demo asobi ni kite ne
meaning: Come over again any time.
source: Saiki Kusuo no Psi Nan S1 (斉木楠雄のΨ難 第1期)

hiragana: み に きて よ
meaning: Come to see!

hiragana: ちょっと まって
meaning: Wait a sec!

hiragana: わたし の め を みて はなして
romaji: watashi no me wo mite hanashite
meaning: Look into my eyes and talk [say this again]!

hiragana: き を つけて
meaning: Be careful! Another example with "ki" - we had "ki ni suru - to mind" before. This sentence literally means "attach your mind", which means to be careful.

kanji: じゃあよかったじゃん
hiragana: じゃあ よかった じゃん
meaning: Well, [this] was good, wasn't it? jan -> casual for "janai". Note that this "jan" is only used to confirm the positive, in the sense of: "It was good, wasn't it?" Tae Kim has an entire section on slang, we already covered quite a bit of it. I add a few more examples, but not all. Most of this is quite easy to understand, if you keep studying with anime, you'll pick up a lot more.

hiragana: まって ってば
meaning: "tteba" indicates exasperation: Wait, I said!
source: Boku no Hero Academia S3 (ep 1-25 jp_en)

hiragana: なっなに し やがる ん
meaning: WHAT THE F*** ARE YOU DOING?!?!?!!!11 Attaching "yagaru" to the verb stem shows contempt for an action. This indicates hatred and contempt, is extremely strong language and not used in everyday conversations.

hiragana: やめさせる
meaning: Make [them] stop. yamesaseru: casuative of yameru (to stop) The causative form is the second to last verb conjugation. It's used to express "to make someone do something". For -ru verbs, replace "ru" with "saseru".

hiragana: させる か
meaning: [You think I] let [you] do [this]? or: [He] made [you] do it? saseru: causative of suru Weird enough, the causative form not only means "to make someone do something", but also "to let someone do something. This really confused me, because I had only learned the causative as "make someone do something". In many cases I then wondered: Why are they forcing him to do it?! In fact, they allowed him to do it, though. Which one is actually meant must be derived from context. So: Causative: to make or to let someone do something. For -ru verbs, replace "-ru" with "-saseru".
source: Fate Stay Night Unlimited Blade Works S1 (JP Eng)

kanji: 俺にだけ約束させるな
hiragana: おれ に だけ やくそく させる な
romaji: ore ni dake yakusoku saseru na
meaning: Don't make / force only me to make a promise! saseru: causative of suru (saseru na is the negative command form). Causative: to make or to let someone do something. For -ru verbs, replace "-ru" with "-saseru".

kanji: ピカチュウに決めさせるの
hiragana: ぴかちゅう に きめさせる の
meaning: [You] let pikachu decide? kimesaseru: causative of kimeru (to decide) Weird enough, the causative form not only means "to make someone do something", but also "to let someone do something. This really confused me, because I had only learned the causative as "make someone do something". In many cases I then wondered: Why are they forcing him to do it?! In fact, they allowed him to do it, though. Note that by letting pikachu decide, they make him do the decision, so this is where the similarity might come from. They're not forcing him though. So: Causative: to make or to let someone do something. For -ru verbs, replace "-ru" with "-saseru".

kanji: どうするかはネロに決めさせる
hiragana: どう する か は ねろ に きめさせる
romaji: dou suru ka ha nero ni kimesaseru
meaning: As for "what do we do?" [We] let nero decide. [Prev. translation was pretty bad, sorry ;): What should we do? Should we make/let nero decide?] Weird enough, the causative form not only means "to make someone do something", but also "to let someone do something. This really confused me, because I had only learned the causative as "make someone do something". In many cases I then wondered: Why are they forcing him to do it?! In fact, they allowed him to do it, though. Which one is actually meant must be derived from context. So: Causative: to make or to let someone do something. For -ru verbs, replace "-ru" with "-saseru".

kanji: すべては彼に決めさせる
hiragana: すべて は かれ に きめさせる
meaning: As for everything, [we] make/let him decide. Causative: to make or to let someone do something. For -ru verbs, replace "-ru" with "-saseru".
source: Boku no Hero Academia S2 (ep 1-25 jp_en)

hiragana: それ は まえ に やった
meaning: As for that, [I already] did it before. mae: before More causative soon...

kanji: 私はずっと前から気付いていましたよ
hiragana: わたし は ずっと まえ から きづいて いました よ
romaji: watashi ha zutto mae kara kidzuite imashita yo
meaning: [A:This guy is like me. B: Yeah, ] As for me, [I] was aware of this for a long time. kidzuku: to notice; to realize; to realise; to become aware (of); to perceive; to sense Corrected in v14.

kanji: コーヒーを入れてきます
hiragana: こーひー を いれて きます
meaning: [I] make coffee and come back. Remark 1: The expression "-te kuru" means: I go, do xxx and come back. In English, you'd probably just say: "I go [into the kitchen] and make coffee" instead of "I make coffee and come back". See ref. Remark 2: literally, "ireru" means to put in or to pour in. In case of coffee or tea, it just means to make coffee or tea. There's a podcast episode in the follow-up deck that explains this in detail ;). ko-hi-: coffee. The weird "-" marks prolong the vowels and are artifacts from romanizing katakana. This is a different Japanese writing system used for spelling loan words from other languages. In katakana, vowels are prolonged using "ー", which results in "-" in the romanization. More causative soon...

kanji: 飲み物はコーヒーでいいかな
hiragana: のみもの は こーひー で いい か な
romaji: nomimono ha ko-hi- de ii ka na
meaning: As for beverage, [I] wonder if coffee is ok.

hiragana: こーひー ください
meaning: A coffee, please.

kanji: 今甘いものが食べたい
hiragana: いま あまいもの が たべたい
meaning: As for now, [I] want to eat sweets. amaimono: sweets; sweet food

kanji: 昔から甘いものが好きだったよね
hiragana: むかし から あまいもの が すき だった よ ね
romaji: mukashi kara amaimono ga suki datta yo ne
meaning: [He/you] liked sweets since long ago, didn't [he/you].

kanji: 早く帰って甘いものが食べたい
hiragana: はやく かえって あまいもの が たべたい
meaning: [I] want to go home quickly and eat sweets.

kanji: コーヒーの前に甘いものを食べさせる
hiragana: こーひー の まえ に あまいもの を たべさせる
romaji: ko-hi- no mae ni amaimono wo tabesaseru
meaning: Before [having] coffee, make [them] eat sweets! tabesaseru: causative of taberu (to eat) The polar bear is talking to an apprentice who's learning to brew good coffee. This sentence is his trick, to make the coffee taste better (just make the coffee tasters eat sweets before the coffee). Causative: to make or to let someone do something. For -ru verbs, replace "-ru" with "-saseru".

kanji: お弁当食べさせてもらっていいかな
hiragana: おべんとう たべさせて もらって いい か な
romaji: obentou tabesasete moratte ii ka na
meaning: I wonder if [he] lets me eat [his] lunchbox. If the causative is used together with ageru, kureru and morau, it almost always means: to let someone do something, not to make someone do it.

kanji: カイともう一度話をします
hiragana: かい と もういちど はなし を します
romaji: kai to mouichido hanashi wo shimasu
meaning: [I] talk to kai once more.

hiragana: はなして やめさせます
meaning: [I] talk [to him] and make [him] stop. A verb in causative form can be conjugated futher (technically, all causative forms are ru verbs).

hiragana: させない よ
meaning: [I won't] let [you] do [it]. This is the negative causative.
source: BOFURI - Itai no wa Iya nano de Bougyoryoku ni Kyokufuri Shitai to Omoimasu (ep 1-12 w_en)

hiragana: ころさせない
meaning: [I] won't let [you] kill [it]! This is the negative causative.

kanji: こんなの聞かせるなんて
hiragana: こんな の きかせる なんて
meaning: [This is really rude...] making [me] listen to something like this! nante: things like; something like (expresses disdain, dislike, astonishment) kikaseru: causative of kiku (to hear, to listen to) Causative: to make or to let someone do something. For -u verbs, change the verb to negative form and then replace "nai" by "seru". Hacky rule of thumb for listening comprehension: If a verb ends on -seru, it's almost always causative. The only exception are -u verbs ending on -su, e.g. hanaseru is the potential form, while the causative e.g. is: hanasu -> hanasanai -> hanasaseru. Editor's remark: your lie in april, 18-18:46

kanji: 帰ったら楽しいお話いっぱい聞かせてね
hiragana: かえったら たのしい おはなし いっぱい きかせて ね
romaji: kaettara tanoshii ohanashi ippai kikasete ne
meaning: When [you] return, let me hear many enjoyable/fun stories. Note that the speaker is not really asking for permission here, she just wants to hear some interesting stories when the guy returns from his trip. Asking for pemission is rather done using "kiite mo ii desu ka" as we learned before. kikasete: causative -te form of kiku. Causative: to make or to let someone do something. For -u verbs, change the verb to negative form and then replace "nai" by "seru". Hacky rule of thumb for listening comprehension: If a verb ends on -seru, it's almost always causative. The only exception are -u verbs ending on -su, e.g. hanaseru is the potential form, while the causative e.g. is: hanasu -> hanasanai -> hanasaseru.

hiragana: きかせて もらう よ
meaning: Come on, let [me / him] hear [it]! If the causative is used together with ageru, kureru, morau or kudasai, it almost always means: to let someone do something, not to make someone do it. Causative: to make or to let someone do something; -u verbs: use negative and replace -nai with -seru. -ru verbs: replace -ru with -saseru. Causative verbs may be conjugated further.

kanji: はい泳がせてください
hiragana: はい およがせて ください
meaning: Yes, please let me swim. If the causative is used together with ageru, kureru, morau or kudasai, it almost always means: to let someone do something, not to make someone do it. Causative: to make or to let someone do something; -u verbs: use negative and replace -nai with -seru. -ru verbs: replace -ru with -saseru. Causative verbs may be conjugated further.

hiragana: およがせて くれ よ
meaning: Let [me] swim! If the causative is used together with ageru, kureru, morau or kudasai, it almost always means: to let someone do something, not to make someone do it. Causative: to make or to let someone do something; -u verbs: use negative and replace -nai with -seru. -ru verbs: replace -ru with -saseru. Causative verbs may be conjugated further.

kanji: ごめんね待たせてしまって
hiragana: ごめん ね またせて しまって
meaning: Sorry, [I] made [you] wait! Causative: to make or to let someone do something; -u verbs: use negative and replace -nai with -seru. -ru verbs: replace -ru with -saseru. Causative verbs may be conjugated further.

kanji: ここで待たせてくださいちょっと具合が悪くて
hiragana: ここ で またせて ください ちょっと ぐあい が わるくて
romaji: koko de matasete kudasai chotto guai ga warukute
meaning: Please let [me] wait here. [My] condition is a bit bad. guai: condition; health; state (of health) Causative: to make or to let someone do something; -u verbs: use negative and replace -nai with -seru. -ru verbs: replace -ru with -saseru. Causative verbs may be conjugated further.
source: Honzuki - Ascendance of a Bookworm S1 (JP Only)

kanji: 静かに飲ませてくれる
hiragana: しずか に のませて くれる
meaning: The speaker is musing about how the owners of this restaurant let their customers enjoy sake to the fullest extend: [In order to enjoy my sake, they] give [me] the favor of letting [me] drink [it] quietly [i.e. without talking to me / disturbing her]. Causative: to make or to let someone do something; -u verbs: use negative and replace -nai with -seru. -ru verbs: replace -ru with -saseru. Causative verbs may be conjugated further. Remark: In the previous translation, I didn't consider the direction of "kureru", changed in v14.

hiragana: だれ に のませた ?
meaning: Who [did you] allow to drink [it]? I.e. the listener let someone drink something and the speaker is upset about it. Causative: to make or to let someone do something; -u verbs: use negative and replace -nai with -seru. -ru verbs: replace -ru with -saseru. Causative verbs may be conjugated further. Remark: Corrected the translation in v14.

hiragana: おわらせる
meaning: Make [them] stop / come to an end! Causative: to make or to let someone do something; -u verbs: use negative and replace -nai with -seru. -ru verbs: replace -ru with -saseru. Causative verbs may be conjugated further.
source: Boku no Hero Academia S3 (ep 1-25 jp_en)

kanji: こんな悲しみ終わらせるんだ
hiragana: こんな かなしみ おわらせる ん だ
meaning: [I] make this sorrow end. Causative: to make or to let someone do something; -u verbs: use negative and replace -nai with -seru. -ru verbs: replace -ru with -saseru. Causative verbs may be conjugated further.

hiragana: きょう は やすみ だ よ
meaning: As for today, [he is on] vacation. Literally, it's "as for today, it's vacation", from context it is clear that it is "his" vacation (some person these guys talk about). yasumi: vacation; holiday; absence; suspension

hiragana: いわせる の か
meaning: [You] make/let [them] say [it]? Reminder: Negative of iu is iwanai. Causative: to make or to let someone do something; -u verbs: use negative and replace -nai with -seru. -ru verbs: replace -ru with -saseru. Causative verbs may be conjugated further.
source: Boku no Hero Academia S3 (ep 1-25 jp_en)

kanji: 辞めた辞めたどうして
hiragana: やめた やめた どうして
meaning: [I] quit. [You] quit?! Why?! yameru: to quit, to resign (it also means: to stop, but this word is written with a different kanji).

kanji: エゾリスたちにおいしいって言わせるまでに
hiragana: えぞりすたち に おいしい って いわせる まで に
romaji: ezorisutachi ni oishii tte iwaseru made ni
meaning: Here we have the coffee apprentice once again. He's trying to learn how to make really good coffee and the "ezorisu - hokkaido squirrels" are judging his skills. However, the poor guy could not convince them. He says: Until [I] make the squirrels say "tasty" [how much more time will it take?! -> next card] Causative: to make or to let someone do something; -u verbs: use negative and replace -nai with -seru. -ru verbs: replace -ru with -saseru. Causative verbs may be conjugated further.

hiragana: ぱん です か
meaning: [Your favorite food] is bread? pan: bread; (sweet) pastry

hiragana: あれ ここ ぱんや な の
meaning: Huh? Is this a bakery? panya: bakery; baker; pastry shop -ya is a suffix used for certain shops. I.e. pan is bread, panya means bakery. The same for niku (meat) nikuya (butcher's shop).

kanji: どれだけかかるんだろう
hiragana: どれ だけ かかる ん だろう
meaning: How much [time] will it take [until the squirrels finally like my coffee?!] kakaru: to take (a resource, e.g. time or money)

hiragana: やつ に こたえる な
meaning: Don't answer him! kotaeru: to answer Reminders: verb + na: negative command form, rudeyatsu: Derogatory way to address someone, don't use this

kanji: 明日は学校に来るのか
hiragana: あした は がっこう に くる の か
romaji: ashita ha gakkou ni kuru no ka
meaning: As for tomorrow, [will] you come to school? ashita: tomorrow

kanji: おいしいって言ってほしいんだ
hiragana: おいしい って いって ほしい ん だ
romaji: oishii tte itte hoshii n da
meaning: Now the polar bear gives some important advice: [You] want [them] to say "oishii".

hiragana: はなしかける な
meaning: Don't talk to me! hanashikakeru: to address (someone), to start a conversation Reminder: verb + na is the negative command form, rude.

hiragana: しらない ばんごう
meaning: An unknown number? (listen, someone is calling this guy, but he doesn't know the incoming number). bangou: number, series of digits

hiragana: 002 みた こと ない ばんごう だ
meaning: 002 - this is a number [I] have not seen before. I cover numbers in a separate deck, which is linked later in this course. This one is easy though: zero-zero-ni (ni is Japanese for two, zero is sometimes used for 0).

hiragana: でんわばんごう しら なー い
meaning: [I] don't know [his] phone number. Remember denwa (phone)? denwabangou is a phone number, but as you learned from the previous card, you can also just say: bangou.
source: 今からあなたを脅迫します

kanji: 私の携帯が携帯電話が
hiragana: わたし の けいたい が けいたいでんわ が
romaji: watashi no keitai ga keitaidenwa ga
meaning: My phone, my cellphone... [seems like she lost it] denwa: phone keitaidenwa: cellphone keitai: short for cellphone

kanji: スマホ持ってないから電話もできないし
hiragana: すまほ もってない から でんわ も できない し
romaji: sumaho mottenai kara denwa mo dekinai shi
meaning: Since [I] don't have a smartphone [I] cannot call [him]. sumaho: smartphone denwa is also a suru-verb: denwa suru - to call someone. Reminder: dekiru is the (irregular) potential form of suru and means "to be able to do" There's also a longer version of "sumaho", but I'll skip this for now.

hiragana: いい ほうほう が ある よ
meaning: [You want them to like your coffee? Well...] A good method exists... [You know the result from an earlier card: Make them eat sweets before! houhou: method; process; manner

kanji: おかえりお風呂にするそれともごはんなんて
hiragana: おかえり おふろ に する それとも ごはん なんて
romaji: okaeri ofuro ni suru soretomo gohan nante
meaning: Welcome home! [Do you want to] take a bath or have a meal? soretomo: or Remark: "ni suru" usually means "to decide on", have a look at the references if you want to know more.
source: 結婚できない男 (kekkon dekinai otoko S1)

kanji: 教室に戻るそれとも部室
hiragana: きょうしつ に もどる それとも ぶしつ
meaning: [Do you] return to the classroom or the club room? soretomo: or

kanji: 椅子から下りてください
hiragana: いす から おりて ください
meaning: Please climb / come down the chair. isu: chair
source: JoJos Bizarre Adventure 黄金の風 (1-25)

kanji: 私の写真誰にも見せないでね
hiragana: わたし の しゃしん だれ に も みせないで ね
romaji: watashi no shashin dare ni mo misenaide ne
meaning: Please don't show my picture to anyone. shashin: picture, photo
source: からかい上手の高木さん

kanji: 僕帰ってもいいですか
hiragana: ぼく かえって も いい です か
romaji: boku kaette mo ii desu ka
meaning: Can I return home? If you want to ask for permission, the "-te mo ii" grammar is more common than the causative.

kanji: 少し見てきてもいいですか
hiragana: すこし みて きて も いい です か
romaji: sukoshi mite kite mo ii desu ka
meaning: Can [I] quickly check [if we have more nice clothes] and come back? The listener is a model who asks for more fancy clothes. The speaker has a lot of respect for her and asks if he can go and check. Also, "-te kuru" means "to xxx and come back", but in English you'd rather say: "I go and xxx", see ref. If you want to ask for permission, the "-te mo ii" grammar is more common than the causative. Translation changed in v14.

kanji: 先生私がやってもいいですか
hiragana: せんせい わたし が やって も いい です か
romaji: sensei watashi ga yatte mo ii desu ka
meaning: Sensei, can I do it [physical action]? If you want to ask for permission, the "-te mo ii" grammar is more common than the causative.

hiragana: あ すわって いい よ
meaning: [You] can sit down. suwaru: to sit, to sit down

kanji: なんでこんなにいろいろあるんだ
hiragana: なんで こんなに いろいろ ある ん だ
romaji: nande konnani iroiro aru n da
meaning: Why are there so many different [kinds of food] -> the speaker has trouble choosing the right dish. iroiro: various; all sorts of

hiragana: この どうが みた か
meaning: Did [you] see this video? douga: video (esp. digital); video clip Especially in Japanese YouTube videos, you will hear the word "douga" a lot, when people say: "In this video..."

hiragana: じゃ たつ ぞ
meaning: [I will] stand up (the speaker is carrying someone on the shoulders, who just got on). tatsu: to stand; to rise; to stand up​

kanji: 人が立ってるのかと思った
hiragana: ひと が たってる の か と おもった
romaji: hito ga tatteru no ka to omotta
meaning: [I was surprised and screamed] because [I] thought somebody is standing [there]? tatsu: to stand; to rise; to stand up​ Reminder: tatteru is short for tatte iru. The speaker was shocked and screamed, because he thought someone might be in the room. However, it was only dresses hanging there. He explains his screaming by saying this. So the "no" here is the typical explanatory one and the "ka" expresses his uncertainty by asking: Was someone there? Altogether, the sentence ending on "ka" is a clause the speaker talks about. Is it clearer now? I add this explanation to the card. It's from natsume's book of friends, s3 e5 after 5:40.

hiragana: とめられる
meaning: Next we cover passive verbs, here are some good news: THIS IS THE LAST VERB CONJUGATION!!!!1 The remainder of Tae Kim's book is very easy I'd say. Hang in there! Passive and potential are actually the same for -ru verbs, so this means: [something] can be stopped (potential form) [something] is being stopped (passive) Passive: Something is done or was done, the "doer" is unknown or not relevant. For -ru verbs, replace -ru by -rareru.

hiragana: たべられる の か な
meaning: Passive and potential are actually the same for -ru verbs, so this means: [something] can be eaten (potential form) [something] is being eaten (passive) Passive: Something is done or was done, the "doer" is unknown or not relevant. For -ru verbs, replace -ru by -rareru.

kanji: この暗さで見られるか
hiragana: この くらさ で みられる か
meaning: Passive and potential are actually the same for -ru verbs, so this means: [something] can be seen in this darkness (potential)? [something] is being seen in this darkness (passive)? kurasa: darkness (kurai - dark + sa (makes i-adjectives to nouns)) Passive: Something is done or was done, the "doer" is unknown or not relevant. For -ru verbs, replace -ru by -rareru.
source: Boku no Hero Academia S3 (ep 1-25 jp_en)

hiragana: きかれる だろう ばか
meaning: [This] is heard [by someone], you moron! Passive: Something is done or was done, the "doer" is unknown or not relevant. For -u verbs, use the negative form, but replace -nai with -reru. Hacky rule of thumb: If a verb ends on -reru, it's most likely passive (or potential). Don't let this intimidate you, I'll add some general advice on the next card.

hiragana: きかれた ぜ
meaning: [It] was heard [by someone] Passive: Something is done or was done, the "doer" is unknown or not relevant. For -u verbs, use the negative form, but replace -nai with -reru. Passive verbs can be conjugated to past tense.
source: JoJos Bizzare Adventure ダイヤモンドは砕けない

hiragana: くわれる って
meaning: [We will] be eaten, you said? Passive: Something is done or was done, the "doer" is unknown or not relevant. For -u verbs, use the negative form, but replace -nai with -reru. Hacky rule of thumb: If a verb ends on -reru, it's most likely passive (or potential).

kanji: 仲間が目の前で食われた
hiragana: なかま が め の まえ で くわれた
romaji: nakama ga me no mae de kuwareta
meaning: [It's dangerous out there, my] comrade was eaten in front of [my] eyes.

kanji: 言われるまで気づかなかった
hiragana: いわれる まで きづかなかった
meaning: [I] didn't notice, until [it] was said. Passive: Something is done or was done, the "doer" is unknown or not relevant. For -u verbs, use the negative form, but replace -nai with -reru. Hacky rule of thumb: If a verb ends on -reru, it's most likely passive (or potential).

hiragana: どう する
meaning: What will [you] do?

hiragana: どう します か
meaning: What will [you] do (regular polite)?

hiragana: どう されます の
meaning: What will [you] do (passive polite)? Using the passive can make a sentence more polite, because you're not addressing a person directly.
source: Boku no Hero Academia S3 (ep 1-25 jp_en)

kanji: どこへ行かれるのかな
hiragana: どこ へ いかれる の か な
romaji: doko he ikareru no ka na
meaning: [I] wonder where [you] go (passive polite) Using the passive can make a sentence more polite, because you're not addressing a person directly.

kanji: ああ聞いたことがある
hiragana: ああ きいた こと が ある
meaning: [I] heard about [this]. We already had a few "koto ga aru" examples before. A few more generic nouns follow now.

kanji: たくさん楽しいことがあったよ
hiragana: たくさん たのしい こと が あった よ
romaji: takusan tanoshii koto ga atta yo
meaning: A lot of enjoyable things happened. takusan: a lot; lots; plenty

hiragana: たいせつ な もの それ は なに
romaji: taisetsu na mono sore ha nani
meaning: An important item? What is it? The difference between "koto" and "mono": mono is usually a tangible thing, such as a wallet, a cabbage, a door, or a coin, while koto is an intangible thing, such as a win, a habit, a wish, or an incident

kanji: 行きたい所だよ行きたい所
hiragana: いきたい ところ だ よ いきたい ところ
romaji: ikitai tokoro da yo ikitai tokoro
meaning: [It is a] want-to-go-there place. Another abstract noun we already had is tokoro. In most cases, it refers to a physical location or place. However.... (next card)

kanji: 優しいところもいっぱいあるんだ
hiragana: やさしい ところ も いっぱい ある ん だ
romaji: yasashii tokoro mo ippai aru n da
meaning: [He] has many gentle places -> He is gentle / kind in many ways. tokoro can also refer to characteristics or places in time.

kanji: 行ったら楽しいかも知れないよ
hiragana: いったら たのしい かもしれない よ
meaning: If [you] go [there], it's maybe enjoyable. kamoshirenai: may; might; perhaps; may be; possibly. It's used to express uncertainty. Technically, kamoshirenai actually is "[clause] ka mo shirenai". The "ka" makes the preceding clause an embedded question, whose answer is "shiru -> shireru (passive) -> shirenai -> not known".

kanji: 前にも言ったかもしれない
hiragana: まえ に も いった かもしれない
meaning: [I] maybe also said [this] before. kamoshirenai: may; might; perhaps; may be; possibly. It's used to express uncertainty. Technically, kamoshirenai actually is "[clause] ka mo shirenai". The "ka" makes the preceding clause an embedded question, whose answer is "shiru -> shireru (passive) -> shirenai -> not known". Note again, that iu (say) and iku (go) have the same past tense (itta).

kanji: 何か意味があるのかもしれない
hiragana: なにか いみ が ある の かもしれない
romaji: nanika imi ga aru no kamoshirenai
meaning: Maybe there's some meaning [to this]. kamoshirenai: may; might; perhaps; may be; possibly. It's used to express uncertainty. Technically, kamoshirenai actually is "[clause] ka mo shirenai". The "ka" makes the preceding clause an embedded question, whose answer is "shiru -> shireru (passive) -> shirenai -> not known".
source: JoJos Bizarre Adventure 黄金の風 (26-39)

kanji: 難しいことかもしれない
hiragana: むずかしい こと かもしれない
meaning: [It's] maybe a difficult thing. muzukashii: difficult kamoshirenai: may; might; perhaps; may be; possibly. It's used to express uncertainty. Technically, kamoshirenai actually is "[clause] ka mo shirenai". The "ka" makes the preceding clause an embedded question, whose answer is "shiru -> shireru (passive) -> shirenai -> not known".

kanji: 私とあなたは似てるかもしれない
hiragana: わたし と あなた は にてる かもしれない
romaji: watashi to anata ha niteru kamoshirenai
meaning: As for you and I, [we] maybe are similar. niru: to resemble; to look like; to be like kamoshirenai: may; might; perhaps; may be; possibly. It's used to express uncertainty. Technically, kamoshirenai actually is "[clause] ka mo shirenai". The "ka" makes the preceding clause an embedded question, whose answer is "shiru -> shireru (passive) -> shirenai -> not known".
source: Mahoutsukai no Yome (The Ancient Magus Bride) ep 13-24

hiragana: でも たのしい かも
meaning: But... maybe [it is] enjoyable. In casual conversations, you can omit "shirenai".

hiragana: そう かもしれん
meaning: Maybe [it is] like that. kamoshiren: masculine, rough version of kamoshirenai.

kanji: 彼女傷つけてしまうかもしれん
hiragana: かのじょ きずつけて しまう かもしれん
meaning: [If I would walk away now without saying a word, I] would hurt her feelings [unintendedly]. The guy sat down next to a girl outside without noticing (he's reading a book). After noticing, he feels in trouble: he's shy and does not dare to talk to her. However, he also does not want to walk away without saying a word, because this would hurt her feelings. kamoshiren: masculine, rough version of kamoshirenai.

kanji: 戦うことになるかもしれません
hiragana: たたかう こと に なる かもしれません
meaning: Maybe [this] will become a fighting matter. kamoshiremasen: teineigo / polite version of kamoshirenai.

hiragana: それ も うそ でしょう
meaning: This is also a lie, isn't it?! deshou: it seems; I think; I guess; I wonder. When voiced as a question, it can also mean "don't you agree"? "deshou" also expresses a bit of uncertainty. However, the uncertainty is less than in case of "kamoshirenai". Keep in mind, that "uncertainty" has a large scale and does not mean someone is completely unsure. It can also be used "when someone is pretty sure something is that way, but not entirely", see ref below.

kanji: 私は必ず勝つでしょう
hiragana: わたし は かならず かつ でしょう
meaning: As for me, [I] think [I] will certainly win. kanarazu: always; without exception; certainly deshou: it seems; I think; I guess; I wonder "deshou" also expresses a bit of uncertainty. However, the uncertainty is less than in case of "kamoshirenai". Keep in mind, that "uncertainty" has a large scale and does not mean someone is completely unsure. It can also be used "when someone is pretty sure something is that way, but not entirely", see ref below. This is especially the case here, because the speaker also uses "kanarazu".
source: The Night Is Short, Walk on Girl

kanji: 友達がびっくりしてるでしょう
hiragana: ともだち が びっくり してる でしょう
meaning: My friends will be surprised, I guess! bikkuri suru: to be surprised; to be amazed deshou: it seems; I think; I guess; I wonder "deshou" also expresses a bit of uncertainty. However, the uncertainty is less than in case of "kamoshirenai". Keep in mind, that "uncertainty" has a large scale and does not mean someone is completely unsure. It can also be used "when someone is pretty sure something is that way, but not entirely", see ref below.
source: Wotakoi Otaku ni Koi ha Muzukashii

hiragana: しらない だろう ね
meaning: [I] guess [they] don't know. The casual version of "deshou" is "darou". darou: seems; I think; I guess

kanji: どうなるかわかっているだろうな
hiragana: どう なる か わかって いる だろう な
romaji: dou naru ka wakatte iru darou na
meaning: [I] guess [you] understand how it will become / what will happen. The casual version of "deshou" is "darou". darou: seems; I think; I guess

kanji: 二人で何話してるんだろう
hiragana: ふたり で なに はなしてる ん だろう
romaji: futari de nani hanashiteru n darou
meaning: [I] wonder what [they] are talking about together / the two of them... futari: two persons

hiragana: つぎ の じゅぎょう なに
meaning: What's the next lesson (casual!)? jugyou: lesson

hiragana: じゅぎょう は ここ まで
meaning: A teacher is speaking, he ends the lesson by saying: As for lesson, [it is] until this.

kanji: 何やってたのよ授業中に
hiragana: なに やってた の よ じゅぎょうちゅう に
romaji: nani yatteta no yo jugyouchuu ni
meaning: What did you do! During class [I mean]. chuu: during (can be appended to some words)

kanji: 俺にだけ約束させるな
hiragana: おれ に だけ やくそく させる な
romaji: ore ni dake yakusoku saseru na
meaning: Don't make only me making a promise! dake: only

hiragana: ふたり だけ で
meaning: Only the two of us [go there].

kanji: 考えてるのは君だけじゃない
hiragana: かんがえてる の は きみ だけ じゃない
romaji: kangaeteru no ha kimi dake janai
meaning: As for thinking, it's not only you [I am also thinking about this].

hiragana: びーる しか ない な
meaning: There's only beer [and really nothing else]. xxx shika nai: only xxx; the difference to "dake" is that "shika nai" emphasizes the lack of everything else. It's always negative.

hiragana: りんご しか たべない
meaning: I eat only apples [and really nothing else]. ringo: apple xxx shika nai: only xxx; the difference to "dake" is that "shika nai" emphasizes the lack of everything else. Note that "shika nai" is always negative, i.e. you can't say: "ringo shika taberu". "ringo dake taberu" however is ok.

kanji: あなたは自分のことしか見てない
hiragana: あなた は じぶん の こと しか みてない
romaji: anata ha jibun no koto shika mitenai
meaning: As for you, [you] can't see anything but yourself. xxx shika nai: only xxx; the difference to "dake" is that "shika nai" emphasizes the lack of everything else. Note that "shika nai" is always negative, i.e. you can't say: "ringo shika taberu". "ringo dake taberu" however is ok.

kanji: でも今しかできないこと
hiragana: でも いま しか できない こと
meaning: But [this is] a can do only now-thing -> it's something that can only be done now. xxx shika nai: only xxx; the difference to "dake" is that "shika nai" emphasizes the lack of everything else. Note that "shika nai" is always negative, i.e. you can't say: "ringo shika taberu". "ringo dake taberu" however is ok.

kanji: そうさ迷惑ばっかりだ
hiragana: そう さ めいわく ばっかり だ
meaning: [This] is nothing but trouble. The counterpart for "shika nai" is "bakkari". It indicates that there's so much of xxx that there's nothing else. I.e. "xxx shika nai" emphasizes the lack of everything else and "xxx bakkari" emphasizes the excessive amount of only xxx.

hiragana: まいにち べんきょう ばっかり で
meaning: Every day there's only studying studying studying... The counterpart for "shika nai" is "bakkari". It indicates that there's so much of xxx that there's nothing else. I.e. "xxx shika nai" emphasizes the lack of everything else and "xxx bakkari" emphasizes the excessive amount of only xxx.

hiragana: あまいもの ばっかり だ な
meaning: Nothing but sweets! The counterpart for "shika nai" is "bakkari". It indicates that there's so much of xxx that there's nothing else. I.e. "xxx shika nai" emphasizes the lack of everything else and "xxx bakkari" emphasizes the excessive amount of only xxx.

kanji: でもね弟とは喧嘩ばっかり
hiragana: でも ね おとうと と は けんか ばっかり
romaji: demo ne otouto to ha kenka bakkari
meaning: But with little brother, there's nothing but quarrels. The counterpart for "shika nai" is "bakkari". It indicates that there's so much of xxx that there's nothing else. I.e. "xxx shika nai" emphasizes the lack of everything else and "xxx bakkari" emphasizes the excessive amount of only xxx.

hiragana: し しあわせ すぎる
meaning: Too much happiness; good fortune -> sounds like the excess is not bad in this case... sugiru: to exceed; to surpass; to be above sugiru is used to express that there's too much of something. For nouns and na-adjectives, simply attach it.

hiragana: あま すぎる
meaning: [You are] too naive, or: [this is] too sweet. amai: we learned it as sweet, but also can mean: naive, see here sugiru: to exceed; to surpass; to be above sugiru is used to express that there's too much of something. For i-adjectives, remove the last "i" and attach it.

hiragana: はずかし すぎる
meaning: Too embarassing! sugiru is used to express that there's too much of something. For i-adjectives, remove the last "i" and attach it.

hiragana: びょういん へ いこう
meaning: Let's go to the hospital [and visit him]. byouin: hospital; clinic

hiragana: やさし すぎる
meaning: [You are] too kind. sugiru is used to express that there's too much of something. For i-adjectives, remove the last "i" and attach it.
source: Enen no Shouboutai _ Fire Force (jp only)

kanji: ななんだなんでこんな場所で寝てるんだ
hiragana: な なんだ なんで こんな ばしょ で ねてる ん だ
romaji: na nanda nande konna basho de neteru n da
meaning: Why are [you] sleeping in this [weird] place? basho: place; location; spot

kanji: それは痛いな痛すぎる
hiragana: それ は いたい な いた すぎる
romaji: sore ha itai na ita sugiru
meaning: This hurts. It hurts too much. sugiru is used to express that there's too much of something. For i-adjectives, remove the last "i" and attach it.

kanji: キマリの隣に誰が寝るか
hiragana: きまり の となり に だれ が ねる か
romaji: kimari no tonari ni dare ga neru ka
meaning: Who is sleeping next to kimari (literally: on kimari's next side)? tonari: next (to); adjoining; adjacent, also: house next door

hiragana: ああ だめ だ ねむ すぎる
meaning: No good, [I'm] too tired. sugiru is used to express that there's too much of something. For i-adjectives, remove the last "i" and attach it.

kanji: お前もちょっと変わった趣味してるよな
hiragana: おまえ も ちょっと かわった しゅみ してる よ な
romaji: omae mo chotto kawatta shumi shiteru yo na
meaning: You also are doing slightly uncommon hobbies, aren't you? shumi: hobby, but also: taste kawaru: to change, but also: to be different / uncommon.

hiragana: むずかし すぎる よ
meaning: [This is] too difficult. sugiru is used to express that there's too much of something. For i-adjectives, remove the last "i" and attach it.

kanji: お母さんもいつも運動してた
hiragana: おかあさん も いつも うんどう してた
meaning: Mother also always worked out / did physical exercise. undou: exercise; physical training; workout

hiragana: にっぽんじん か おまえ
meaning: Are you Japanese? -jin: suffix to indicate nationality: nihon + jin = Japanese person. Reminder: nihon + go: Japanese language

hiragana: こわ すぎる ね
meaning: [This is] too scary. sugiru is used to express that there's too much of something. For i-adjectives, remove the last "i" and attach it.

kanji: あれどの家にだっけどこに
hiragana: あれ どの いえ に だ っけ どこ に
romaji: are dono ie ni da kke doko ni
meaning: Huh? Which house was it? Where [should I go]? dono: which; what (way)​ da kke: was it?; I think it was ...? used e.g. when someone is trying to remember something.

hiragana: しゅっしん は にっぽん
meaning: As for [your] origin, [is it] Japan? -> Are you from Japan? shusshin: one's origin (e.g. city, country, parentage, school)

hiragana: みえ すぎる
meaning: Too much is visible! sugiru is used to express that there's too much of something. For verbs, attach it to the verb stem. mie: verb stem of mieru - to be visible. It's not the stem of miru - to see, this would be mi sugiru.
source: Boku no Hero Academia_ Futari no Hero

kanji: 病院や医者には何もできません
hiragana: びょういん や いしゃ に は なに も できません
romaji: byouin ya isha ni ha nani mo dekimasen
meaning: Both the hospital and the doctor among others could not do anything. byouin: hospital; clinic Reminder: "ya" is used for an incomplete listing of nouns. It means "and" and implies that there are more instances.

kanji: 何しているのこんな時間にこんな場所で
hiragana: なに して いる の こんな じかん に こんな ばしょ で
romaji: nani shite iru no konna jikan ni konna basho de
meaning: What are [you] doing? At this time in this place? basho: place; location; spot

kanji: そしてこれが隣の部屋にあった
hiragana: そして これ が となり の へや に あった
romaji: soshite kore ga tonari no heya ni atta
meaning: And this was in the room next door (looks like they are investigating something and probably found the note in the guy's hand in the room next door). tonari: next (to); adjoining; adjacent, also: house next door Remark: The "ga" here sounds a bit like a "mo", but it's indeed a "ga", see Blood+, ep 19, 21:20+ for reference & context. Don't worry if you don't understand the "ga" perfectly, it's the speaker's fault :D.

kanji: 誰に言われたか知らないけど趣味が悪すぎる
hiragana: だれ に いわれた か しらない けど しゅみ が わる すぎる
romaji: dare ni iwareta ka shiranai kedo shumi ga waru sugiru
meaning: [I] don't know who told [you to do so] but: [Their] taste is too bad. Here, the speaker was addressed using the witch of envy's name (which is bad). She asks the listener: I don't know who told you to use this name, but their taste is too bad. shumi: hobby, but also: taste
source: Re Zero kara Hajimeru Isekai Seikatsu (Eng + Jp)

hiragana: たべ すぎた
meaning: [I] ate too much. sugiru is used to express that there's too much of something. For verbs, attach it to the verb stem.

hiragana: たべ すぎちゃった
meaning: [This was so tasty that I automatically] ate to much. Reminder: sugichatta is from sugite shimatta - unintended actions, often with a bad outcome. sugiru is used to express that there's too much of something. For verbs, attach it to the verb stem.

hiragana: のみ すぎた
meaning: [I] drank too much. sugiru is used to express that there's too much of something. For verbs, attach it to the verb stem.

kanji: 悪い冗談にもほどがある
hiragana: わるい じょうだん に も ほど が ある
romaji: warui joudan ni mo hodo ga aru
meaning: For bad jokes, there's a limit (seems like someone pushed it too far by telling some bad jokes). hodo: extent; degree; limit.

hiragana: なく ほど うれしい か ｡
meaning: Are [you] delighted / happy to the extend that [you] cry -> Are you so happy that you cry? hodo: extent; degree; limit.

kanji: 俺はこの男ほど優しくないぞ
hiragana: おれ は この おとこ ほど やさしくない ぞ
romaji: ore ha kono otoko hodo yasashikunai zo
meaning: As for me, [I] am not friendly to the extent of this guy -> I am not as friendly as this guy! Imagine a good cop / bad cop interrogation going on here and the suspect has not yet said anything. So now it's time for the bad cop to continue. hodo: extent; degree; limit.

kanji: 死ぬほど恐ろしかったわ
hiragana: しぬ ほど おそろしかった わ
meaning: [I] was scary to the die-extend -> It was so scary I could die. hodo: extent; degree; limit.
source: JoJos Bizzare Adventure ダイヤモンドは砕けない

kanji: 悲しいさ死ぬほど悲しい
hiragana: かなしい さ しぬ ほど かなしい
meaning: [I] am sad, die-degree sad -> I am so sad I could die. hodo: extent; degree; limit.

kanji: あれほどの元気はありませんよ
hiragana: あれ ほど の げんき は ありません よ
romaji: are hodo no genki ha arimasen yo
meaning: To this-degree lively / healthy / well is not there -> I am not that genki. hodo: extent; degree; limit.

hiragana: わらえる ほど に ね
meaning: [I was tasty] to a can-laugh extend. hodo: extent; degree; limit. Remark: The "ni" directs what is hidden in the previous sentence of the conversation towards "waraeru hodo": The ramen at this shop was sooo good, to the extend I could laugh.

hiragana: しつれい に も ほど が ある
romaji: shitsurei ni mo hodo ga aru
meaning: For impoliteness, there's a limit! shitsurei: discourtesy; impoliteness​

hiragana: ほんとうに たかい です わ ね
meaning: This is really high. takai: high / expensive

kanji: あなたが高いのは聞いています
hiragana: あなた が たかい の は きいて います
romaji: anata ga takai no ha kiite imasu
meaning: I heard that you are expensive (could also mean: tall)

hiragana: 30めーとる の たかさ から
meaning: [This has] a height of 30 meters. takasa: height By replacing the "i" of an i-adjective with "sa" you nominalize it (we already had oishii -> oishisa before).
source: Saiki Kusuo no Psi Nan S1 (斉木楠雄のΨ難 第1期)

kanji: 熱はまだあるじゃないか
hiragana: ねつ は まだ ある じゃない か
romaji: netsu ha mada aru janai ka
meaning: As for temperature / fever, isn't it still there?-> [You want to go out, but] don't you still have temperature? mada: still (don't mix it up with mata - again)

kanji: めんまはまだ帰ってこない
hiragana: めんま は まだ かえって こない
meaning: As for menma, [she] still hasn't returned / didn't come home yet. mada: still (don't mix it up with mata - again)

kanji: めんままだ髪長いのか
hiragana: めんま まだ かみ ながい の か
romaji: menma mada kami nagai no ka
meaning: Is menma's hair still long? mada: still (don't mix it up with mata - again) kami: hair

hiragana: ちがう ちがう よ
meaning: Wrong, [this optinion / anwer is] wrong. chigau: to differ (from); to vary; to not match the correct (answer, etc.)

hiragana: ちがう だろ きりやま
meaning: [I] guess kiriyama is wrong. chigau: to differ (from); to vary; to not match the correct (answer, etc.)

hiragana: ちがいます か
meaning: Is [this answer] wrong? chigau: to differ (from); to vary; to not match the correct (answer, etc.)

kanji: 違う違うただのバイトだよ
hiragana: ちがう ちがう ただ の ばいと だ よ
romaji: chigau chigau tada no baito da yo
meaning: No, no, [it's] just an ordinary side job. tada: ordinary, common chigau: to differ (from); to vary; to not match the correct (answer, etc.)

kanji: 昔と全然違うんだけど
hiragana: むかし と ぜんぜん ちがう ん だ けど
romaji: mukashi to zenzen chigau n da kedo
meaning: [Look at how the city has changed.] It's completely different from the olden days. Note that the "to" particle is used to indicate a comparison here. Whenever you're confused by some particle use, you might want to look at this list.

hiragana: あの とき の みょう な ひと
romaji: ano toki no myou na hito
meaning: [It's] the weird person from that time [before]. toki: time; hour; moment​ or also: occasion Here, the speaker is meeting some strange person she met before.
source: Boku no Hero Academia S2 (ep 1-25 jp_en)

kanji: あのとき僕が言ってほしかったのは
hiragana: あの とき ぼく が いって ほしかった の は
romaji: ano toki boku ga itte hoshikatta no ha

Especially when used as "xxx wake da", it translates to what I wrote above, but it as usual depends a bit on the context.
